NT01.challenges: The main challenge is to demonstrate quantitatively that the country is on track to meet the -11% vs. BAU by 2035; it is critical to publish periodically and comparably: (i) the updated sectoral series (energy, agriculture, IPPU, waste) with recent years (post-2021), (ii) the official BAU scenario used for NDC 3.0 and its methodology, and (iii) progress reports that convert policies/actions into estimated reductions (tCO₂e) by measure, to verify real contributions by sector.
NT01.progress: Since 2019, Panama has advanced toward this target mainly through (a) the updating and strengthening of national GHG inventories and climate transparency, (b) the adoption of climate policy instruments to guide mitigation by sectors, and (c) concrete sectoral measures in energy/transport, waste, and planning for short-lived climate pollutants (methane, hydrofluorocarbons (HFC)). However, quantitatively demonstrating progress “toward -11% vs. BAU by 2035” requires maintaining a robust and public time series of emissions by sector and periodically comparing it with the official business-as-usual scenario. First, a key structural advance is the strengthening of the measurement base. The National Climate Transparency Platform (SSINGEI) reports that, taking as reference the last year of its published series (2021), Panama estimated 20.519.64 kt CO₂e of total emissions and a sectoral distribution of Energy 813.439.96 kt CO₂e, Agriculture 4.150.21 kt CO₂e, Waste 1.312.64 kt CO₂e and IPPU 1.616.51 kt CO₂e. At the same time, it indicates that the LULUCF sector recorded higher removals (net “positive” capture balance in that year), which supports the country’s carbon negativity, although this target is formulated excluding LULUCF and focuses on energy, agriculture, IPPU and waste. Second, Panama has been updating its commitments framework. The Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) (submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in 2025) reaffirms the unconditional target of reducing emissions by 11% by 2035 compared to the BAU scenario for the energy, IPPU, waste and agriculture sectors (excluding LULUCF), and states that the country could achieve a greater reduction if it receives international support (Republic of Panama, 2025). Complementarily, the regional NDC tracking platform in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), under the Panama Nature Pledge, also summarizes this commitment as a central objective (NDC-LAC, n. d.). Third, Panama strengthened the policy scaffolding to implement mitigation. The National Climate Action Plan (adopted in 2022) organizes actions by sectors and sets out decarbonization measures, especially in energy, including targets and lines of action related to energy transition, transport and efficiency (MiAMBIENTE, 2022). At the sectoral level, clearer advances are observed in energy/transport and waste. In low-carbon mobility, Panama approved Law 295 of 2022 that promotes electric mobility and subsequently regulated it through an executive decree (Republic of Panama, 2022; Republic of Panama, 2023). These regulations create enabling conditions to reduce emissions from land transport (a relevant component within the energy sector in inventories). In parallel, in waste, initiatives are reported for energy recovery from biogas in Cerro Patacón; for example, a news note indicated that in 2020, 29.8 GWh were generated from landfill biogas (cited source: ETESA/CND), which points to methane capture/use with mitigation co-benefits (The Visitor Panamá, 2021). Panama promoted in 2023 a Roadmap for the mitigation of Short-Lived Climate Pollutants (SLCP) with actions in sectors such as agriculture/livestock and waste, and in recent years has communicated the process of developing these roadmaps (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). In 2024 it was published and its strategy proposes mitigation targets for the year 2050 with respect to the projected baseline, highlighting (Roccard, J. et al, 2024): Agriculture and livestock: 12% reduction in methane. Waste: 31% reduction in methane. Energy: 44% reduction in methane and 28% reduction in black carbon. Industrial processes and product use: 95% reduction in HFC.
NT01.actions: Panama strengthened the policy framework to implement mitigation (National Climate Action Plan (adopted in 2022)). The Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in 2025 reaffirms the unconditional target of reducing emissions by 11% by 2035. Panama approved Law 295 of 2022 that promotes electric mobility and subsequently regulated it through an executive decree (Republic of Panama, 2022; Republic of Panama, 2023). Panama promoted a Roadmap for the mitigation of Short-Lived Climate Pollutants (SLCP) with actions in sectors such as agriculture/livestock and waste.
NT01.effectiveness: 2019–2025 sectoral progress in GHG reduction: Energy Sector Consolidation of the renewable electricity matrix Between 2019 and 2024, Panama maintained an electricity matrix with a high share of renewable sources (hydroelectric, wind and solar), reducing dependence on fossil fuels in electricity generation. The diversification of the matrix and renewable energy auctions have contributed to reducing the carbon intensity of the electricity sector (ASEP, 2023; Ministerio de Ambiente, 2022). In addition, the update of the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) reaffirmed the energy transition as a central mitigation axis (República de Panamá, 2022). Electric Mobility Law and electrification of transport The enactment of Law 295 of 2022 established tax incentives for the import and use of electric vehicles, as well as targets for the progressive transition of public transport (Law 295, 2022). The National Electric Mobility Strategy promoted the installation of charging infrastructure and the incorporation of electric buses (Ministerio de Ambiente, 2020). Agriculture and Land Use Sector Million Hectares Alliance and forest restoration The Million Hectares Alliance promoted the restoration of forest landscapes and sustainable production systems, including silvopastoral systems (Ministerio de Ambiente, 2023). These actions increase carbon capture and reduce emissions associated with forest degradation, contributing to the AFOLU component of the national GHG inventory (Ministerio de Ambiente, 2022). Sustainable and resilient agriculture The strengthening of sustainable agricultural practices, including efficient fertilizer management and climate adaptation, has been part of the agricultural sector plans (MIDA, 2021). Industry Sector Energy efficiency and cleaner production programmes Between 2019 and 2024, programmes for energy audits and efficiency in industrial processes were strengthened, with support from international cooperation and environmental regulatory frameworks (PNUD, 2021). The promotion of voluntary corporate carbon footprint reports also made it possible to improve the management of industrial emissions (Ministerio de Ambiente, 2022). Waste Sector Improvement in waste management and methane reduction The modernization of sanitary landfills and the strengthening of integrated waste management have made it possible to advance in reducing methane emissions from the final disposal of solid waste (Autoridad de Aseo Urbano y Domiciliario, 2023). The national GHG inventory has incorporated methodological improvements to estimate emissions from the waste sector, allowing greater traceability (Ministerio de Ambiente, 2022).

NT02.challenges: 1) Restore 100,000 ha with quality and permanence Availability and prioritization of land: identify degraded areas with high ecological and social viability. Tenure and legal security: tenure conflicts hinder agreements, investment and maintenance. Establishment and maintenance costs: restoration requires sustained investment (nurseries, fences, fire management, invasive species control, replacement of plants) over several years. Climate risks and disturbances: droughts (Arco Seco), fires, extreme events and floods can reduce survival and make replanting necessary. 2) “Effective conservation” and not only declarative Management, control and compliance: surveillance, control of logging/hunting/fires and compliance with regulations are needed; without that, conservation is not effective. Institutional capacity and decentralization: personnel, budget, logistics and territorial presence to monitor and support actions in corridors. Effectiveness monitoring: there is a lack of consistent indicators to demonstrate ecological results (connectivity, habitat recovery, biodiversity, water). 3) Specific restoration of 2,500 ha of mangrove Coastal land-use pressures: urbanization, infrastructure, shrimp farms, fill, hydrological changes and pollution. Complex restoration: in mangroves, if water flow/salinity is not restored, planting fails. Multi-actor governance: it requires strong coordination among environmental authorities, municipalities, private actors and communities. 4) Intervene in 25,000 agricultural ha and increase productivity by 20% Adoption by producers: resistance to change, initial costs and perception of risk (especially small producers). Technical assistance and extension: continuous support is required for silvopasture/agroforestry, soil management, water, forage and animal health. Access to financing and incentives: without credit/blended finance and payments for results, scale is difficult. 5) Operationalize 3 corridors (Azuero, Coclé, Veraguas) Define functional boundaries and zoning: a corridor requires agreements on land use, cores, connectors and buffer zones. Real interinstitutional coordination: agriculture, environment, land-use planning, municipalities and local actors; institutions must act as a team and in a coordinated manner. Fragmented connectivity: road infrastructure, urban expansion and productive mosaics can cut key connectors. Social acceptance and local governance: without clear mechanisms for participation, benefits and conflict resolution, implementation is weakened. 6) Reduce unplanned agricultural expansion by 30% Lack of binding land-use planning: in several territories the instruments exist, but they are not applied or do not have practical force. Contradictory incentives: if there are economic signals that favor expansion (subsidies, prices, informality), the pressure continues. Limited control and enforcement: insufficient monitoring and sanctioning in the face of unauthorized land-use change. Productive alternatives: if a profitable route is not offered (sustainable intensification, productive restoration), expansion remains the “easiest” option.
NT02.progress:
Vegetation restoration Between 2019 and the present date (December 2025), the most publicly documented advances for Panama in a target such as National Target 10 (restoration + biological corridors + carbon capture in LULUCF + agricultural productivity) are observed mainly in: (i) the implementation of the Programa Nacional de Restauración Forestal (PNRF) and its monitoring systems, (ii) territorial restoration/corridor initiatives (Azuero, Veraguas and projects in the Corredor Biológico Mesoamericano), and (iii) specific actions for mangrove restoration and productive restoration (agroforestry/silvopastoral). Within the framework of the PNRF, the Ministerio de Ambiente indicates that these actions are monitored with institutional tools (e.g., Sistema de Monitoreo de Restauración and forest monitoring) and that the 2021–2025 target (51,000 ha) is supported by Executive Decree No. 137 of 21 May 2021 (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). In terms of biological corridors and restoration at the landscape scale, MiAMBIENTE has documented processes of establishment/territorial management in key regions. In Veraguas, for example, work was reported to create a biological corridor between the La Yeguada and Alto Guarumo forest reserves, supported by actions such as reforestation, natural regeneration and agroforestry/silvopastoral practices; as of July 2022, progress had been made with 1,356 hectares restored and 26,538 seedlings of adapted native species (MiAMBIENTE, 2022). In Azuero, restoration and resilience interventions were promoted that explicitly include the creation of corridors and watershed restoration through the implementation of the Fondo de Desarrollo Verde project, obtaining the following results: Table 1. Restoration figures of the Fondo de Desarrollo Verde in the province of Los Santos. Restoration Area (ha) Natural recovery in intervened forest 1088 Recovery of degraded areas on livestock farms 1887 Water rehabilitation in mangrove ecosystems 24.13 Total 2999.13 Where 69 producers participated, of whom 15 were women (MiAMBIENTE, 2023a). Likewise, the “Azuero Verde” initiative was presented as an effort with pillars that include watershed restoration, biological corridors and rural development (MiAMBIENTE, 2024a, 2024b). Complementarily, recent technical climate documents of the country have indicated as a line of action the creation of biological corridors with emphasis on Azuero, Coclé and Veraguas as a climate change adaptation measure and with the broad participation of the private sector, organizations, networks and local leaders (UNFCCC, 2025). Regarding the mangrove component (2,500 ha by 2035), recent public evidence shows specific actions with operational figures. In 2025, MiAMBIENTE reported restoration activities that included the planting of 300,000 mangrove propagules and the restoration of 150 ha of mangrove in Bahía de Chame (MiAMBIENTE, 2025a). In the same period, follow-up and community restoration days were reported in the mangroves of Chame, consistent with the line of nature-based solutions and effective conservation of coastal ecosystems (MiAMBIENTE, 2025b). Although these numbers are still far from the threshold of 2,500 ha proposed for 2035, they do constitute a verifiable basis for implementation and scaling up. Panama has developed concrete actions for the restoration of coastal and inland wetlands, mainly through projects implemented with the support of Wetlands International – Oficina Panamá, with two documented projects, which together total approximately 156.2 hectares restored or in the process of restoration. The first project corresponds to mangrove restoration on Isla Galeta (province of Colón), carried out between 2018 and 2024, with a restored area of 6.2 ha, and the second project was carried out in Laguna de Las Lajas (San Félix, province of Chiriquí) between 2017 and 2025, covering an approximate area of 150 ha. (Blanco & Yellachich, 2023). The Ministerio de Desarrollo Agropecuario (MIDA) under the Programa de Adaptación al Cambio Climático a través del Manejo Integrado de Recursos Hídricos en Panamá, Proyecto Medidas de Adaptación al Cambio Climático para la Cría de Ganadería Sostenible en la Cuenca Media y Baja del Río Santa María (2019-2021), reports the establishment of 600 ha under silvopastoral systems on 120 farms. From 2000 to 2024, Panama has implemented one of the most robust restoration, conservation and sustainable production schemes in the country through the Programa de Incentivos Económicos Ambientales (PIEA) of the Autoridad del Canal de Panamá, aimed at the protection of water resources and the restoration of productive landscapes in the Cuenca Hidrográfica del Canal de Panamá (CHCP), obtaining the following results: Table 2. However, the PNRF explicitly recognizes productive modalities (silvopastoral, agroforestry, plantations) as part of the reforested restoration reported and monitored (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). Finally, regarding the target of “1 million tCO₂e in LULUCF”, the country has climate transparency architecture and national inventories that account for emissions and removals, including the LULUCF sector (MiAMBIENTE, n.d.; UNFCCC, 2022).

Coral restoration Panama’s coral reefs, located mainly in the Caribbean (Bocas del Toro) and in the eastern tropical Pacific (Parque Nacional Coiba and Golfo de Chiriquí), have experienced progressive deterioration associated with rising sea temperature, bleaching events, coral diseases, sedimentation, eutrophication and local pressures such as unregulated tourism (Eakin et al., 2019; Fong et al., 2021). The Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) has been a key actor in generating knowledge that underpins coral restoration in Panama. Research has documented the dynamics of bleaching, mortality and partial reef recovery, as well as the differential response of species and genotypes to thermal stress (Eakin et al., 2019; Lesser et al., 2020). These studies have made it possible to identify corals with greater thermal tolerance, fundamental information for modern restoration approaches that prioritize climate resilience (STRI, 2022). The study “Evaluación de la eficiencia de dos estructuras para jardines de coral de la especie Acropora cervicornis (Scleractinia: Acroporidae) en el Parque Nacional Portobelo”, evaluated the efficiency of two types of coral nursery structures (clothesline and fixed) for the restoration of Acropora cervicornis in Bahía Huertas, Parque Nacional Portobelo. Eighty coral fragments were cultivated, which initially represented 9.71 m of extension, and after nine months a total growth of 15.3 m of new coral was estimated. The clothesline-type structure concentrated 95.4 % of the total growth, with average growth rates close to 5.7 cm/month and 100 % survival, while the fixed structure showed lower growth (≈2.8 cm/month) and 45 % mortality. The results show that clothesline-type nurseries are technically and economically more efficient for coral restoration, by reducing algal colonization and maximizing the growth and survival of fragments, constituting a viable tool for the recovery of degraded reefs in the Panamanian Caribbean (Bernal et al., 2023). The study “Restauración de arrecifes degradados en el Parque Nacional Portobelo mediante dos estructuras de jardines de corales” evaluated the active restoration of degraded coral reefs in Parque Nacional Portobelo (Panama) through the implementation of Acropora cervicornis coral gardens in two types of structures (clothesline and pedestal). The fragments showed a high survival rate (≈90 %) and an increase close to 50 % in branching, with no significant differences between structures. The oceanographic conditions (temperature between 29–33 °C, stable pH and dissolved oxygen) were suitable for coral growth, showing that coral nurseries are a viable tool to accelerate reef recovery and strengthen ecological resilience in marine protected areas of the Panamanian Caribbean (González Muñoz et al., n.d.). In terms of active restoration, pilot projects in the Panamanian Caribbean have used in situ coral nurseries (tree- or table-type structures), with key species such as Acropora cervicornis and Acropora palmata, followed by transplants to degraded reefs. Although the scientific literature reports reduced spatial scales (specific sites rather than extensive hectares), initial survival rates above 60–80 % have been recorded in nurseries during the first months, under controlled conditions and with periodic maintenance (Lirman & Schopmeyer, 2016; STRI, 2022). These results confirm the technical viability of coral restoration, although they also show its high dependence on the reduction of local pressures and the control of thermal stress. In the Panamanian Pacific, particularly in Coiba, active restoration has been more limited, due to the high natural oceanographic variability and the recurrent influence of ENSO events, which generate extreme temperature fluctuations. In this context, the predominant strategy has been passive restoration, focused on the protection of marine areas, the control of human activities and long-term ecological monitoring, which is consistent with the scientific evidence suggesting that effective conservation can be more cost-effective than active restoration in highly variable systems (Glynn et al., 2018; MiAmbiente, 2023). In summary, Panama has a solid scientific basis for coral restoration, led by research by STRI and national universities; however, the main challenge lies in transferring scientific knowledge to larger-scale restoration programs, articulated with the reduction of local pressures, integrated coastal management and sustainable financing, in order to guarantee lasting benefits for biodiversity, coastal protection and the livelihoods associated with reefs.
NT02.actions: 1) Framework measures (policies, programmes and institutional arrangements) NDC 3.0 / Nature Pledge as an integrating climate–biodiversity–land framework, which explicitly establishes the restoration target of 100,000 ha (includes 2,500 ha of mangrove) and indicates that implementation translates into policies and measures with key actors. Enabling sectoral instruments that NDC 3.0 itself identifies as the basis for climate and territorial action: National Climate Change Plan for the Agricultural sector (2019) Strategic Guidelines for the Energy Transition Agenda (2020) National Forest Restoration Programme (2020) National Gender and Climate Change Plan (2021) Integrated Waste Management Law (mentioned as part of the framework) 2) Measures to “restore and place under effective conservation 100,000 ha” (includes mangroves and agricultural lands) Government–FAO alliance to mobilize investments and restore 10,000 ha as an initial tranche within the national target of 100,000 ha by 2035, aligning financing, technical assistance and territorial implementation. Programme/Project “Alianza por el Millón” as a public-private platform led by MiAMBIENTE/MIDA for restoration of degraded areas, protection of watersheds, creation of buffer zones and support for biological corridors. Restoration modalities (key to ensuring that part of the 100,000 ha are agricultural and mangroves): NDC 3.0 indicates that the 100,000 ha are distributed in modalities such as agroforestry systems, silvopastoral systems and reforestation in mangroves (this aligns directly with the component of 25,000 ha of agricultural land and 2,500 ha of mangrove). National reforestation campaigns/actions reported by MiAMBIENTE (example 2025) that show implementation on the ground and annual accumulation (e.g., reforestation reported at national scale). 3) Measures to operationalize 3 biological corridors (Azuero, Coclé, Veraguas) Azuero Corridor Azuero Verde Initiative (MiAMBIENTE/MIDA): explicit focus on restoring watersheds, creating biological corridors, rehabilitating protected areas and promoting a green economy. Veraguas Corridor Biological corridor integration project between protected areas in Veraguas (e.g., Alto Guarumo–La Yeguada): includes intervention through restoration/reforestation in a delimited area. Coclé Corridor Wetlands/mangroves approach and coastal restoration with demonstration projects and territorial governance (cases of mangrove and wetland restoration in the Arco Seco/Coclé used as a basis for intervention and scaling up).

NT03.challenges: 1) Expansion Availability and territorial viability Identify additional areas with high ecological value without generating social conflicts. Make new declarations compatible with property rights and existing productive uses. Limitations in coastal areas with high real estate and tourism pressure. Land and marine use conflicts Agricultural activities, industrial fishing, infrastructure and mining may overlap with priority areas. In the marine sphere, fishing and logistics interests may hinder expansions. 2) Inclusion Intercultural governance Guarantee Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) processes. Articulate indigenous governance systems with the national legal framework. Avoid the recognition of OECM implying loss of territorial autonomy. 3) Planning Interinstitutional coordination Overlap of competencies among environment, fishing, agriculture, territorial planning and municipalities. Lack of full integration between environmental planning and territorial development. Effective participation Participatory processes may be long and complex. Need for technical resources to facilitate broad and inclusive consultations. 4) Development of management plans Limited technical information Lack of updated hydrological and ecological studies in some basins. Lack of systematic monitoring of aquatic biodiversity. Anthropogenic pressures Agricultural expansion in upper areas. Pollution from agrochemicals and discharges. Deforestation in water recharge areas. 5) Management and monitoring Management effectiveness Not all protected areas have periodic METT-type evaluation. Gap between legal declaration and actual operational management. Financial resources Insufficient recurring budget for surveillance, monitoring and technical personnel. Dependence on external financing. Monitoring systems Need to strengthen geospatial systems and interoperable databases. Lack of uniform indicators for ecological connectivity. 6) Ecological connectivity Landscape fragmentation Road infrastructure and urban expansion interrupt natural connectors. Difficulty in ensuring ecological continuity between terrestrial and marine areas. Regional coordination Corridors require agreements among provinces and multiple local actors. 7) Climate change as a cross-cutting factor Sea level rise affects marine protected areas. Extreme events deteriorate infrastructure and ecosystems. Need to integrate ecosystem-based adaptation.
NT03.progress: Since 2019, Panama has advanced in the expansion and strengthening of the SINAP mainly through two routes: (a) significant increases in marine protection (especially 2021 and 2023) and (b) gradual improvements in management instruments (management plans, effectiveness evaluations, and coordination with watershed management), although gaps persist to reach 40% terrestrial and 60% marine/inland waters by 2035. Expansion of coverage and consolidation of the SINAP (2019–2025) In terms of terrestrial and inland coverage, the most comparable consolidated international information shows that Panama has remained around 31% of the territory under protected areas, without yet reaching the 40% proposed for 2035. In the global reference database (WDPA/Protected Planet), Panama records 31.35% terrestrial and inland water coverage and 114 protected areas (with 104 national designations), with data reported as of December 2025 (UNEP-WCMC, 2025a). For marine coverage, the pattern is one of accelerated expansion since 2021. The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) “Country Dossier” (based on the World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA), with an explicit note on registration delays) reported for May 2021 marine coverage of 11.6% (32 areas; 38,489.5 km²) and documented that in June 2021 Panama expanded the protected marine surface by extending the Cordillera de Coiba to 67,742 km² (increase >50,000 km²), estimating that with this the country reached 30% marine coverage (Secretariat of the CBD, 2021). That 2021 expansion was also communicated by STRI, detailing the increase of 50,518.84 km² and a national total of 98,228.25 km² of marine protected areas, also emphasizing the regional connectivity of the Corredor Marino del Pacífico Este Tropical (Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI), 2021). Subsequently, in March 2023, Panama expanded the Área de Recursos Manejados Banco Volcán from 14,201.13 km² to 93,390.0 km² (+79,178.71 km²), and the Ministry of Environment reported that with this the country reached 54.33% of its protected marine area (MiAmbiente, 2023a). This change is recorded in Executive Decree No. 2 (2 March 2023) published in the Official Gazette (Republic of Panama, 2023). A study published in 2023 identifies the Gran Golfo de Chiriquí as an area of high ecological relevance due to the presence of critical habitats; in this region migratory routes (migravías) used by highly mobile species such as the olive ridley turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea), the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), the humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae), and large pelagic fish are documented. A central contribution of the document is the description of marine migravías as functional units of connectivity. At the regional level, the Migravía Coco–Galápagos stands out, with an approximate extent of 240,000 km². In Panama, the Migravía Coiba–Malpelo is identified as strategic for the conservation of sharks, rays, turtles, and cetaceans, by linking Parque Nacional Coiba with deep oceanic areas and seamounts. Although Panama has advanced significantly in the designation of marine protected areas and in the recognition of marine corridors, challenges persist related to fragmentation of the marine landscape, illegal fishing, climate change, and the limited integration of marine corridors into marine spatial planning. Nevertheless, the consolidation of these migravías represents a key tool to reduce the risk of extinction of priority marine species, strengthen ecosystem resilience, and meet national and global biodiversity targets (Vergara-Chen & Del Cid, 2023). Note: international figures (WDPA/Protected Planet) and official national figures may differ due to methodology, cartographic base, and update times; this is explicitly recognized in the CBD dossier for Panama (Secretariat of the CBD, 2021). Management, monitoring, and connectivity standards Regarding management quality/standards, Panama has increased the use of effectiveness evaluations and has reported progress, although with asymmetries between terrestrial and marine. In 2021, the CBD dossier reported that 71.7% of terrestrial protected areas and 11.3% of marine ones had management effectiveness evaluations (PAME) (Secretariat of the CBD, 2021). As of December 2025, WDPA/Protected Planet records 37 areas in Panama with registered effectiveness evaluations (UNEP-WCMC, 2025a). As for management plans, the institutional reports show that the country has been updating instruments, but carries historical delays. The MiAmbiente 2020 Report recorded 13 current management plans and 15 expired plans that required updating (MiAmbiente, 2020). Additionally, the 2022 Management Report (institutional synthesis) noted, among other milestones, the modification/update of the management plan of Parque Internacional La Amistad incorporating Strategic Environmental Assessment, which is consistent with the orientation toward more robust standards (MiAmbiente, 2023b). In relation to the “management plans in 10 priority watersheds,” Panama has a public Integrated Watershed Management platform that lists management plans by watershed (Santa María River, Tabasará, Pacora, Chucunaque, Indio, Santa María, Bayano, and Chiriquí Viejo), with links to documents/downloads and status (MiAmbiente, n.d.). This shows progress toward watershed-based territorial planning, although it does not automatically equate to “protected area management plans” within each watershed; in practice, it is a key framework for the strict protection of areas of high ecological value and connectivity (MiAmbiente, n.d.). In summary, Panama shows clear progress in the marine dimension (jumps in 2021 and 2023, with decrees and large-scale expansions) and gradual progress in the dimension of management standards (management plans, effectiveness evaluations, and better integration with watershed management). However, with the available public evidence, the country still does not reach the aspiration of 40% terrestrial (it remains ~31%) and must continue closing gaps in: (i) updating and validity of management plans, (ii) systematic evaluation of effectiveness (PAME) in the marine sphere, (iii) monitoring and control, and (iv) harmonization of metrics (WDPA vs national figures) for consistent official reporting (Secretariat of the CBD, 2021; UNEP-WCMC, 2025a; MiAmbiente, 2023a).
NT03.actions: 1) Expansion of the coverage of terrestrial and marine protected areas Panama has progressively increased the area under official protection through the creation and expansion of terrestrial and marine protected areas within the Sistema Nacional de Áreas Protegidas (SINAP) (MiAmbiente, 2022). The country has consolidated biological corridors and marine protected areas in fulfillment of the 30x30 commitment established in the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022). 2) Strengthening of SINAP through updating management plans Management plans have been developed and updated for key protected areas, incorporating: Ecological zoning. Connectivity criteria. Adaptive management. Community participation. Ecosystem-based planning is consistent with the IUCN guidelines (2020) on effective management of protected areas. 3) Integration of OECM and indigenous territories Panama has advanced in the recognition of Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (OECM), including indigenous territories and traditional use areas that contribute to conservation (CBD, 2022). The inclusion of indigenous peoples strengthens territorial governance and responds to international standards of participatory conservation (IPBES, 2019). 4) Land-use planning and watershed approach Land-use planning has been promoted with a watershed and ecological connectivity approach, integrating protected areas with productive zones and biological corridors (MiAmbiente, 2022). The landscape and watershed approach is recommended by the IPCC (2022) as a key mechanism to increase climate resilience and conservation. 5) Establishment of international monitoring standards Panama has strengthened environmental monitoring systems through: National inventories. Biodiversity monitoring. Integration of geospatial tools. Management effectiveness evaluation (METT). Effectiveness evaluation is a standard promoted by IUCN and UNDP (2020) to ensure quality in the management of protected areas. 6) Marine conservation and ecological connectivity The country has strengthened marine protection in the Pacific and Caribbean, including mangrove, reef, and seagrass ecosystems, aligned with international ocean conservation targets (CBD, 2022). The protection of marine ecosystems also contributes to climate resilience and blue carbon (IPCC, 2022). 7) Participation and inclusive governance Participatory processes have been developed for: Validation of management plans. Consultation with local communities. Interinstitutional coordination. Participation is key to the sustainability of conservation (IPBES, 2019).

NT04.challenges: Reduction of extinction risk (≥10% of priority species) Insufficient systematic population monitoring for several priority species. Gaps in data on demographic trends and distribution. Lack of periodic assessments such as an updated national Red List. Isolation of populations that reduces genetic flow. Illegal activities Poaching and wildlife trafficking. Illegal extraction of forest species. Unregulated fishing of vulnerable species. NT04.progress: Since 2019, Panama’s progress toward the target of reducing the extinction risk of priority native species (≥10%), strengthening in situ and ex situ conservation, and maintaining/restoring genetic diversity (including banks and collections) can be grouped into three lines: (1) strengthening ex situ management programs and infrastructure, (2) generating evidence and targeted actions for emblematic species and human–wildlife conflicts, and (3) frameworks and cooperation for the conservation of migratory marine species (e.g., sea turtles). Components of the target: Management measures to halt human-induced extinctions by 2035 and reduce extinction risk, particularly of threatened species. Panama has a list of threatened species published in Official Gazette No. No. 28187-A (2016) “by which the process for the preparation and periodic review of the list of threatened fauna and flora species of Panama is established, and other provisions are issued”; this list is currently under review to be updated and to define national threat levels according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN); according to the designated threat category, they will have priority when defining conservation strategies, plans, or programs. In 2023, the Ministry of Environment provided support through the provision of inputs to the ex situ conservation program Proyecto de Rescate y Conservación de Anfibios de Panamá (PARC), aimed at the conservation of harlequin frogs, classified in the Critically Endangered (CR) category in the List of Threatened Flora and Fauna Species of Panama, in accordance with Resolution No. DM-0657-2016. During 2024, population management of Proyecto de Rescate y Conservación de Anfibios de Panamá (PARC) focused on priority conservation species, including Andinobates geminisae, Oophaga vicentei, Triprion spinosus, Agalychnis lemur, Atelopus varius, Atelopus certus, Atelopus limosus, Atelopus glyphus and Atelopus zeteki. In this period, successful reproduction was achieved for all species of harlequin frogs and poison dart frogs under management, as well as for the crowned frog (Triprion spinosus) and the lemur tree frog (Agalychnis lemur). Notably, reproduction of the harlequin frog (Atelopus limosus), founder of a population surviving the chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), was achieved. In March 2025, the Tropical Amphibian Resilience Initiative (TARI), led by the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) and the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, was launched with the objective of halting the extinction of threatened frogs in Latin America. Through this initiative, Proyecto de Rescate y Conservación de Anfibios de Panamá (PARC) was significantly strengthened through the provision of financial, technological, and scientific resources. Thanks to support from the Bezos Earth Fund, the capacities of the Amphibian Rescue Center in Gamboa were expanded, improving infrastructure and specialized equipment to increase and maintain captive populations of priority species. Likewise, the creation of a regional biobank and the implementation of advanced genetic protocols were promoted, complementing ex situ conservation efforts, and integrating PARC into a regional amphibian resilience network that strengthens the exchange of data, knowledge, and strategies, aligning local actions with the global objectives of protecting genetic diversity and preventing extinctions. Currently (2025), the Centro de Conservación e Investigación de Felinos Silvestres is under construction; this center will be the first national platform for rehabilitation, pre-release, and reintroduction of felines affected by human activities. It will allow the functional reintegration of individuals into the natural environment, their monitoring through GPS collars and camera traps, and will strengthen national capacities in feline management and conservation. Its operation will contribute to generating verifiable results on population recovery. 2. Management measures to maintain and restore genetic diversity among all species. In terms of biological corridors and restoration at the landscape scale, MiAMBIENTE has documented processes of establishment/territorial management in key regions. In Veraguas, for example, work was reported to create a biological corridor between the La Yeguada and Alto Guarumo forest reserves, supported by actions such as reforestation, natural regeneration, and agroforestry/silvopastoral practices; as of July 2022, progress had been made with 1,356 hectares restored and 26,538 seedlings of adapted native species (MiAMBIENTE, 2022). In Azuero, restoration and resilience interventions were promoted that explicitly include the creation of corridors and watershed restoration through the implementation of the Fondo de Desarrollo Verde project, obtaining the following results: Table 1. Restoration figures of the Fondo de Desarrollo Verde in the province of Los Santos. Restoration Area (ha) Natural recovery in intervened forest 1088 Recovery of degraded areas on livestock farms 1887 Water rehabilitation in mangrove ecosystems 24.13 Total 2999.13 Where 69 producers participated, of whom 15 were women (MiAMBIENTE, 2023a). Likewise, the “Azuero Verde” initiative was presented as an effort with pillars that include watershed restoration, biological corridors, and rural development (MiAMBIENTE, 2024a, 2024b). Complementarily, recent national climate technical documents have identified as a line of action the creation of biological corridors with emphasis on Azuero, Coclé, and Veraguas as a climate change adaptation measure and with broad participation from the private sector, organizations, networks, and local leaders (UNFCCC, 2025). 3. Measures to manage interactions between humans and wildlife to minimize human–wildlife conflicts. For species highly sensitive to habitat loss and persecution, such as the jaguar (Panthera onca), Panama shows measurable progress in applied research: MiAMBIENTE reported captures and monitoring with GPS telemetry since 2019 (first marked individual), with additional captures in 2022 and reports of movement/home range areas in approximate ranges (50–250 km², according to the institutional report), reinforcing the use of spatial data to guide connectivity, conflict management, and territorial prioritization (Ministerio de Ambiente, n.d.). This line is complemented by recent publications that position research as a jaguar conservation tool in Darién (Moreno et al., 2024); the results indicate that, although Darién National Park maintains relatively healthy populations, in mixed landscapes human–jaguar conflict represents the main cause of mortality; between 1989 and 2023, 395 dead jaguars were documented in Panama, with Darién being the province with the highest number of cases, mainly due to retaliation associated with livestock losses. The article highlights that the scientific information generated has been translated into concrete recommendations for decision-makers and local communities, promoting sustainable livestock management practices, anti-predation measures, and silvopastoral systems as strategies to reduce conflict; and with a 2025 scientific article that documents, for the first time in Panama, the spatial ecology of jaguars with GPS tracking in a transformed landscape, the results show that home ranges were relatively small compared to other Mesoamerican regions, varying between 35 and 131 km², suggesting high landscape productivity and partial adaptation to disturbed environments. The study showed high spatial overlap among individuals (average 59%), accompanied by temporal segregation, indicating mechanisms of coexistence and territoriality. Jaguars showed preference for primary and secondary forests, regeneration areas, and zones near water bodies, while they actively avoided livestock pastures, confirming the importance of forest remnants as functional corridors. Although approximately 31% of the study area has been deforested, the results show that jaguars can persist in productive landscapes as long as there is ecological connectivity, minimum forest cover, and prey availability (Moreno et al., 2025). Panama plays a strategic role in the continental conservation of the jaguar (Panthera onca), by guaranteeing connectivity between the populations of Mesoamerica and South America. The species is distributed mainly in the Atlantic forests, from the lowlands to the mountains of the central mountain range, as well as in the Azuero region and the Pacific of Darién, where it coexists with productive landscapes and rural communities. The main sources of conflict between humans and wildlife associated with the jaguar are retaliation for livestock depredation, which constitutes the predominant cause of human-induced mortality for the species; added to this are habitat loss and fragmentation and the decline of its natural prey; the same sources of conflict occur with the puma (Puma concolor). As a basis for more effective conflict management and conservation of the species, Panama carried out the first National Jaguar Census and of its main prey species in the eastern sector of the country. Based on the extrapolation of estimates to the available habitat, it is estimated that this region could harbor approximately 350 individuals, a significant proportion of which is found within protected areas and indigenous territories. Although uncertainty persists regarding the status of the species outside the national protected areas system, the results indicate that eastern Panama has the potential to sustain, in the long term, a viable jaguar population, provided that the identified anthropogenic pressures are controlled. Recent publications that position research as a jaguar conservation tool in Darién (Moreno et al., 2024), the results indicate that, although Darién National Park maintains relatively healthy populations, in mixed landscapes human–jaguar conflict represents the main cause of mortality; between 1989 and 2023, 395 dead jaguars were documented in Panama, with Darién being the province with the highest number of cases, mainly due to retaliation associated with livestock losses. The jaguar (Panthera onca) has been monitored through GPS telemetry since 2019, generating key spatial information for ecological connectivity, territorial prioritization, and conflict management. Recent studies show that, despite landscape transformation, jaguars can persist if connectivity, minimum forest cover, and prey availability are maintained (Moreno et al., 2024; 2025). To address human–jaguar conflict, the following actions have been carried out through the indicated actors: Ministry of Environment, strategic allies, and international financing: Implementation of farm management plans and anti-predation measures for livestock by jaguar on livestock farms located in critical areas corresponding to 10 livestock farms (6 managed by men and 4 by women), between Darién (621ha) and Chepo (238ha), which include sustainable livestock management practices and construction of infrastructure to reduce depredation (installation of 6-wire electric fences with solar panels, light and sound alarms, secure maternity sheds, and installation of drinking troughs within the paddocks). Training and technical support for producers and local communities, generating replicable models of coexistence between livestock raising and wildlife (jaguar biology and conservation, conflicts with humans, good livestock practices to improve production and coexistence with wildlife). These actions have shown a reduction in depredation incidents and in jaguar deaths by retaliation, demonstrating the effectiveness of preventive approaches. Civil society organizations and complementary projects: Fundación Natura, ANCON and YAGUARÁ, as manager and administrator of environmental funds, supports conservation and sustainable management projects in watersheds, marine-coastal areas, and biodiversity zones, including those that benefit landscape management on farms and priority watersheds. Through its programs, it finances initiatives for ecosystem restoration, farm management plans, anti-predation measures for livestock from jaguar and puma attacks, water resource management, community monitoring of conservation objects, and strengthening local capacities for biodiversity conservation in areas with productive activities and wildlife. The main actors directly affected by these conflicts are livestock producers and rural and indigenous communities whose livelihoods may be impacted by depredation. The actors involved in the implementation and support of the measures include environmental authorities, civil society organizations, academic institutions, and international partners. The researchers MSc. Josué Ortega, director of Fundación Somos Selva, and Dr. Claudia Rengifo, professor in the Department of Communicable Diseases and Public Health of the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine of the University of Panama, in recent years have been promoting applied research to understand the ecology of the coyote (Canis latrans) in Panama and its relationship with rural and urban/peri-urban landscapes. This work seeks to describe habitat use, activity patterns, diet, and ecological role, as well as to directly document human–coyote interactions associated with depredation and the social perception of the species. To this end, scientific data have been generated through tools such as tracking by GPS transmitters, camera traps, systematic observations, and captures, in order to produce evidence that can guide management decisions and science-based coexistence strategies. Based on these scientific findings, prevention/anti-predation measures have been designed and validated and environmental education actions have been developed, working directly with local actors to reduce losses, reduce persecution of wildlife, and strengthen preventive management practices. In addition, a One Health approach is incorporated, using the coyote as a sentinel species to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the risks and dynamics of diseases that affect domestic animals, many of them zoonotic in Panama, comparing rural and urban scenarios and articulating efforts among conservation, animal health, and public health. Taken together, this work represents a relevant technical contribution to the national biodiversity report, by integrating research, conflict management, education, and health, with emphasis on practical and replicable solutions in the national territory. In parallel, in human–wildlife conflicts, MiAMBIENTE reported the formation/activation of an intersectoral group to define and implement concrete actions that reduce economic impacts on producers and risks to conservation, which is key to meeting the target in “critical areas” where coexistence conditions the persistence of populations; this type of conflict or problem implies a comprehensive approach, in which actions of research, farm management, awareness-raising, education, and application of the regulatory framework are complemented (Ministerio de Ambiente, 2022).
NT04.actions: 1) Updating lists of priority species and action plans Panama has strengthened the identification of threatened species through national assessments aligned with IUCN criteria (2022) and reports to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD, 2022). The Ministry of Environment has developed action plans for priority species, including wild fauna at risk and threatened flora (MiAmbiente, 2022). 2) In situ conservation in protected areas and biological corridors The strengthening of the National System of Protected Areas (SINAP) has made it possible to protect critical habitats for priority species, contributing to in situ conservation (MiAmbiente, 2022). The habitat conservation approach is recommended by IPBES (2019) as the main strategy to reduce extinction risk. 3) Ex situ conservation and germplasm banks Panama has collections and germplasm banks aimed at conserving the genetic diversity of agricultural and forest species, under the coordination of national institutions (MIDA, IDIAP) and universities (IDIAP, 2021). Ex situ conservation complements in situ conservation, in accordance with what is established in the CBD (2022) and FAO (2019). 4) Ecological restoration and genetic connectivity Forest and mangrove restoration projects have been implemented that favor ecological connectivity and genetic flow between populations (MiAmbiente, 2022). The IPCC (2022) notes that connectivity is key to maintaining adaptive capacity in the face of climate change. 5) Sustainable management of wild species Panama has made progress in regulating the trade and sustainable use of species through the implementation of the CITES Convention and national wildlife regulations (CITES, 2023). Sustainable management contributes to maintaining viable populations and reducing anthropogenic pressures (IPBES, 2019). 6) Management of human–wildlife conflicts In critical areas, actions have been implemented such as: Progress in protocols for addressing conflicts. Environmental education programs. Coordination with rural communities. Conflict management is considered essential for conserving large and medium-sized species in productive landscapes (IUCN, 2021). 7) Strengthening scientific research and monitoring Biodiversity monitoring programs and genetic studies for priority species have been developed, with academic support and international cooperation (MiAmbiente, 2022). Continuous monitoring is recommended by IPBES (2019) to assess population trends.

NT05.challenges: 1) Complexity of transnational organized crime Illegal wildlife trafficking is frequently linked to transnational criminal networks that use formal and informal trade routes, which makes detection and prosecution difficult (UNODC, 2020). Panama, due to its strategic geographic position, faces additional challenges as a transit country, which requires permanent international cooperation (CITES, 2023). 2) Limitations in technical and forensic capacities Effective control of trafficking requires: Specialized taxonomic identification. Forensic tools. Traceability systems. The lack of technical capacities can weaken judicial processes and reduce effective convictions (UNODC, 2020). 3) Sustained interinstitutional coordination Although there are cooperation mechanisms among MiAmbiente, Customs, Ministerio Público and security forces, maintaining constant operational coordination and standardized protocols represents an institutional challenge (MiAmbiente, 2022). The Global Biodiversity Framework highlights the need to strengthen multisectoral governance to combat environmental crimes (CBD, 2022). 4) Gaps in prosecution and sanction The effectiveness of control depends on the application of dissuasive sanctions. However, environmental crimes may face procedural delays or reduced penalties, which limits the preventive effect (UNODC, 2020). 5) Digital trade and new trafficking modalities The use of digital platforms for the illegal commercialization of species represents an emerging challenge that requires specialized technological monitoring (UNODC, 2020). 6) Balance between control and respect for traditional uses It is necessary to differentiate between illegal trafficking and sustainable traditional uses by Indigenous Peoples and local communities. IPBES (2019) highlights that policies must recognize traditional rights to avoid social conflicts and ensure legitimacy. 7) Health risks and zoonotic surveillance Illegal wildlife trade increases risks of transmission of zoonotic diseases, which requires integration between environmental and health authorities (WHO, 2021; UNEP, 2020). Intersectoral health-environment coordination still represents an operational challenge. 8) Awareness-raising and cultural change Internal and external demand for wild species drives trafficking. Reducing this demand requires sustained environmental education and behavior change campaigns (CBD, 2022). 9) Financing and sustainability of operations Effective control implies continuous investment in: Equipment. Training. Technology. Border surveillance. Financial sustainability is identified as a critical factor in the fight against environmental crimes (UNODC, 2020).
NT05.progress: Between 2019 and the present, Panama has shown progress mainly in interinstitutional coordination, operational tools, and strengthening criminal prosecution linked to illegal wildlife trafficking, although gaps in consolidated information persist. A relevant change was the creation and implementation of the Equipo Multidisciplinario Especializado Ambiental (EME-Ambiente) as an interinstitutional mechanism between MiAMBIENTE, the Ministry of Security, and the Public Prosecutor's Office, formalized since 24 May 2021 through a cooperation agreement (Organization of American States (OAS), 2023). In terms of results reported by the scheme itself, it is documented that, during the initial period of operation, EME-Ambiente coordinated 17 operations, of which 12 were carried out jointly with international institutions (OAS, 2023). In a later note, MiAMBIENTE reported having carried out about 19 national and international operations and indicated the provision of 2 pick-up vehicles and drones to support investigation/prosecution of environmental crimes, including illegal species trafficking (MiAMBIENTE, 2022). In 2022, a catalog of the most trafficked protected fauna and flora species was presented as a tool for identification, intended for security, border, and customs authorities (National Police, SENAFRONT, and Customs), with an explicit focus on combating the trafficking of flora and fauna (MiAMBIENTE, 2022). In the institutional communication, examples of frequently rescued species are listed (e.g., ocelot/manigordo ( Leopardus pardalis) , jaguarundi ( Puma yagouaroundi) , howler monkey ( Alouatta palliata) , black spider monkey ( Ateles fusciceps) , ( Caiman crocodilus) , macaws and parrots), which points to practical prioritization by taxonomic groups and capture pressure (MiAMBIENTE, 2022). Although there is no consolidated annual series of fauna seizures by route/market in a single official public source, there are specific figures that show operational activity: Rescue and relocation of fauna: MiAMBIENTE reported 326 specimens rescued and relocated in the first half of 2023, and indicated that 102 received medical-veterinary care in the course of the year up to that point (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). Precious timber trafficking case (linked to networks and enforcement): In an operation for illegal trafficking of cocobolo ( Dalbergia retusa ), three people were reported apprehended and the seizure/transfer of 19 logs (and the text also refers to 25 logs in custody), in addition to a reference price of up to USD 3,000 per ton on the black market, highlighting the economic component of the crime (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). Evidence from the criminal justice system (2023–2025) The Public Prosecutor's Office publishes complaint statistics from the Sistema Penal Acusatorio for environmental crimes. In 2024, the crime “Trafficking of wildlife species” (art. 410) recorded 18 complaints, compared with 30 in 2023 (Public Prosecutor's Office, 2024). For the period January–May 2025, the same crime (410) appears with 5 complaints (preliminary figures) (Public Prosecutor's Office, 2025). These figures reflect the dynamics of judicialization (complaints), but do not directly equate to seizures, convictions, or a real reduction in trafficking; even so, they show that the phenomenon is classified as an offense, recorded, and prosecuted in the criminal system. Zoonotic approach and “One Health” articulation (2024) The target explicitly incorporates the reduction of zoonotic pathogen risks. In 2024, Panama hosted a zoonotic disease prioritization process/workshop under the One Health approach, with participation from the human, animal, and environmental health sectors, which is consistent with the health risk component associated with trafficking and illegal handling of wildlife (Ministry of Health of Panama, 2024).
NT05.actions: 1) Strengthening of the legal framework and implementation of CITES Panama has strengthened the implementation of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) through customs controls, export/import permits and compliance mechanisms (CITES, 2023). The country has national wildlife regulations that govern capture, transport and trade, under the authority of the Ministry of Environment (MiAmbiente, 2022). 2) Creation and strengthening of interinstitutional mechanisms Coordinated actions have been strengthened among: MiAmbiente National Customs Authority Public Prosecutor's Office National Border Service National Police Interinstitutional cooperation is considered a good international practice to combat crimes against wildlife (UNODC, 2020). 3) Technical training and capacity strengthening Panama has participated in regional training programs in species identification, evidence handling and criminal prosecution of illegal trafficking (CITES, 2023). Strengthening technical capacities is key to reducing impunity in environmental crimes (IPBES, 2019). 4) Promotion of legal and sustainable trade The country has promoted compliance with CITES requirements for legal trade in authorized species, ensuring non-detriment findings (Non-Detriment Findings) where applicable (CITES, 2023). This contributes to differentiating sustainable trade from illicit trafficking. 5) Public health and zoonoses approach The regulation of the trade and transport of wild fauna also responds to the need to reduce risks of transmission of zoonotic diseases, as warned by WHO (2021). The link between illegal trafficking and public health has been recognized internationally following the COVID-19 pandemic (UNEP, 2020). 6) Respect for traditional uses and indigenous peoples National regulations recognize sustainable traditional uses of species by indigenous peoples, in coherence with the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD, 2022) and principles of indigenous rights. The differentiation between illegal trafficking and sustainable traditional use is essential for social legitimacy and effective conservation (IPBES, 2019). 7) International and regional cooperation Panama participates in regional networks to combat wildlife trafficking and in international cooperation mechanisms for information exchange (CITES, 2023; UNODC, 2020).

NT06.challenges: One of the main challenges is the construction of a clear and verifiable national baseline on the rate of introduction and establishment of IAS. The National Biodiversity Strategy recognizes the need to strengthen monitoring, diagnostic, and inventory systems as a condition for measuring progress in biodiversity (Gaceta Oficial Digital, 2018; CBD, 2018). Without consolidated indicators and comparable annual data series, demonstrating the 10% reduction may be methodologically complex. Another relevant challenge is effective interinstitutional coordination. Although the National Strategy contemplates coordination mechanisms among environmental, agricultural, and maritime entities (Gaceta Oficial Digital, 2018), practical implementation requires system interoperability, real-time information exchange, and clear joint response protocols. In border areas, the high volume of international trade represents a permanent risk. Panama depends on phytosanitary and quarantine controls carried out by the Ministerio de Desarrollo Agropecuario (MIDA), whose bulletins show the magnitude of the effort required to intercept pests and potentially invasive organisms (MIDA, 2022). However, the constant pressure of trade increases the probability of accidental entries. In the maritime sector, the country faces the challenge of effectively implementing the International Convention for the Control and Management of Ballast Water, a key instrument for preventing invasive marine introductions (Asamblea Nacional, 2016; Autoridad Marítima de Panamá, n.d.). Technical inspection and compliance by maritime operators require permanent specialized capacities. Likewise, early detection and rapid response continue to be an operational challenge. Although national planning contemplates the monitoring and control of IAS (Gaceta Oficial Digital, 2018), effective eradication or containment depends on timely financing, trained personnel, and agile administrative decisions. In continental and marine aquatic environments, the regulatory framework establishes measures for the control of introduced exotic species (FAOLEX, n.d.). However, the regulation of deliberate introductions, escapes in aquaculture, and ornamental trade remains a critical point. From the health point of view, the integration of the “One Health” approach is still a process under consolidation. Invasive species can facilitate vectors or emerging pathogens, which requires greater coordination between environment and public health (MIDA, 2022). Finally, the social component constitutes an additional challenge. The intentional release of ornamental species or exotic pets requires permanent educational campaigns and effective compliance mechanisms. The Global Biodiversity Framework establishes as a priority the prevention of new introductions and the control of invasive species as a condition for protecting biodiversity (Secretaría del CBD, 2024; WWF, 2024), which implies strengthening both regulatory measures and awareness-raising actions.
NT06.progress: Since 2019, Panama already had explicit guidelines to prevent the entry and spread of invasive alien species within its national biodiversity planning, including actions to strengthen technical capacities and control at points of entry (MiAmbiente, 2018). Although the document predates 2019, it is relevant because it has served as a guiding framework for the period 2019–present and to justify investments and control actions (MiAmbiente, 2018). Customs currently in 2025 is creating an interinstitutional platform for controlling the entry through ports, airports, and borders of products and by-products of wild species. In the wetlands sphere, Panama reported in its National Report for Ramsar COP14 (which compiles progress up to 2021) the prioritization of activities linked to invasive alien species, including identification, control/eradication, and management measures to avoid introduction and establishment (Ramsar, n. d.). Main finding: the country has planning frameworks that recognize the threat of invasive species and propose measures; however, these frameworks do not always include a public national indicator that directly measures the “rate of introduction/establishment” to demonstrate a 10% reduction by 2030. (Ramsar, n. d.; MiAmbiente, 2018). Prevention at borders: agricultural quarantine and phytosanitary control One of the most robust prevention mechanisms (avoiding new introductions) is the MIDA Agricultural Quarantine system, responsible for inspecting cargo and controlling risks of pests and pathogens associated with the movement of agricultural goods (MIDA, n. d.). In terms of recent figures (useful as a proxy for “introduction pressure”), MIDA reported that its Executive Directorate of Agricultural Quarantine intercepted 1,498 pests in imported products during the second quarter of 2025, these interceptions were distributed in different inspection categories: 1, 226 pests were detected in food samples, 134 on container floors and packaging, 110 in non-edible samples and 28 from seizures. Among the most common species detected are mealybugs, which are a type of pest that affects a wide variety of plants, including indoor plants, fruit trees, ornamentals, and agricultural crops. Grain weevils also stand out, mainly affecting stored cereals, both in the field and in warehouses. Another type of pest detected was wood beetles, which damage both trees and structures such as houses and furniture. The increase in interceptions during this second quarter is attributed both to the season and to the greater movement of international cargo recorded in this period, according to Agricultural Quarantine personnel of MIDA (MIDA, 2025). In addition, Panama activated preventive measures in response to regional risks of species/pests with invasive potential and sanitary impact. A clear example is the national phytosanitary alert for the giant African snail ( Achatina fulica ) in 2021, declaring national measures to prevent its introduction and strengthening inspection at points of entry and phytosanitary surveillance (MIDA, 2021a, 2021b). For control (not only prevention), Panama has used management strategies aimed at invasive species already established. The most documented case is the lionfish ( Pterois spp.), invasive in the Caribbean. In 2020, the Autoridad de los Recursos Acuáticos de Panamá (ARAP) issued a resolution authorizing the capture of lionfish in specific areas of the Caribbean (ARAP, 2020). Subsequently, control actions have continued through capture tournaments and local awareness/management activities, reported by MiAmbiente, including events in Guna Yala (2021) and Portobelo/others (2024) (MiAmbiente, 2021; MiAmbiente, 2024a; MiAmbiente, 2024b). These public notes usually highlight the holding of events and their reduction objective, but they do not always publish standardized numbers (biomass extracted, densities before/after) to quantify population reduction at the national scale. Therefore, progress is clear in “control mechanism,” but less demonstrable in “reduction of the establishment of new species” or “quantified reduction of the invasive species” due to the lack of published series. Recent literature and academic work have attempted to quantify the presence of invasive species. For example, a thesis (Universidad de Panamá) reports that 54 alien species of arthropods and chordates have been reported as invasive in Panama (Rodríguez, 2022).
NT06.actions: To advance toward the target of reducing by 10% the rate of introduction and establishment of new invasive alien species by 2030, Panama has implemented a set of regulatory, operational, and technical measures coordinated among various State institutions. First, the National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (2018–2050) explicitly incorporates the prevention, control, and management of invasive alien species as a priority line of action, including the strengthening of interinstitutional and monitoring mechanisms (Gaceta Oficial Digital, 2018; Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), 2018). In the area of border prevention, the Ministry of Agricultural Development (MIDA), through the Executive Directorate of Agricultural Quarantine (DECA), has strengthened phytosanitary and zoosanitary controls at ports, airports, and land borders, implementing inspections, import requirements, and phytozoosanitary licenses to reduce the risk of introduction of pests and invasive organisms (MIDA, n. d.-a; MIDA, n. d.-b). As evidence of these controls, in 2025 more than 600 pest interceptions were reported in the first quarter of the year, reflecting the strengthening of the preventive surveillance system (MIDA, 2025a). In the marine sphere, Panama implemented the International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships’ Ballast Water and Sediments (BWM 2004) through Law 41 of 2016, under the supervision of the Panama Maritime Authority (AMP), with the objective of preventing the introduction of invasive marine species through maritime transport (National Assembly, 2016; Panama Maritime Authority, n. d.). Likewise, in the aquatic sector, the regulatory framework establishes specific measures for the regulation and control of invasive aquatic species and introduced exotic species, including provisions for education, prevention, and management (FAOLEX, n. d.). Regarding monitoring and early detection, the Ministry of Environment has incorporated IAS monitoring within the programs of the National System of Protected Areas (SINAP), strengthening inventories and early warning mechanisms, in accordance with the guidelines of the National Biodiversity Strategy (Gaceta Oficial Digital, 2018). In terms of scientific support, the Aquatic Resources Authority of Panama (ARAP) has promoted the use of technical and genetic tools for the identification and study of invasive species, contributing to improving the country’s technical response capacity (ARAP, 2015).
