NT07.challenges: 1) Reduction of nutrient losses One of the main challenges is diffuse pollution from the agricultural sector, particularly due to the intensive use of nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers. The National Biodiversity Strategy recognizes the need to strengthen sustainable soil management and watershed protection to reduce impacts on aquatic ecosystems (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). Likewise, the lack of a consolidated baseline on nutrient losses makes it difficult to measure progress toward the 50% target, since runoff and leaching monitoring is not systematically integrated at the national level (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). 2) Dependence on pesticides and hazardous substances The agricultural sector maintains a significant dependence on conventional agrochemicals, which represents a challenge for the transition toward less risky alternatives. Panama regulates the import and use of pesticides through phytosanitary and sanitary frameworks (MIDA, 2021; MINSA, 2019), however, field monitoring and traceability continue to be limited. At the international level, Panama is a Party to the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions, which establish obligations for the management of hazardous chemical substances (PNUMA, 2017). The challenge lies in fully harmonizing these commitments with local productive practice. 3) Prevention of plastic pollution Although the country adopted legislative measures such as Law 1 of 2018 (reduction of plastic bags) and Law 187 of 2020 (single-use plastics), territorial compliance and recycling infrastructure still present gaps (Asamblea Nacional, 2018; Asamblea Nacional, 2020). In addition, the transition toward a circular economy requires strengthening integrated waste management and promoting changes in consumption patterns (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). 4) Adoption of clean technologies The substantial increase in clean technologies faces financial and technical barriers. The transition toward cleaner production requires investment in energy efficiency, effluent treatment and industrial modernization, in coherence with climate and biodiversity commitments (CDB, 2018). The lack of robust economic incentives and accessible green financing mechanisms limits the speed of adoption in small and medium-sized enterprises. 5) Institutional coordination and governance Pollution reduction involves multiple sectors (environment, agriculture, health, industry, trade). Although the General Environmental Law establishes the principle of interinstitutional coordination (Asamblea Nacional, 1998), effective implementation requires greater integration of information and monitoring systems. 6) Climate change as an aggravating factor The increase in extreme events can increase nutrient runoff and the mobilization of contaminants toward bodies of water, exacerbating cumulative impacts (CDB, 2018). This implies that reduction targets must consider future climate scenarios.
NT07.progress: Since 2019, Panama's progress linked to the national target of reducing pollution from nutrients, pesticides/hazardous substances, and plastic pollution shows clear progress in the regulatory framework and planning (especially in plastics and pesticide control), while public evidence of quantified reductions (e.g., “50% less nutrient losses” at the country scale) still appears fragmented and more available at the level of specific programs/territories than as a consolidated national balance. In the plastic pollution component, the country strengthened its regulatory framework by regulating Law 187 of 2020 through a decree published in the Official Gazette (May 2022), establishing criteria and institutional responsibilities for the reduction and progressive replacement of single-use plastics, including the requirement for a National Strategic Plan with targets, indicators, and follow-up/monitoring methodologies (Digital Official Gazette, 2022). This regulatory advance has been complemented by public policy signals and recent planning oriented toward the circular economy: MiAmbiente has disseminated estimates of Panama’s annual generation of plastic waste (e.g., 191,580 tons/year, cited from IDB) and commitments to reduce the sale/import of single-use plastics and virgin resin by 2030 (Ministry of Environment of Panama, 2023). In 2025, in addition, a “roadmap/plan” was publicly presented projecting that, if the proposed actions are implemented, Panama could reduce plastic pollution by 67% by 2040 (Swissinfo, 2025) and set a threshold of 12% of mismanaged plastic waste by 2040 (La Estrella de Panamá, 2025; La Prensa, 2025). Although these projections do not yet amount to achieved results, they do constitute relevant progress in scenario-based planning and in establishing an accountability framework. In terms of the magnitude of the challenge, official statements have also reported orders of magnitude of municipal solid waste (approx. 4,800 tons/day, 1.7 million/year), useful for contextualizing the pressure on management systems and the urgency of reducing leakage into rivers and coasts (Ministry of Environment of Panama, 2025). In the pesticides and hazardous substances component, the most verifiable progress is seen in regulatory measures and the strengthening of controls. In 2025, a resolution was issued in the Official Gazette prohibiting the registration of active pesticide ingredients of extreme and high hazard (toxicological categories Ia and Ib WHO; or 1 and 2 in GHS/RTCA) that had not previously been registered in the country, and establishing exceptional conditions for special permits under defined criteria (Digital Official Gazette, 2025). This type of decision is consistent with the target of “reducing risks associated with pesticide use” through regulation and reinforces the coordinated role of MIDA–MINSA described in the resolution itself (Digital Official Gazette, 2025). In parallel, MIDA has continued promoting technical instruments to guide good practices; for example, in 2025 it published/updated a Manual of Procedure for Good Agricultural Practices, which serves as implementation support to reduce risks from the inappropriate use of inputs (Ministry of Agricultural Development, 2025). With respect to this component, toxicology studies have been carried out using aquatic insects with the following findings: Cornejo et al. (2019a) evaluated the combined effects of pesticides, nutrient enrichment, and habitat alteration on macroinvertebrate communities in the Chiriquí Viejo River basin (Panama). Thirteen sites were sampled in 20 campaigns between 2015 and 2017. The results show that: Pesticide toxicity (TUmax), soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP), and sedimentation significantly affect the abundance, richness, and composition of macroinvertebrates. The BMWP/PAN index responded to pesticide toxicity, while SPEAR did not show the same sensitivity, possibly because BMWP/PAN is adapted to local fauna. Antagonistic interactions between stressors were detected, that is, the combined effects were smaller than expected according to their individual effects. The study highlights the need for bioassays with tropical species and the joint analysis of multiple stressors to understand agricultural impacts in tropical regions. 2. Cornejo et al. (2021a) evaluated the acute sensitivity (LC50) of three tropical detritivores (Anchytarsus sp., Hyalella sp., Lepidostoma sp.) to: Chlorpyrifos (organophosphate insecticide) Bifenthrin (pyrethroid insecticide) Chlorothalonil (fungicide) The results indicate that: The tropical species showed high sensitivity, with 50% mortality at concentrations between 0.04 and 2.7 μg L⁻¹. Chlorpyrifos was the most toxic. Through species sensitivity distribution curves (SSD), it was shown that these tropical species are among the most sensitive, even compared with standard species such as Daphnia magna. The study shows that extrapolating data from temperate species may underestimate ecological risk in tropical regions. 3. Cornejo et al. (2021b) experimental in microcosms evaluated how chlorpyrifos and chlorothalonil affect: Survival and growth of detritivores Sporulation and richness of aquatic fungi (hyphomycetes) Leaf litter decomposition rates Main findings: Chlorpyrifos significantly reduced the survival of detritivores, especially Hyalella. Chlorothalonil more strongly affected microbial decomposers. The combination of pesticides had additive effects, further reducing total decomposition. The loss of detritivore diversity amplified the negative effects on ecosystem functioning. The study demonstrates that pesticides not only affect individual organisms, but also key ecosystem processes such as nutrient recycling. 4. Pérez et al. (2023) evaluated the agricultural impact detected through leaf litter decomposition, leaf litter decomposition as a functional indicator in tropical lowland streams in the Panama Canal basin, comparing areas with: Low intervention (LI) Medium intervention (MI) High intervention (HI) Three types of leaves were used (local native, non-local native, and exotic). Key results: In tropical lowland streams, decomposition was mainly microbial (>60%). Only in the presence of detritivores did the species Alnus acuminata clearly discriminate between levels of intervention, with greater decomposition in less impacted areas. Detritivore activity, although low in these systems, reflected land-use impacts. The study confirms that leaf litter decomposition is a functional indicator sensitive to agricultural intervention, even in tropical systems where detritivores are scarce. Regarding nutrients (losses to the environment), the strongest publicly available progress tends to be presented as sectoral/territorial monitoring and management, rather than as an aggregated national achievement. For example, in the Panama Canal Watershed, ACP maintained a surveillance program with high sampling intensity: in 2020 it reported 606 samples at 40 stations and 14,720 results, with specific evaluation of nitrates and orthophosphates, and found that orthophosphates were undetectable in 90% of the samples analyzed (Panama Canal Authority, 2021). These data illustrate installed monitoring capacity and can serve as a line of evidence for trends at critical sites, but they do not yet substitute for a country indicator on “50% less nutrient losses.” On the infrastructure and sanitation front (key for nutrients and organic matter), the Panama Sanitation Program and the Juan Díaz Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP) have been identified as central pieces; for example, treatment capacity of 5,500 liters/second and benefit coverage for more than 700,000 people have been publicized, and the applicable technical framework for effluent quality and disposal is mentioned (e.g., COPANIT 35-2019) (CAPAC, 2024). This type of expansion and standardization is consistent with reducing nutrient pressures in receiving bodies.
NT07.actions: 1) Strengthening of the environmental regulatory framework The country has adopted specific legislation to reduce plastic pollution, including Law 1 of 2018, which progressively prohibits polyethylene plastic bags, and Law 187 of 2020, which regulates the progressive reduction and substitution of single-use plastics (National Assembly, 2018; National Assembly, 2020). These standards are aligned with the national roadmap for the progressive elimination of plastics. Resolution DM 0496 of 2025 by which the use, commercialization and distribution of single-use plastics and expanded polyethylene (fom) are prohibited in all protected areas and national parks of the Rep. of Panama. 2) Reduction of nutrient losses in the agricultural sector The Ministerio de Desarrollo Agropecuario (MIDA) has promoted the adoption of Good Agricultural Practices (BPA), which include the rational use of fertilizers and integrated soil management to reduce runoff and leaching of nutrients into water bodies (MIDA, 2021). In addition, the implementation of management plans in priority watersheds seeks to reduce diffuse pollution by nitrogen and phosphorus, contributing to the protection of water sources and aquatic ecosystems (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). 3) Regulation and control of pesticides and hazardous chemical substances Panama regulates the import, registration and use of pesticides through phytosanitary and public health regulations, under the supervision of MIDA and the Ministerio de Salud (MINSA). These regulations seek to reduce environmental and health risks associated with agrochemicals (MIDA, 2021; MINSA, 2019). At the international level, Panama is Party to the Stockholm (persistent organic pollutants), Rotterdam (prior informed consent) and Basel (transboundary movements of hazardous wastes) conventions, strengthening the control of hazardous substances and their international trade (UNEP, 2017). 4) Integrated waste management and circular economy The country has promoted the National Policy for Integrated Waste Management and strategies linked to the circular economy, aimed at reducing waste generation and promoting recycling, recovery and clean technologies (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). These actions include: Recycling and source separation programs. Regulation of sanitary landfills. Promotion of extended producer responsibility. Incentives for innovation in clean technologies. 5) Prevention of plastic pollution In addition to legislation on single-use plastics, Panama has developed national environmental education campaigns and action plans to reduce marine plastic pollution, in line with international commitments and targets of the Global Biodiversity Framework (National Assembly, 2020; CBD, 2022). 6) Promotion of clean technologies in productive sectors The country has integrated cleaner production and energy efficiency criteria within its climate and environmental policies, promoting: Efficient use of resources. Effluent treatment technologies. Sustainable agriculture and silvopastoral systems. Industrial innovation with a lower environmental footprint. These measures are aligned with the National Biodiversity Strategy and national climate commitments (CBD, 2018).

NT08.challenges: The target implies not only conserving species, but organizing their use, integrating sustainable products/services and ensuring real benefits for vulnerable populations, indigenous peoples and local communities, while maintaining the ecological viability of wild populations. This is consistent with the approach of the Global Biodiversity Framework on sustainable, safe and legal use, harvest and trade (CBD, 2022a) and on sustainable management to generate benefits (CBD, 2022b). 1) Define and prioritize the “20 species” with verifiable criteria An initial challenge is to have a transparent and technically grounded process to select priority species (by threat, cultural/economic value, pressure of use, management potential, ecological role), and to update it periodically. The need for planning and lines of action for sustainable use is contemplated in the National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2018–2050 (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). 2) Insufficient biological data for closed seasons and management plans To demonstrate “sustainable management,” information is required on population size, reproduction rates, mortality, distribution, connectivity, critical habitat and trends. Without these data, it is difficult to define extraction limits, seasons, quotas or measures by species and region, as required by the sustainability and “non-overexploitation” approaches of the Global Framework (CBD, 2022a; CBD, 2022b). 3) Pressure from illegal trade and unregulated use Overexploitation and illegal trafficking can neutralize sustainable management efforts. Within the SDG framework, target 15.7 calls for urgent measures to end poaching and trafficking of protected species and address demand and supply (United Nations, 2015). In addition, CITES requires Parties to report seizures through annual illegal trade reports, which shows the importance of the compliance and traceability component (CITES, n. d.). 4) Governance and implementation: permits, enforcement and institutional capacity Although Panama has a general framework to promote the sustainable use of natural resources (National Assembly, 1998), the challenge is to sustain in the field: sufficient inspectors/rangers, transport and marketing controls, post-permit follow-up and effective sanctioning, interinstitutional coordination (environment–customs–security–health–sectoral authorities). The typical gap is not “lack of regulation,” but implementation capacity (National Assembly, 1998; MiAMBIENTE, 2018). 5) Traceability and sustainable value chains (from territory to market) The target requires that the products/services derived from wild species (e.g., ecotourism, artisanal fishing, non-timber forest products, handicrafts, etc.) have: traceability, sustainability standards, control of intermediation, access to markets and fair prices. Without this, the benefits may be concentrated in intermediaries and not in communities, weakening the social legitimacy of management (CBD, 2022b; MiAMBIENTE, 2018). 6) Benefit distribution and social safeguards Ensuring that benefits are socially fair and reach vulnerable populations implies clear rules (associativity, sharing agreements, transparency), and conflict resolution mechanisms. The Global Framework emphasizes protecting and respecting customary sustainable use by indigenous peoples and local communities (CBD, 2022a; CBD, 2022b). 7) Cultural relevance, consent and rights in indigenous territories In indigenous territories, the challenge is to apply management schemes that respect their own governance systems and traditional uses, avoiding the “criminalization” of sustainable cultural practices and promoting participatory agreements. This approach is aligned with the National Biodiversity Strategy and with the Global Framework (MiAMBIENTE, 2018; CBD, 2022a). 8) “Safe” approach and health risks (zoonoses) in use and trade Sustainability today also incorporates the health security component: the Global Framework makes explicit that use/harvest/trade must be “safe” and reduce risks of pathogen spillover (CBD, 2022a). This requires protocols (handling, transport, slaughter, markets), surveillance and coordination with public health. 9) Climate change and habitat loss as factors that reduce “sustainable yield” Even with good management, populations may decline if habitat degrades or if extreme events alter reproductive cycles/food availability. Therefore, sustainable management usually requires parallel habitat protection/restoration actions (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). 10) Stable financing and monitoring/management costs Planning and managing 20 species with robust monitoring requires sustained financing (personnel, science, control, community incentives). Without stable resources, the plans remain on paper and are not sustained over time (MiAMBIENTE, 2018).
NT08.progress: Since 2019, the most clearly documented progress and with the greatest numerical traceability for “sustainable management” of wild species comes from the fisheries sector, for three reasons: (i) there is an updated legal framework, (ii) volumes and composition by species are reported, and (iii) governance approaches such as co-management and control/monitoring measures have expanded. Legal framework and sustainability approach: Law 204 of 18 March 2021 (fisheries/aquaculture) makes explicit the purpose and objectives of ensuring conservation, renewal, and permanence of aquatic resources and promotes “sustainable use” (Autoridad de los Recursos Acuáticos de Panamá (ARAP), 2021). Co-management (shared governance): ARAP formalizes and promotes “co-management zones for responsible fishing,” defined as a mode of governance with shared responsibility among ARAP, local authorities, coastal communities, and fishers. (ARAP, n. d.). Species-specific management measures (e.g. closed seasons): The closed season for Caribbean lobster ( Panulirus argus ) appears documented at least for 2019 and 2020 through specific resolutions, which is consistent with effort management and protection of reproductive cycles (ARAP, 2019, 2020). Recent figures: In the Informe de Pesca y Acuicultura 2024 (annual summary 2023–2024), Panama reports 138,722 total tons (fisheries + aquaculture); large-scale fishing totals 116,514 t and small/medium-scale 4,804 t; the aquaculture sector reports 17,403 t. (ARAP & Autoridad Marítima de Panamá (AMP), 2024). In addition, the same report breaks down volumes for commercial species/groups (examples, 2024): Small pelagics (anchoveta/herring): 113,004 t (97% of large-scale fleet catch). Trawl shrimp (examples): white shrimp 514 t, red 465 t, cabezón 267 t, Fidel 81 t. Longline/trawl (examples): yellowfin tuna 731 t, dolphinfish 230 t, spotted snapper 235 t, cabezón 268 t, sole 166 t. These data show that Panama already has (i) statistics/record systems by species and (ii) management instruments (closed seasons, monitoring, co-management) that are the operational basis for declaring “sustainable management” in a broad set of aquatic species (a significant block toward “20 species,” although the target asks for “priority” species and with explicit benefits). Sustainable products and services linked to biodiversity: a) Nature tourism services with management rules (cetaceans) Panama has regulations that define sighting modalities (e.g., scientific and educational), which is consistent with the notion of “sustainable services” associated with wild fauna (cetaceans) when applied with control and compliance (Gaceta Oficial Digital, n. d.). b) Community conservation/local management (recent examples) There is public evidence of strengthening the approach of community and indigenous participation in biodiversity governance, being host of the first global meeting of the body in charge of strengthening the participation of indigenous peoples and local communities in the protection of global biodiversity (although this does not always translate into “20 priority species” with quantitative traceability). (MiAmbiente, 2025). Experiences of community forest management in Darién are also documented with complementary productive components (agroforestry/enrichment), which can be linked to livelihoods and conservation (MiAmbiente, 2025). c) Conservation programs with figures (sea turtles as an example of a priority species) Although target 28 emphasizes “sustainable management” and benefits, in practice Panama reports robust quantitative results on certain beaches/sites for sea turtles (species of high conservation value, and in some cases with community participation and educational tourism). Example: at Playa La Marinera (2022–2023 season), MiAmbiente reports: 83,068 nests recorded in arribadas, 2,966 solitary nestings, 11,263 hatched nests and 645,724 hatchlings released (including records of green turtle Chelonia mydas in addition to olive ridley Lepidochelys olivacea ) (MiAmbiente, 2023). As for terrestrial species, there are Conservation Action Plans: Action Plan for the Conservation of Amphibians in Panama Panama is one of the countries with the greatest amphibian diversity in Mesoamerica, but also one of the most affected by chytridiomycosis (caused by Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis ), habitat loss, and climate change (ANAM, 2011; IUCN, 2022). The Action Plan for the Conservation of Amphibians of Panama was developed by the then Autoridad Nacional del Ambiente (ANAM) in coordination with research centers such as the Instituto Conmemorativo Gorgas and the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute. Main strategic lines: Population and epidemiological monitoring of threatened species. Implementation of ex situ conservation programs, such as the Proyecto de Rescate y Conservación de Anfibios de Panamá (PARC). Restoration and protection of critical habitats in protected areas. Research on genetic resistance to the chytrid fungus. Environmental education and community participation. The plan prioritizes endemic and critically threatened species such as Atelopus zeteki and Craugastor evanesco , whose population decline has been dramatic since the 2000s (ANAM, 2011; IUCN, 2022). 2 . National Action Plan for the Conservation of the Jaguar (Panthera onca) and a key umbrella species for ecological connectivity in Panama. The National Action Plan for the Conservation of the Jaguar was prepared by the Ministerio de Ambiente (MiAMBIENTE) in alignment with the Jaguar Corridor 2030 Initiative promoted by the Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Desarrollo (PNUD) and Panthera (MiAMBIENTE, 2018; PNUD, 2020). Main axes of the plan: Identification and conservation of priority biological corridors, especially between Darién, Chagres, and La Amistad. Reduction of human–wildlife conflict through: Implementation of silvopastoral systems. Electric fences and preventive livestock management. Strengthening control against illegal hunting. Monitoring through camera traps. Community education in rural areas. The plan recognizes that habitat fragmentation and retaliation for livestock depredation constitute the main threats (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). 3 . Conservation Plan for the Harpy Eagle ( Harpia harpyja ) The harpy eagle is the national bird of Panama and is listed as vulnerable globally (IUCN, 2022). Panama developed a National Conservation Program for the Harpy Eagle, led by MiAMBIENTE in partnership with the Peregrine Fund and scientific organizations (MiAMBIENTE, 2019). Key components: Protection of active nests in Darién, East Panama, and other forested regions. Satellite monitoring and tracking of released individuals. Rehabilitation and release programs. Environmental education in rural communities. Protection of primary forests where the species depends on emergent trees for nesting. The program emphasizes the conservation of large expanses of continuous forest, given the species’ sensitivity to deforestation (MiAMBIENTE, 2019). 4. Other Relevant Action Plans in Panama In addition to the species mentioned, Panama has developed or participates in plans for: Sea turtles, within the framework of the Inter-American Convention for the Protection and Conservation of Sea Turtles (CIT). Central American tapir ( Tapirus bairdii ), an endangered species. Marine species under the National Biodiversity Plan and the National Biodiversity Strategy (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). This shows operational capacity for monitoring/management by species and potential to integrate “services” (education/responsible tourism) and local benefits, but to meet the target it would be necessary to make explicit (i) which are the “20 priority species” and (ii) what “sustainable products/services” and benefits (income, employment, value chains) are associated with each one, with verifiable indicators.
NT08.actions: Regulatory and public policy framework The National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2018–2050 incorporates strategic lines for the sustainable management of native species, the sustainable use of biological resources, and the participation of local communities (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). In the forestry and wildlife sphere, Panama regulates use through permits, management plans, and closed seasons when applicable, under the supervision of the Ministry of Environment (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). In situ management and conservation plans The country has implemented management plans for priority species (including forest, marine, and terrestrial fauna species), particularly within the National System of Protected Areas (SINAP), strengthening in situ conservation (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). In the marine sphere, the Aquatic Resources Authority of Panama (ARAP) regulates sustainable fishing, establishes closed seasons and quotas for marine species of commercial interest, contributing to the sustainability of wild populations (ARAP, 2020). Sustainable management and generation of economic benefits Panama has promoted sustainable use schemes that integrate products and services derived from wild species, such as: Community forest management. Sustainable artisanal fishing. Ecotourism in protected areas. Agroforestry systems with native species. These schemes seek to generate income for rural communities and indigenous peoples, reducing pressures on ecosystems (MiAMBIENTE, 2018; United Nations, 2015). Integration of indigenous peoples and local communities The Constitution and the Panamanian environmental framework recognize the collective rights of indigenous peoples over their territories and natural resources. The sustainable management of species in indigenous territories is developed through participation and prior consent mechanisms (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). Likewise, the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework highlights the importance of sustainable use and the fair distribution of benefits derived from biological resources (CBD, 2022), aligning with the national target. Ex situ conservation and scientific strengthening The country has strengthened germplasm banks and biological collections, as well as scientific research programs to ensure the genetic conservation of priority species (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). These actions allow: Recovery of threatened populations. Restocking in degraded ecosystems. Maintenance of genetic diversity. Legal trade and trafficking control Panama is a Party to the CITES Convention, which strengthens the regulation of international trade in threatened species and promotes their sustainable use (CITES, 1973). Oversight of legal trade helps prevent overexploitation and guarantees that use generates benefits without compromising conservation.

NT09.challenges: 1) Align the national ABS framework with the new multilateral DSI mechanism and the Cali Fund Panama already has regulations on access and control of the use of biological/genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge (e.g., Executive Decree No. 19 of 2019 and the previous regime), but it must now harmonize these instruments with Decision 16/2 (DSI and multilateral mechanism) to avoid overlaps, gaps and, especially, risks of a “double track” in obligations or procedures. Practical challenge: translating global modalities (Cali Fund/multilateral mechanism) into internal procedures that are compatible with national ABS (permits, contracts, monitoring, beneficiaries, etc.). 2) Define precisely the operational scope of “DSI” in national instruments Decision 16/2 creates a global scheme for benefits derived from the use of DSI; without clear operational definitions in regulations, guides and forms, there may be uncertainty for universities, laboratories, companies and authorities about what falls under DSI, when the multilateral mechanism applies and how the use and generation of benefits are documented. 3) Implement FPIC consistently in new frameworks and decisions Panama has a normative basis for FPIC (e.g., Law 37 of 2016) that establishes the right to consultation and prior, free and informed consent for indigenous peoples and its exercise through traditional institutions. The challenge is to operationalize it in a uniform, predictable and verifiable manner in future administrative and regulatory practice. Associated risk: inconsistencies between sectors/territories or between what a new sectoral regulation requires and the standards and timelines of the FPIC process. 4) Ensure effective participation and benefit-sharing for indigenous peoples and local communities The target requires that indigenous peoples and local communities participate effectively in benefit-sharing. In practice, this implies: clear rules of representation, internal agreements, financial transparency, complaint and dispute resolution mechanisms, and safeguards for traditional knowledge. The FPIC regime and the existence of frameworks on traditional knowledge are enabling factors, but their integration into ABS/DSI requires detailed procedures. 5) Monitor and demonstrate “80% compliance” of new frameworks (indicators, audit and traceability) The target sets a quantifiable threshold (80% of new frameworks fully complying). The challenge is to build a monitoring system that makes it possible to: Identify what counts as a “new legal/administrative/policy framework” Assess “full compliance” with Nagoya and with the DSI/Cali Fund component Maintain evidence (files, FPIC records, benefit agreements, reports). 6) Institutional capacity and intersectoral coordination ABS/DSI/FPIC is not only MiAMBIENTE: it involves research, health, agriculture, trade/IP, customs, foreign affairs, etc. Even with decrees in force, the challenge is to sustain technical and legal capacities (assessment, benefit negotiation, compliance verification, records management, use control), and to coordinate decisions among entities. The need for capacity-building and guidance tools is reflected in recent initiatives for institutional support and FPIC guides. 7) Legal certainty for users (academia, private sector, cooperation) without weakening rights For the system to work, users must have clarity on: steps, timelines, costs, competent authority requirements for access, use, transfer of material what FPIC requires and when how DSI is managed (multilateral/Cali Fund). If the system is perceived as uncertain, informality or “non-compliance” due to lack of knowledge may increase. 8) Coordination between traditional knowledge and access to genetic resources in specific cases Decree 19 of 2019 contemplates access to associated traditional knowledge where applicable; the challenge is to standardize criteria: when there is associated traditional knowledge, how it is documented, how it is protected and how the benefit is shared without exposing sensitive information. 9) Prepare for the operational architecture of the Cali Fund Decision 16/2 defines the multilateral mechanism and indicates that the global fund is called the Cali Fund; in addition, there is operational documentation/mandates for its implementation under the UN fiduciary architecture. The challenge for Panama is to define focal points, coordination mechanisms, and how to prioritize/channel benefits at the national level (including criteria for beneficiaries and projects), while maintaining coherence with FPIC and with national priorities.
NT09.progress: Since 2019, Panama has made significant progress in building (and beginning to operate) the legal-administrative framework for Access to Genetic Resources and Fair and Equitable Benefit-Sharing (ABS), including associated traditional knowledge, although it is not yet publicly evident (with consolidated data) whether the country is already approaching the threshold of 35% of access agreements with clear benefit-sharing mechanisms set out in its target. In regulatory terms, Panama already had the approval of the Nagoya Protocol (Law 57 of 2012), which provides the international basis for the ABS regime (Official Gazette, 2012; CBD, 2011; National Assembly of Panama, 2012). The most visible operational leap since 2019 occurred with the adoption of Executive Decree No. 19 (26 March 2019), which regulates access and control of the use of biological and genetic resources, and incorporates relevant requirements for equity and rights, such as Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) when access involves indigenous communities/collective lands/areas under special regimes (Digital Official Gazette, 2019; WIPO Lex, 2019). This regulation is a key prerequisite for moving from general commitments to enforceable procedures (CBD, 2011). In implementation, between 2019–2020 the completion of an institutional strengthening effort with cooperation support was reported, aimed at consolidating a “national regulatory system” on access to biological/genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge (MiAmbiente, n.d.; UNDP, 2020). In parallel, MiAmbiente reported the launch/promotion of an information system for scientific permit and access procedures (UNDP, 2020). In addition, operational instruments were formalized, such as Resolution DM-0197-2020 (published in the Official Gazette) approving forms and formats for applications and permits for access to and use of genetic/biological resources (Ministry of Environment, 2020). As for quantitative evidence (publicly available), MiAmbiente reported that in 2020 it processed 143 scientific permits, of which 14 corresponded to “permits for access to genetic resource for non-commercial purposes (ARG)” and 80 to “access to biological resource (ARB)” (Ministry of Environment, 2021). In a later report, MiAmbiente reported that through its section on access to genetic/biological resources, 1,025 permits were processed (Ministry of Environment, 2022). Although these figures do not automatically amount to “ABS agreements with benefit-sharing” (they involve diverse types: permits, exports/imports, etc.), they do show administrative operability and a volume of management that allows (if systematized) better measurement of compliance with the target. An additional indicator of progress—more aligned with Nagoya—is the use of the ABS Clearing-House: Panama appears with published certificates/IRCC, which shows that in certain cases the country issues permits that may constitute internationally recognized certificates (ABS Clearing-House, n.d.). For example, there are IRCC associated with scientific permits linked to collections for sequencing/genomics, which connects with traceability and compliance in the ABS scheme (ABS Clearing-House, n.d.; CBD, 2011). In capacities and participation, training activities on ABS negotiations and benefit-sharing are reported, including a gender approach and the Nagoya framework, with national actors (MiAmbiente, 2022). There are also signs of greater incorporation of indigenous peoples and of the “access to genetic resources and benefit-sharing” agenda in national target processes, which is important so that benefit-sharing is legitimate and applicable when there is associated traditional knowledge (MiAmbiente, 2024). An emerging challenge (2019–2025) is the dimension of digital sequence information (DSI): at the global level, the Convention adopted at COP15 decision 15/9 creating a multilateral mechanism and a fund for benefit-sharing from the use of DSI, and at COP16 modalities were adopted (decision 16/2, “Cali Fund”) (CBD, 2022; CBD, 2024; United Nations, 2024). This matters for Panama because even with a good “classic” ABS regime (based on physical access), part of the value can be captured via DSI, so it will be key to harmonize national policies with that international mechanism (CBD, 2022; CBD, 2024).
NT09.actions: 1) Legislative and regulatory measures already adopted in Panama (basis for ABS–FPIC) a) Approval of the Nagoya Protocol (international ABS framework) Panama approved the Nagoya Protocol through Law 57 of 4 October 2012, expressly cited in the recitals of the national regulation on access and control of the use of biological and genetic resources. Relevance for the 2028–2030 target: it enables national frameworks to align with Nagoya and strengthen ABS procedures. b) Regulation on access to genetic/biological resources and traditional knowledge with FPIC and benefits Executive Decree No. 25 of 29 April 2009 regulates access to genetic/biological resources and access to associated traditional knowledge, establishing a system based on FPIC and mutually agreed terms, to ensure fair and equitable sharing of benefits; it also provides for contracts/commitments and transfer of material. c) Specific regulation (2019) for access and control of use, benefits and associated traditional knowledge Executive Decree No. 19 of 26 March 2019 approves the regulation for access and control of the use of biological and genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge (when applicable), for commercial and non-commercial purposes. It includes among its objectives: to regulate access and use, ensure fair and equitable sharing through Benefit-Sharing Agreements, and strengthen institutional capacity and participation of nationals. d) FPIC law for indigenous peoples (mandatory for legislative/administrative measures affecting collective rights) Law No. 37 of 2 August 2016 establishes the right to prior, free and informed consultation and consent; it provides for its mandatory nature and its exercise through traditional institutions and mechanisms of indigenous peoples. e) Protection of traditional knowledge through a special regime of collective rights (intellectual property) Law No. 20 of 26 June 2000 creates a special regime to protect collective rights and traditional knowledge of indigenous peoples, through a registration system (including the associated institutional framework). 2) Administrative and capacity-building measures already carried out a) Legal-institutional strengthening and consultations for ABS/Nagoya MiAMBIENTE reported the completion of a project (3 years) aimed at strengthening legal, policy and institutional capacities for national ABS frameworks, generating trust between users and providers and strengthening the capacities of indigenous peoples and local communities to implement Nagoya, including workshops and participatory consultations. b) Guidance tools to apply FPIC UNDP Panama published an FPIC Guide (October 2024) to guide good practices and compliance with the rules of indigenous congresses in consultation processes. 3) Measures pending or under adjustment to comply with the DSI component and “Cali Fund” (Decision 16/2) Decision 16/2 (COP16, 1 Nov 2024) adopted the multilateral mechanism for benefit-sharing from the use of DSI and the Cali Fund, administered by the UN through the Multi-Partner Trust Fund Office, and invites Parties to align their national ABS measures on DSI to avoid duplication. Implication for Panama: although Panama already has an ABS–FPIC framework (2009/2019 + Law 37), to meet the 2028–2030 target it will have to operationalize in practice (through internal regulations/protocols) elements such as: Procedures to articulate national ABS with the multilateral DSI mechanism (avoid “double charging” or overlaps). Institutional arrangements and protocols to identify beneficiaries, channel benefits and ensure effective participation of indigenous peoples and local communities in accordance with the rules of the multilateral mechanism.

NT10.challenges:
1) From “project EIA” to “risks and impacts across the entire value chain” EIA is a strong instrument for specific projects (with approval and conditions), but the target requires going further: incorporating biodiversity impacts and dependencies in the supply and value chain (raw materials, suppliers, transport, use and useful life), as set out by GBF-T15. The challenge is to adapt capacities and requirements so that companies report on the value chain (not only the project site).

2) Lack of a mandatory and uniform biodiversity reporting standard (quality and comparability) The 2030 Agenda promotes that companies—especially large and transnational ones—integrate sustainability information into their reporting cycles (SDG 12.6), but the practical challenge is to move from voluntary/dispersed disclosure to consistent, auditable and comparable reports. Although there is a voluntary ESG Guide (Latinex/BID Invest) that promotes transparency, its voluntary nature may not guarantee 50% coverage or methodological uniformity.

3) Limited technical capacities to measure biodiversity (data, metrics, baseline) Assessing impacts on biodiversity requires baseline, biological and geospatial indicators, and traceability of pressures (land use, deforestation, fragmentation, species, habitats). In practice, many companies do not have the teams, data or internal methodologies to measure biodiversity rigorously. There is a risk of superficial (narrative) reports without verifiable metrics.

4) Oversight and monitoring: gap between “meeting requirements” and “managing real impacts” The environmental assessment framework relies on oversight processes and on instruments such as PAMA and audits, regulated by specific regulations and administrative procedures. The challenge is framed in ensuring sufficient monitoring (inspection, verification, sanction) so that commitments do not remain only in documentation and so that the results are integrated into corporate public reporting.

5) Economic and market incentives still insufficient to scale up disclosure Reporting impacts and biodiversity management has costs (data, monitoring, audit, traceability). Without financial/fiscal incentives or clear requirements from buyers/financiers, many companies—especially local suppliers in transnational chains—may not prioritize reporting, despite the policy orientation toward cleaner production.

6) Integration of “cleaner production” with biodiversity (not only pollution/efficiency) The National Cleaner Production Policy promotes pollution prevention, efficiency and improvements in productive processes. The challenge is to broaden its effective application toward explicit biodiversity results (land/water footprint, habitat, connectivity, species), and not limit it to energy efficiency, waste or basic compliance.

7) ABS and compliance transparency: limited sectoral scope and low public visibility Panama has a framework for access and control of the use of biological/genetic resources and benefit-sharing (ABS). The challenge is: (i) that relevant companies publicly and verifiably report their ABS compliance (as requested by GBF-T15); and (ii) to coordinate “who reports what” when foreign partners, DSI and/or multilateral agreements are involved (as applicable).

8) Coverage: identify and classify “high-impact and transnational companies” To measure the “50%”, an operational definition is required (sectors, thresholds, criteria) and a verifiable registry of target companies. Without this, it is difficult to measure progress and require compliance in a manner consistent with the SDG 12.6 approach (large/transnational).

9) Consumer information: turning technical reports into useful information for sustainable consumption GBF-T15 requires that companies provide the information necessary to promote sustainable consumption patterns. Its challenge is to standardize labels, environmental claims, traceability and verifiable messages for consumers and make them accessible and comparable across companies/sectors.

10) Interinstitutional coordination and regulatory coherence Effective implementation requires coordination among environmental authorities, the productive sector/competitiveness (cleaner production), the securities/finance market (ESG disclosure) and the competent authority for ABS. The EIA regulation and the ABS framework exist, but the challenge is to integrate them into a “system” that pushes 50% of companies to report under consistent criteria.
NT10.progress: Since 2019, Panama's progress toward the target that at least 50% of high-impact and transformative companies incorporate and disclose information on biodiversity in their value chain (and make transparent compliance with access and benefit-sharing – Access and Benefit-Sharing Clearing-House (ABS Clearing-House) when applicable) is observed mainly along three lines: (1) strengthening voluntary ASG/ESG reporting (environmental, social and governance) and transparency in capital markets, (2) consolidation of public-private frameworks for social responsibility and accountability, and (3) development of capacities and processes for ABS (Nagoya), which connects directly with the “compliance” component required of companies. This approach aligns directly with Target 15 of the Kunming-Montreal Framework, which asks countries to adopt legal/administrative/policy measures so that companies and financial institutions assess and disclose dependencies, impacts, risks and ABS compliance, and also provide relevant information to consumers (CBD, 2022/2023). First, Panama shows concrete progress (although still mostly voluntary) in the creation of tools to standardize corporate disclosure. A relevant milestone is the Guide for the voluntary reporting and disclosure of ASG factors promoted by Latinex with support from BID Invest, which documents that, in a sample of 16 issuers, 56% had published some type of ASG report, and that the market had more than 219 issuers operating through Latinex, with the explicit objective of improving transparency and comparability of information (Bolsa Latinoamericana de Valores (Latinex), 2021). Complementarily, the evolution toward instruments for measuring and recognizing sustainability performance is reflected in the Voluntary Sustainability Index (IVS) (e.g., 2024 edition), which shows the existence of a local scheme to classify issuers by sustainability practices (with the presence of 20 classified issuers, distributed by levels), composed of 55% banks, 20% specialized finance, 10% discretionary consumption, 5% energy, 5% telecommunications and 5% manufacturing, have been classified in the 2024 Ranking (Banistmo, S.A., BAC International Bank, INC, AES Panama Generation, Holdings S. DE R.L., Global Bank Corporation, Banco Promerica de Costa Rica, S.A., MMG Bank Corporation, Caja de Ahorros, Banesco, S.A. Soluciones de Microfinanzas, S.A. (Microserfin), Corporación Interamericana para el Financiamiento de Infraestructura, S.A. (CIFI), Mercantil Banco, S.A., Productos Alimenticios Pascual, S.A., Telecomunicaciones Digitales, S.A., Banco General, S.A., ST. Georges Bank & Company INC., Empresas MELO, Latin_American Kraft Investment, Inc. , Sustainable Urban Revitalization FUND, INC., Banisi, S.A., Prival Bank, S.A.). While this does not yet amount to a national obligation of “biodiversity reporting” for 50% of high-impact companies, it does constitute enabling infrastructure to scale up corporate public disclosure (Latinex,2024). Second, from the State, public-private coordination frameworks have been articulated for social responsibility and accountability, which serve as “scaffolding” to require (or encourage) transparency and due diligence. The National Public-Private Social Responsibility and Human Rights Plan (led from the country's economic institutional framework) structures areas of action, lines of work, and proposes follow-up with periodic publication of reports (which, in terms of this target, is relevant for “public information” and the traceability of commitments, even when the plan is not exclusive to biodiversity) (Ministerio de Comercio e Industrias (MICI), 2022). Third, Panama records progress linked to the access and benefit-sharing (ABS) compliance component that KM-GBF Target 15 itself mentions as part of the transparency package expected for companies “where applicable” (CBD, 2022/2023). In practice, MiAmbiente reported the closing of the strengthening project to implement the Nagoya Protocol, with results aimed at consolidating a national regulatory system on access to biological/genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge, including training processes and consultations (Ministerio de Ambiente de Panamá, s. f.). This progress is key because the national target requires companies to make transparent their ABS compliance when they use genetic resources or traditional knowledge: without clear procedures and institutional capacities, corporate transparency becomes difficult to verify.
NT10.actions: 1) Obligation to assess impacts and manage environmental measures in high-impact projects Law 41 of 1998 (General Environmental Law): requires that activities/works/projects that generate environmental risk have a prior Environmental Impact Study (EIA), and includes stages of evaluation, approval and monitoring/oversight of the environmental program (PAMA), creating a formal obligation for high-impact business projects. Current regulation of the EIA process (Executive Decree No. 1 of 2023): updates definitions, criteria and procedures of the EIA as an “early warning” instrument for decision-making, reinforcing requirements for prevention, mitigation, correction and compensation of impacts. It obliges high-impact companies to identify, assess and manage impacts (including biodiversity when applicable) and leaves documentary traceability (EIA, PAMA, conditions), the basis for corporate reporting and accountability. 2) Environmental audit and compliance instruments (control and verification) Law 41 incorporates the environmental audit as a methodology to evaluate environmental performance and regulatory compliance, enabling verification mechanisms (mandatory or voluntary according to regulations). It facilitates companies with complex operations reporting performance (compliance, gaps, improvement plans), including risks to biodiversity. 3) National Cleaner Production Policy (clean technologies and prevention) National Cleaner Production Policy, approved through Executive Decree 36 of 2007, promotes the minimization of pollution at the source, efficiency and adoption of cleaner practices/technologies in the productive sector. It offers the policy framework for companies (especially high-impact ones) to shift to sustainable production, reducing pressures on ecosystems and biodiversity. 4) National ABS framework for compliance transparency (access to genetic resources and benefits) Executive Decree No. 19 of 2019 regulates access, use and the fair and equitable distribution of benefits derived from the use of biological and genetic resources (ABS), applicable to commercial and non-commercial uses, establishing permits, conditions and obligations. It makes it possible to require companies (e.g., biotechnology, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, applied research) to make transparent that they comply with permits/conditions and benefit-sharing agreements, and to report their due diligence in ABS. 5) FPIC and safeguards for participation of indigenous peoples in decisions that affect them Law 37 of 2016 establishes the right to consultation and free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) for indigenous peoples, mandatory for legislative/administrative measures that affect collective rights. It is a basis for corporate frameworks and practices to incorporate social due diligence (participation, agreements, safeguards), especially when impacts and value chains are related to territories and traditional knowledge. Taken together, Panama already has an enabling “package” that: obliges high-impact companies to assess impacts (SEIA/EIA) and manage measures (PAMA), enables verification (audits) and control, guides toward cleaner production, promotes public disclosure (ESG) in the capital market, and establishes ABS and FPIC rules relevant to transparency and rights. Several of these tools are not a “single regime” of mandatory reporting for all companies, but rather a set of instruments (permits, ABS, FPIC) and disclosure guides (ESG) that, combined, can support the requirement for reporting and due diligence in high-impact sectors.

NT11.challenges: Fragmentation and heterogeneity of data Law 33 of 2018, which establishes the policy for integrated waste management under the “Basura Cero” approach, creates the national legal framework; however, building a baseline requires homogeneous information systems among municipalities and operators (Asamblea Nacional, 2018). The National Integrated Waste Management Plan (PNGIR) recognizes the need to have consolidated data on generation and composition to guide strategic decisions (AAUD, 2017). Territorial dispersion and variability in weighing and recording systems hinder comparability and consistency. Technical limitations in direct measurement and characterization Establishing a robust baseline implies carrying out periodic characterization studies (sampling by socioeconomic strata, seasonal analysis, waste audits). The PNGIR highlights that generation and composition are fundamental inputs for designing reduction and recovery policies (AAUD, 2017). Without systematic measurement, the figures may depend on indirect estimates, which limits precision for monitoring reductions by 2030. Final disposal infrastructure and operational control The effectiveness of the baseline depends on having disposal sites with reliable records of waste entry. Technical reports indicate that waste management in Panama presents operational and infrastructure challenges that affect traceability and control (PNUD, 2023). If dumps or sanitary landfills do not have certified weighing or adequate entry control, national data may underestimate or overestimate real volumes. Measurement of food waste Food waste represents a complex component to quantify, since it occurs in households, retail trade and supply chains. The Food Waste Index Report 2024 of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP, 2024) notes that many countries still lack complete national baselines and that the available data are usually partial or subnational. In Panama, initiatives such as those promoted by FAO to reduce waste in wholesale markets show sectoral progress, but still require integration into a consolidated national baseline (FAO, 2025). Interinstitutional coordination Law 33 of 2018 establishes the general framework, but its implementation involves multiple actors: municipalities, Autoridad de Aseo, Ministerio de Ambiente, health sector and trade (Asamblea Nacional, 2018). The lack of standardized reporting protocols can generate inconsistencies in data and methodologies. Sustained financing and technical capacity PNUD has highlighted that the challenge of waste management in Panama is not only regulatory, but also financial and technical (PNUD, 2023). Building and maintaining a baseline implies investment in: Digital reporting systems. Municipal training. Periodic audits. Certified measurement equipment. Without sustained resources, the baseline can become a one-time exercise without continuity. Behavior change and prevention at source Reducing waste in households and businesses depends on changes in consumption patterns and domestic management. The 2030 Agenda, in its SDG 12.3, establishes the reduction of food waste as a global target (United Nations, 2015). Without awareness campaigns, incentives and separation at source, measurement does not necessarily translate into effective reduction.
NT11.progress: In the period 2019–to date, relevant progress is shown in the regulatory framework and in the generation of technical evidence, although with signs that the national baseline (composition + generation + food waste) is still being built in a fragmented manner through initiatives and specific studies. In regulatory terms, Law 33 of 2018 (Zero Waste Policy) continues to be the enabling framework for structuring the information system and the national waste statistics: it establishes the policy and the framework for action for integrated management and creates reporting/statistics obligations (for example, assigning the Cleaning Authority the role of establishing methods for collecting and publishing national statistical reports). As of 2019, implementation has been strengthened with regulations focused on critical flows, especially single-use plastics: the regulation linked to Law 187 (2020) defines the purpose and objective of the progressive reduction and replacement of these plastics, with an explicit focus on reducing environmental and health impacts. In terms of data availability, there is public evidence that measures the magnitude of the challenge and justifies the need for a baseline: it has been reported that in Panama each person generates between 0.7 and 1.2 kg of waste per day, which is equivalent to ~4,400 tons daily nationwide (estimates cited in analyses of municipal management and the need to know composition). However, the diagnosis itself recognizes gaps regarding what type of waste predominates in many municipalities, which precisely points to the central gap of the target: systematic and comparable characterization to build a national baseline (UNDP, n.d.). In parallel, since 2019 there has been an increase in characterization studies that provide pieces for the baseline, although they still do not amount to a standardized national characterization. During the pandemic, a household per capita generation of 0.409 kg/inhabitant/day was estimated in the province of Panama (with 27% error and standard deviation 0.23) and a relative increase in organic and hazardous waste in the composition was reported (useful findings for adjusting differentiated management, collection routes and treatment) (Requena et al, 2021). Another household-scale characterization study (June 2020) estimated a PPC of 0.667 kg/inhabitant/day and found a physical composition with predominance of food waste (42.86%), followed by plastic (39.28%) and paper (17.86%) (Tello et al, 2020). Although these studies are valuable, their scope (household/specific areas, exceptional pandemic conditions) limits their extrapolation as a national baseline without a broader and periodic statistical campaign. In programmatic/strategic terms, the recent agenda incorporates circular economy and recovery, including explicit lines for organic waste and food (e.g., initiatives and pre-feasibility studies for the recovery/redistribution of food and organic waste within the framework of a sectoral roadmap). This is consistent with the part of the target relating to food waste, but the evidence consulted suggests that the country is making more progress in the design of instruments and initiatives than in a quantified and traceable national baseline of food waste (for example, with harmonized metrics by link in the chain and by type of actor).
NT11.actions: Legal framework for integrated waste management Panama strengthened its regulatory framework through Law 33 of 30 January 2018, which establishes the integrated waste management policy and creates the Urban and Household Cleaning Authority as the entity responsible for the planning and regulation of the collection and final disposal service (National Assembly, 2018). This law promotes source reduction, recycling, recovery and shared responsibility, laying the foundations for generating systematic information on waste generation and composition. National Policy for Integrated Waste Management The Ministry of Environment (MiAMBIENTE) has promoted the National Policy for Integrated Waste Management, aimed at improving planning, strengthening traceability and promoting the circular economy (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The policy includes: Development of inventories and diagnostics. Improvement of national statistics. Promotion of source separation. Strengthening of recycling infrastructure. These actions are essential to consolidate a national baseline of generation and composition. Regulation for reduction of plastics and single-use waste Law 1 of 2018 (plastic bags) and Law 187 of 2020 (single-use plastics) establish progressive reduction measures, generating information on substitution and changes in consumption patterns (National Assembly, 2018; National Assembly, 2020). These regulations contribute to reducing waste sent to final disposal and facilitate the measurement of progress. Strategies linked to food waste Panama has incorporated the food waste reduction approach in coherence with SDG 12.3, which establishes halving global per capita food waste (United Nations, 2015). Although the country is still consolidating a specific national baseline for food waste, food security and organic waste management policies are moving toward: Food use and donation programmes. Composting and organic recovery. Consumer education.
