NT12.challenges: Despite these regulatory and strategic advances, there are no nationally harmonized official data indicating a real quantified reduction (in % or tons) of mismanaged plastic pollution between 2019 and 2025. The diagnosis of the Plataforma de Acción Plásticos uses 2022 as the baseline (380 000 tons/year with 88 % mismanaged), but comparative figures by year are not reported to measure the trend since 2019. This constitutes an important gap for evaluating progress toward national Target 12. Likewise, formal recycling rates are low at the city and national level, and there is still a deficit of separation and recycling infrastructure at scale, with only pilot programs and multisectoral collaboration, but no consolidated industrial infrastructure that would allow large volumes of recovered plastic to be processed (Resilient Cities Network, 2023; Casa Solution, 2025). In the 2019–2025 period, Panama has strengthened the legal framework to reduce single-use plastics, established environmental incentives to promote sustainable practices, and developed a Hoja de Ruta de Acción por los Plásticos that addresses the circular economy. In addition, sectoral measures such as the ban on plastics in protected areas starting in 2026 consolidate the transition toward lower levels of pollution. However, the absence of annual quantitative data on the effective reduction of mismanaged plastics prevents confirming whether Panama has covered half the way toward the 50 % reduction set out in national Target 12. This underscores the need for robust monitoring systems, national waste and recycling statistics, and clear intermediate targets for 2030.
NT12.progress: Panama faces a considerable challenge in plastic waste management. It is estimated that the country generates more than 380 000 tonnes of plastic waste per year, of which approximately 88 % ends up mismanaged (that is, in uncontrolled landfills, open dumps or other environmental destinations such as rivers and coasts) (Plataforma de Acción Plásticos, 2025). Regulatory framework for single-use plastics Since the end of 2019, Panama has implemented and strengthened legislation to restrict single-use plastics, a key component for reducing mismanaged plastic pollution. In July 2019, single-use plastic bags were banned, making Panama the first country in Central America to apply this measure nationally (Waste360, 2019). Subsequently, Law 187 of 2 December 2020 was adopted, which regulates the progressive reduction and replacement of single-use plastics, with phases for the elimination of various items (for example, stirrers, can rings, disposable items) between 2021 and 2023 (The Bocas Breeze, 2020). Additionally, Law 223 of 8 June 2021 established environmental incentives for companies that reduce or sustainably manage plastic pollution and promote the circular economy and the development of recycling industries (Quijano & Associates, 2021). In 2025 the Ministry of Environment reported that Panama has taken “significant steps to reduce plastic pollution” through the gradual elimination of bags, straws and other single-use plastics, in addition to advancing towards a circular economy with a climate focus (MiAmbiente, 2025). As of January 2026, the prohibition on the use of plastics and foam in protected areas of the country is scheduled, including disposable bottles, cups, plates and non-biodegradable bags, which will strengthen the protection of sensitive ecosystems (MiAmbiente, 2025). Circular economy strategies and recycling infrastructure In 2025 Panama launched the Hoja de Ruta de Acción por los Plásticos, a national strategy to address plastic pollution and accelerate the transition towards a circular economy for plastics, with the participation of the public sector, civil society, academia and international cooperation. This roadmap proposes more ambitious targets than National Target 12, such as reducing mismanaged plastic pollution by 80 % by 2040 (Plataforma de Acción Plásticos, 2025). Media and technical observer projections also point to efforts to transform up to 58 % of plastic management through recycling, reduction, innovation and better disposal systems by 2040, which could translate into avoiding up to 235 000 tonnes of plastic waste polluting the environment if implemented effectively (Casa Solution, 2025). Local examples of recycling and reuse include initiatives such as Panama City recycling around 60 tonnes of marine plastic by transforming it into urban furniture, although these figures remain very low compared with the total generated; in the city, only 2 % of the 34 000 ton/month of solid waste is recycled (Resilient Cities Network, 2023).
NT12.actions: 1) Progressive elimination of single-use plastics Panama adopted Law 1 of 19 January 2018, which regulates and progressively prohibits the use of polyethylene plastic bags in commercial establishments, marking the beginning of the transition toward reusable or biodegradable alternatives (Asamblea Nacional, 2018a). Subsequently, Law 187 of 2 December 2020 expanded the regulatory scope by establishing the reduction and progressive substitution of single-use plastic products, such as containers and utensils, promoting alternative and reusable materials (Asamblea Nacional, 2020). These measures constitute direct legal instruments to reduce the generation of plastic waste at the source. 2) Comprehensive waste management and circular economy framework Law 33 of 30 January 2018, which establishes the comprehensive waste management policy under the “Basura Cero” approach, promotes the reduction, reuse, recycling and recovery of solid waste, including plastics (Asamblea Nacional, 2018b). The National Comprehensive Waste Management Plan (PNGIR) reinforces the need to strengthen recycling infrastructure, improve source separation systems and increase material recovery rates (AAUD, 2017). 3) National Policy on Comprehensive Waste Management and circular economy The Ministry of Environment (MiAMBIENTE) has promoted the National Policy on Comprehensive Waste Management, aimed at consolidating the circular economy approach, encouraging the recovery of recyclable materials and shared responsibility (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). This instrument recognizes that reducing plastic pollution requires not only regulation, but transformation of the production model. 4) Environmental education and awareness campaigns The State has promoted citizen awareness campaigns on plastic reduction and source separation, in line with international commitments on marine pollution (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). Strengthening environmental culture is key to reducing mismanaged plastic pollution. 5) Strengthening recycling infrastructure The implementation of Law 33 and the PNGIR contemplates the strengthening of: Collection centers. Municipal recycling programs. Formalization of recyclers. Public-private partnerships for material recovery. These elements are fundamental to reducing plastic waste sent for final disposal (AAUD, 2017).

NT13.challenges: Consolidation of a comprehensive and coherent regulatory framework Although Panama is a Party to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, full implementation requires harmonizing environmental, agricultural, health, and trade legislation under a unified biosafety system (CBD, 2000). The challenge lies in avoiding regulatory overlap and ensuring coherence among risk assessment, import authorizations, and monitoring mechanisms. Strengthening technical and scientific capacities The Protocol requires rigorous scientific assessments based on the precautionary principle (CBD, 2000). However, the development of national capacities in: Molecular biology, Environmental risk assessment, Bioinformatics, Post-release monitoring, requires sustained investment in human resources and specialized laboratories. The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework also recognizes the need to strengthen scientific capacities and technology transfer (CBD, 2022). Complex interinstitutional coordination Biosafety involves multiple sectors: environment, agriculture, health, foreign trade, and customs. The lack of permanent coordination mechanisms can generate gaps in: Control of LMO imports. Oversight of experimental trials. Post-authorization follow-up. The Cartagena Protocol underscores the importance of clearly designated competent authorities and coordinated administrative mechanisms (CBD, 2000). Public participation and social consensus The target establishes that the strategy must be “agreed upon.” The Protocol promotes public participation and access to information on living modified organisms (CBD, 2000). The challenge consists of: Guaranteeing informed participatory processes. Reducing misinformation about biotechnology. Balancing scientific innovation with social concerns. Integration with the Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) regime The use of biotechnology may involve genetic resources and traditional knowledge. Panama has specific regulations on access and benefit-sharing (National Assembly, 2019). The challenge consists of ensuring coherence among: Biosafety (Cartagena), ABS (Nagoya), Rights of indigenous peoples, New technologies such as gene editing. Post-release monitoring and traceability The establishment of monitoring systems following the commercial release of LMOs requires: Standardized technical protocols. Laboratory infrastructure. Interoperable information systems. Without these elements, it is difficult to verify environmental impacts or apply corrective measures. Sustainable financing Effective implementation of the Protocol depends on financial resources for: Training. Scientific equipment. Regulatory development. Information systems. The CBD has indicated that resource mobilization and international cooperation are key to strengthening the implementation of biodiversity instruments (CBD, 2022). Accelerated evolution of biotechnology New techniques such as gene editing (CRISPR) pose regulatory challenges that are not always clearly contemplated in traditional biosafety frameworks. The challenge consists of updating regulatory frameworks without slowing responsible scientific innovation.
NT13.progress: From 2019 to date (December 2025), Panama’s progress linked to the implementation of the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (biosafety) shows progress above all in institutional strengthening, updating/operation of sectoral committees, technical training, regulatory public consultation, and practical application of risk analysis. Verifiable progress (2019–2025): 1) Enabling legal framework and interinstitutional governance Panama has the formal approval of the Protocol and a national framework law that creates the biosafety institutional framework: Law 72 of 2001: approves the Cartagena Protocol. (Legislative Assembly of Panama, 2001). Law 48 of 2002: creates the National Biosafety Commission (CNB), defines its composition (includes MIDA, MINSA, MiAmbiente, MICI, etc.), establishes a Technical Secretariat, and explicitly incorporates the logic of risk analysis, follow-up/monitoring, and coordination with sectoral committees. (Legislative Assembly of Panama, 2002). This is key because the target requires a legal/administrative framework that enables specific measures and coordination; Law 48 already contemplates instruments (sectoral committees, Technical Secretariat, risk analysis, participation, and interinstitutional liaison) that function as the “architecture” of the system. 2) Capacity strengthening and technical cooperation (2019–2021) Starting in 2019, training and strengthening activities were recorded, consistent with “strengthened national capacities”: On the Panama Biosafety Project platform, for example, the “Launch Workshop of the Agreement with the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB)” (15 Oct 2019) is recorded as a milestone of technical cooperation. (Panama Biosafety Project, 2019). In 2021, strengthening processes are reported, with participation of the National Biosafety Commission (CNB) and three sectoral committees (agriculture, health, and environment). (Panama Biosafety Project, 2021). These milestones support that, since 2019, there has been investment in technical capacity (risk analysis, management/use of GMOs/LMOs, exchange of experiences), an essential component of the Protocol. 3) Regulatory measure “under development/consultation”: genetically modified foods (approx. 2023) Progress aligned with “administrative and policy frameworks” is the public consultation led by MINSA to review a draft resolution on genetically modified foods, whose stated purpose is to regulate Law 48. (Ministry of Health of Panama, n.d.). Although the page does not by itself amount to a final promulgated regulation, it does show a process of updating/regulation and participation (a “consensual” component in the procedural sense) linked to the biosafety regime. 4) Measure “in operation”: risk assessment + formal decision/recommendation on a genetically modified organism (GMO) (2024–2025) A strong indicator of practical implementation is the CNB Resolution (published in the Official Gazette, 25 April 2025) where: It is recorded that the Sectoral Committees on Health and Environment processed information and carried out risk assessment; The importation and commercialization of Aedes aegypti OX5034 (GMO) is recommended and an Annual Monitoring and Follow-up Plan 2025 is required with a deadline (30 calendar days after publication). (National Biosafety Commission for GMOs, 2025). This document demonstrates, with date and institutional traceability, that Panama applies (i) risk assessment, (ii) administrative decision, (iii) follow-up/monitoring conditions, and (iv) intersectoral coordination; all of this is consistent with the operational core of the Cartagena Protocol (risk assessment/management and post-authorization measures). 5) “Institutionalized” measure: functioning of the CNB and sectoral committees (current structure and publicly described) As of 2026, Panama has carried out the first authorization for commercial release of a GMO contained in Resolution 006-2025 after having carried out an exhaustive environmental risk assessment process. Added to this is the authorization for confined research contained in Resolution 007-2026. The National Biosafety Commission is also working on the new regulation of the resolution on new breeding techniques and has closed the technical review process and the advice of international counterparts. Within the framework of the creation of the National Bioeconomy Strategy, together with the United Nations University and the Latin America Office for Biotechnology, a specialized training and capacity-strengthening program has also been formed for the CNB as well as for the sectoral commissions on environment, agriculture, and health [E1]. The CNB remains in permanent session in view of the significant number of applications received between 2023 and 2026, holding monthly meetings. The three sectoral commissions have remained in periodic sessions associated with 1 application for commercial release, 1 application for confined research and importation, 2 applications for review of follow-up and monitoring plans, and one application for export of GMOs. The CNB also continues with the follow-up of previous research applications such as the one associated with CNB Resolution 08-2017 by which the authorization granted by the Agricultural Biosafety Sectoral Committee to the Panama United States Commission for the Eradication and Prevention of the Screwworm - COPEG is endorsed to carry out the first phase of research on the genetically modified Screwworm Fly Cochlyomya hominivorax. In this regard, it has also advanced with the guide for the management of unauthorized transboundary movement of genetically modified organisms at the request of the national regulatory agencies. As opportunities for improvement, the CNB will work during 2026 on the guides and procedure manuals for processing applications and the flowcharts necessary for guidance to applicants, while at the same time increasing its associated capacity in reducing evaluation times and strengthening the technical secretariat. [E1] Bioeconomy in Panama: Senacyt leads national strategy toward the sustainable future – Panama news Daily newspaper of Panama Novedades This is consistent with an “implementation” that does not depend only on old laws, but on operational mechanisms that remain active and are articulated to process applications and manage risks.
NT13.actions: 1) Ratification and incorporation of the Cartagena Protocol Panama is Party to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, which constitutes the international legal framework for regulating the transboundary movement of living modified organisms (LMOs) (CBD, 2000). Ratification implies national obligations to develop regulatory systems and mechanisms for risk assessment and management. 2) Environmental institutional framework and competent authority The Ministry of Environment (MiAMBIENTE) acts as the national competent authority on biodiversity and biosafety, in coherence with the General Environmental Law (Law 41 of 1998) and its institutional evolution (National Assembly, 1998). This framework provides the basis for integrating biosafety within the national environmental system. 3) Creation and strengthening of technical capacities Through international cooperation and projects financed by the Global Environment Facility (FMAM/GEF), Panama has strengthened technical capacities for: Scientific risk assessment. Training of specialists. Participation in the Biosafety Clearing-House (CBD, 2000). 4) Integration with the access and benefit-sharing (ABS) regime The national framework for access to genetic resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits, established through specific regulations, complements the implementation of the Cartagena Protocol, ensuring coherence between biosafety and ABS (National Assembly, 2019). This allows the development and use of biotechnology to respect sovereign rights over biological resources. 5) Intersectoral coordination (environment–agriculture–health–trade) The safe management of biotechnology requires coordination among: Environmental authorities. Phytosanitary and agricultural authorities. Health sector. Customs and foreign trade. This multisectoral approach is consistent with the obligations of the Cartagena Protocol (CBD, 2000). 6) Public participation and transparency The Cartagena Protocol establishes the importance of public information and participation in decisions related to LMOs (CBD, 2000). Panama has incorporated public consultation mechanisms within environmental regulatory processes, strengthening the legitimacy of the national strategy.

NT14.challenges: 1) Complete inventory and comparability: identify 100% of incentives A central challenge is to define, locate, and classify all incentives (fiscal, budgetary, credit, regulatory, tariffs, exemptions, fuels/energy, agriculture, fisheries, transport, land-use planning, etc.) under a single methodology to decide whether they are “harmful” or “positive.” This usually requires budget traceability, review of regulations, and assessment of direct and indirect effects on biodiversity (CBD Secretariat, n.d.). 2) Measuring harm and prioritization: identify “the most harmful” Even once identified, the challenge is to quantify which incentives generate the greatest pressure (deforestation, overfishing, pollution, unplanned expansion, fragmentation), and to prioritize “the most harmful” with evidence. The target emphasizes starting with the most harmful, which requires impact assessments and transparent prioritization criteria. 3) Political economy: sectoral resistance and transition costs Eliminating or reforming subsidies can affect competitiveness, production costs, and prices, generating resistance from productive actors. 4) “Fair and effective processes”: social safeguards, consultation, and legitimacy The target requires fairness and effectiveness. In practice, this implies designing participatory processes (private sector, producers, local governments, civil society) that reduce conflict and ensure legitimacy. The Pacto de Panamá con la Naturaleza underscores the need for implementation with citizen contributions and coordination to address environmental crises, which reinforces the focus on inclusive processes (Gobierno de Panamá, 2025; MiAMBIENTE, 2025). 5) Interinstitutional coordination and regulatory-fiscal coherence Incentive reform is usually dispersed among economic and sectoral entities (MEF, MICI, MIDA, ARAP, municipalities, etc.) and not only in the environmental authority. Without a robust coordination mechanism, there may be partial reforms that contradict each other or shift the harm to another sector (“leakage” of the impact). 6) Increase positive incentives by 30%: financial capacity and “additionality” Increasing positive incentives (payments for ecosystem services, restoration, conservation, bioeconomy, green finance) faces two challenges: Mobilizing new resources (not just relabeling existing spending) and Guaranteeing additionality (that the incentive generates measurable conservation/sustainable use results). Panama has promoted instruments such as Fondo Panamá Natural and the reactivation/operation of Fondo Reforesta, but scaling them requires financial sustainability, allocation rules, and results monitoring (MiAMBIENTE, 2025; MiAMBIENTE, 2025; Asamblea Nacional, 2017). 7) Monitoring and verification: demonstrate “50% reformed/eliminated” and “30% increased” The target implies verifiable metrics: which incentives were identified (complete universe), which were reformed/eliminated (and their mitigated “level of harm”), how much positive incentives grew, and what results they achieved. This requires a monitoring system with indicators and budgetary/administrative evidence, consistent with sustainable financing frameworks and accountability. The Marco de Financiamiento Sostenible de Panamá illustrates the effort to structure criteria and reporting of sustainable financial instruments, which can support the traceability of positive incentives (MEF, 2024). 8) Risk of unintended impacts: substitution by “equivalent” incentives When a subsidy is eliminated, another instrument may arise that, without explicit intention, reproduces the same effect (e.g., exemptions, soft loans, or infrastructure that encourages expansion into sensitive areas). Therefore, the target emphasizes effective reforms, and the challenge is to design controls to prevent the “reappearance” of the harmful incentive under another format.
NT14.progress: 1. Regulatory and public policy framework The National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2018-2050 (EPANB) had already established National Target 16 to “eliminate or reform incentives harmful to biodiversity and promote positive incentives for its conservation” and defined indicators such as “number of harmful subsidies identified and eliminated” and “number of positive incentives created” (Ministry of Environment, 2018). Starting in 2019, this orientation is reinforced in several instruments: The National Environment Strategy 2021-2031 (ENA), approved by Executive Decree No. 12 of 2022, incorporates as a line of action “promote National Target 16 of the EPANB” and includes as an indicator the number of beneficiaries of incentives for biodiversity conservation compared to the number of applicants, assigning resources and identifying the Ministry of Environment (MiAmbiente) and the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) as responsible entities (MiAmbiente, 2022; UNDP & MiAmbiente, 2022). The Long-Term Strategy for Low-Emission Development (ELP 2050) and the second nationally determined contribution (NDC2) refer to the need to align fiscal instruments with the ecological transition, mentioning the EPANB and the ENA as frameworks for reviewing economic and financial incentives (Government of Panama, 2024). Since 2019 Panama has participated in the UNDP BIOFIN initiative. In 2023-2025 progress was made in the preparation of a Biodiversity Financing Plan, which analyzes public and private spending, identifies gaps and proposes instruments such as the review of subsidies and the expansion of positive incentives (UNDP & MiAmbiente, 2023, 2025). Taken together, these instruments do not yet mean the elimination of 50% of harmful subsidies, but they do create the policy architecture needed to identify such subsidies and scale up positive incentives. 2. Progress in identifying and reforming harmful subsidies Although there is not yet a sectoral and quantified inventory of subsidies harmful to biodiversity, important steps can be observed: National Registry of Incentives and Subsidies (RENIS) In 2025 a legislative initiative was introduced proposing the creation of RENIS under the MEF. The registry would be responsible for periodically evaluating the “profitability” and relevance of all incentives and subsidies, and would make it possible to modify or eliminate those that fail to meet the objectives for which they were created, lack economic justification or generate market distortions and inequity (Panamá América, 2025). Although the bill is general in nature (not exclusive to biodiversity), the creation of a registry and periodic evaluations is a key step in being able to identify and clean up subsidies with negative impacts on ecosystems (for example, in energy, agriculture or fisheries). Public discussion on the rationalization of subsidies Various economic analyses and official statements between 2024-2025 recommend “touching subsidies” and targeting them to those who really need them, emphasizing the evaluation of their fiscal cost and their alignment with equity and efficiency (La Estrella de Panamá, 2025; TVN, 2024). These debates constitute a favorable context for reorienting subsidies that encourage practices that degrade biodiversity. Fisheries subsidies In 2025 Panama ratified the World Trade Organization Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies through Law 470 of 29 May 2025, committing to prohibit subsidies that support illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing and fishing of overexploited stocks, as well as certain operations on the high seas (Destino Panamá, 2025). Although the agreement is global, its implementation in Panama will imply reviewing and eventually eliminating fisheries subsidies that negatively affect marine biodiversity, in line with the national target. Since 2019, more progress has been made in the creation of tools (plans, registries, ratification of agreements) than in the presentation of concrete data on percentages of subsidies already eliminated. 3. Progress in positive incentives for conservation and sustainable use Clear figures exist in the expansion of positive incentives, especially in payments for environmental services and in the certification of sustainable productive practices. 3.1. Environmental Economic Incentives Program (PIEA), Panama Canal The PIEA of the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) has grown notably in the last decade and its results have been consolidated in the 2019-2024 period: In the Canal watershed, 17 628 ha have been established under reforestation, agroforestry and silvopastoral systems schemes; more than 6.2 million trees have been planted and 6 150 ha of forest are maintained under payment for environmental services (PES) schemes (Panama Canal Authority, 2024). These incentives have benefited approximately 16 485 people, organized in around 148 communities, with a cumulative investment close to 41 million balboas, and an annual payment of B/.130 per hectare of protected forest, considered the highest PES in the region (Panama Canal Authority, 2024; El Capital Financiero, 2025; Hub.com.pa, 2025). This is an emblematic case of a positive economic incentive that promotes forest conservation, the restoration of productive landscapes and the improvement of rural livelihoods, cited internationally as an example of payment for ecosystem services (OECD, 2025). 3.2. Biodiversity-positive production systems The project “Sustainable Production Systems and Conservation of Biodiversity” (SPCB), implemented by MiAmbiente with support from the World Bank and closed in 2019, continued generating impacts in subsequent years by leaving capacities and incentives in place: 1 611 ha of coffee, cocoa, banana and vegetable farms in buffer zones of protected areas were certified under environmental and biodiversity standards; of these, 626 ha received MiAmbiente’s “biodiversity-friendly products” certification, 77 ha organic certification and 908 ha a denomination of origin with sustainability criteria (World Bank, 2020). 30 productive subprojects were implemented and 5 commercial alliances were established for biodiversity-friendly products, directly or indirectly benefiting 152 119 people (World Bank, 2020). These instruments generate market incentives for productive practices compatible with conservation, aligned with the part of the target that requires “increasing positive incentives by 30%”. 3.3. Other financial and policy instruments The Water, Protected Areas and Wildlife Trust Fund, created in 2017 and strengthened with estimated annual contributions of 7 million dollars, has made it possible to finance the management of the National System of Protected Areas, functioning as a mechanism of financial incentives for conservation (World Bank, 2020). In 2025, the Development Bank of Latin America (CAF) approved a loan of 300 million dollars to promote sustainable forest management and the green economy in Panama, with components aimed at financial incentives for activities that reduce deforestation and improve ecosystem resilience (CAF, 2025). 4. Assessment Strong progress in policy and financing frameworks, but weak data on the magnitude of harmful subsidies and their effective reform. No reports were found indicating percentages of 50% of harmful subsidies reformed or eliminated. Real growth in positive incentives, especially through the PIEA and other PES and product certification schemes, with specific figures on hectares intervened, families benefited and amounts invested. This points in the direction of “+30% positive incentives”. The 2019-2025 period can be interpreted as a phase of preparation and expansion of pilot instruments, rather than full compliance with the target.
NT14.actions: 1) Incorporation of the approach in the Pacto de Panamá por la Naturaleza The Pacto de Panamá por la Naturaleza recognizes the need to review economic incentives that negatively affect biodiversity and strengthen positive financial mechanisms aligned with climate, biodiversity and land (Gobierno de Panamá, 2022). This policy instrument constitutes the strategic basis for advancing in the identification and reform of harmful subsidies. 2) Global Biodiversity Framework and national alignment Panama has aligned its national targets with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, particularly with Target 18, which establishes the progressive reduction of harmful incentives and the increase of positive incentives (CDB, 2022). This alignment implies: Inventories of fiscal and sectoral incentives. Assessment of the environmental impacts of subsidies. Gradual reforms in productive sectors. 3) Creation and strengthening of positive financial instruments Panama has promoted innovative environmental financing mechanisms such as: Fondo Panamá Natural, aimed at channeling resources toward conservation and climate resilience (Gobierno de Panamá, 2023). Fondo Reforesta, focused on forest restoration and degraded lands. Carbon markets and payments for ecosystem services. These instruments constitute positive incentives that promote conservation and sustainable use. 4) Regulatory framework for forest incentives and restoration Forest legislation and restoration programs establish incentives for reforestation and sustainable management, contributing to redirecting resources toward activities compatible with biodiversity (Asamblea Nacional, 1994). 5) Integration with climate policies and green transition The Ley Marco de Cambio Climático y Transición Verde establishes bases for reorienting incentives toward low-carbon and sustainable activities, reducing economic distortions that favor environmentally harmful practices (Asamblea Nacional, 2022). 6) Transparency and budget evaluation The review of subsidies requires budgetary and fiscal analyses. Panama has progressively incorporated environmental assessments within public planning, in coherence with the integration of biodiversity into decision-making (CDB, 2022).

NT15.challenges: 1) Organized crime, illegal logging, and territorial control in “hotspots” A determining challenge is the intensification of illegal logging associated with criminal groups and extraction/trade networks, especially in areas such as Darién, where pressure and operational complexity raise the cost of surveillance and prosecution (MiAMBIENTE, 2024). In addition, official reports have warned of significant losses and pressures in critical provinces, suggesting that territorial control and the focus on “hotspots” will continue to be a structural challenge (MiAMBIENTE, 2024a). 2) Land-use change and agricultural expansion as a persistent driver Although the target focuses on “illegal deforestation,” in practice the boundary between illegality, occupation, and land-use conversion can be diffuse. National reports recognize the expansion of the agricultural/livestock frontier and poor practices as relevant pressures on forests (CBD Secretariat, 2014). This complicates “zero illegality” because part of the loss is connected with productive dynamics and settlements that require comprehensive solutions (planning, incentives, control, and economic alternatives). 3) Land tenure, territorial conflicts, and local governance Tenure insecurity, conflicts over access to land and resources, and invasions/occupations increase deforestation and hinder law enforcement. Specialized literature on forests and REDD+ documents that lack of tenure clarity and illegal activities are factors that weaken forest governance and complicate sustained results (Wiley, 2013; FAO, 2010). In Panama, it has also been documented that territorial conflicts and pressures on territories with high forest cover can increase threats from illegal logging and land grabbing (Ucpress, 2018). 4) Operational capacity for oversight and prosecution of environmental crime Achieving “zero” implies not only detection, but also response, seizure, sanction, follow-up, and deterrence. Even with institutional offensives, the challenge is to sustain personnel, logistics, territorial presence, and coordination with justice and security in order to break criminal chains (MiAMBIENTE, 2024). If sanction is not timely or networks are not dismantled, illegality tends to shift to other areas (“balloon effect”). 5) Traceability and control of the timber supply chain Even with control actions in the field, if illegal timber manages to enter commercial channels, illegal deforestation persists. The national expansion of traceability and forest control systems is a relevant advance, but it also entails challenges: full coverage, interoperability, control on roads/ports, and effective verification at points of sale and processing (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). A robust traceability system requires compliance and oversight to prevent falsification or timber “laundering.” 6) Monitoring: from maps to early warnings and rapid response Panama has been strengthening forest monitoring frameworks in the REDD+ context; however, technical documents from UN-REDD indicate that an early warning system is not automatically mandatory and requires specific design, resources, and response protocols (UN-REDD, 2021). The challenge is not only to “see” the change (satellite), but to react quickly, verify in the field, and activate sanctioning processes. 7) Economic incentives: making the forest “worth more standing” than converted The target requires positioning forests as productive and environmental assets with benefits greater than their conversion. The challenge is to scale incentives (results-based payments, PSA, carbon, funds) and ensure that they reach producers and communities in pressure zones, with clear rules and low transaction costs. REDD+ experiences highlight that, in addition to illegality, there are pressures from slash-and-burn agriculture, expansion of development, and other factors that demand economic and governance solutions (Ecosystem Marketplace, 2021). 8) Climate risks and fires that worsen degradation and facilitate conversion Droughts, fires, and extreme events can degrade forests and facilitate land-use changes. In Panama, the combination of deforestation and fires has been identified as important challenges for the country (La Estrella de Panamá, 2020). This adds a risk management and fire prevention component as part of the “zero illegal deforestation” strategy.
NT15.progress: Between 2019 and the present, Panama has advanced on two key fronts to move closer to the goal of zero illegal deforestation: (a) regulatory and operational strengthening of control (including traceability) and (b) oversight and sanction actions. However, the available evidence also shows that pressure on forests and the illegal timber trade persist, so the country is still in a consolidation phase to achieve total and effective coverage in 100% of concessions and permits. In terms of traceability and control, the country has a regulatory framework that supports the Sistema de Trazabilidad y Control Forestal (STCF) (linked to the management of timber flow and the control of transport and commercialization), and has been promoting its progressive implementation as a forest governance tool (Organización Internacional de las Maderas Tropicales [OIMT/ITTO], 2023; STCF Panamá, n. d.). In addition, evaluations of forest projects report that Panama developed and validated pilot monitoring/control systems in critical regions (e.g., East Panama and Darién) and strengthened institutional capacities (for example, training of technical staff and coordination with mechanisms such as forest oversight and responsible purchasing networks) (OIMT/ITTO, 2023). At the operational level, the STCF has a digital platform for user access/registration, which is consistent with the objective of traceability throughout the chain (STCF Panamá, n. d.). Since 2024–2025, more restrictive regulatory measures associated with risks of illegality and control weaknesses have been observed. For example, decisions were issued to provisionally suspend the granting of forest transport guides originating from natural forest and/or managed natural regeneration areas (República de Panamá, Ministerio de Ambiente, 2024a) and, subsequently, the suspension for five years of forest harvesting permits in natural forests nationwide was announced, based on powers under forest legislation, the measure was adopted through Resolution No. DM 0587-2024 of 10 December 2024, ‘by which regulatory measures are adopted on forest harvesting in natural forests of the State Forest Heritage nationwide and other provisions are issued (MiAmbiente, 2025a). These measures suggest a shift toward the principle of regulatory precaution against illegal logging, while traceability, control and verification instruments are strengthened. Regarding results and data on cover loss, international reference indicators show that Panama continues to record tree cover loss (which does not automatically equate to “illegal deforestation,” but is a sign of pressure and land use/cover change). Using the standard Global Forest Watch threshold (>30% canopy cover), Panama reported approximate tree cover loss of 33,994 ha (2019), 27,314 ha (2020), 24,390 ha (2021), 17,327 ha (2022) and 25,086 ha (2023) (Global Forest Watch, 2024a; Global Forest Watch, 2024b). For 2024, Global Forest Watch indicates natural forest losses on the order of 17 thousand ha (Global Forest Watch, 2025). These data are useful for contextualizing the challenge: even with regulatory strengthening and control platforms, forest cover loss and risks of illegality remain relevant and require real-time control and complete traceability at the national scale. Finally, oversight provides direct evidence of the persistence of the problem: in recent years, operations, seizures, sanctions and complaints linked to the trade/transport of timber without the proper documentation have been reported, including fines and criminal actions for trafficking in protected timber species (MiAmbiente, 2024a; MiAmbiente, 2025b; MiAmbiente, 2025c). This pattern is consistent with a scenario where the State increases control action, but still faces gaps (inspection capacity, complete traceability in all permits, and effective control of the chain) to achieve the goal of “zero” illegal logging in a verifiable manner.
NT15.actions: 1) Forest Monitoring System and satellite technology Panama has strengthened its National Forest Monitoring System (SNMF) within the framework of the REDD+ Strategy, incorporating satellite monitoring tools and periodic reports on forest cover (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). Monitoring makes it possible to: Detect changes in forest cover. Identify areas of illegal deforestation. Generate early warnings. 2) REDD+ Strategy and results-based payments Panama developed its National REDD+ Strategy, aimed at reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, improving governance and promoting sustainable management (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). In 2023, Panama received results-based payments under the Green Climate Fund for emission reductions associated with the forest sector, strengthening economic incentives to conserve forests (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). 3) Reforesta Fund and forest restoration Law 69 of 2017 created the Reforesta Panamá Fund, intended to finance forest restoration and sustainable management programs (National Assembly, 2017). This instrument promotes the forest as a viable economic alternative to its conversion. 4) Panama Nature Pledge The Pacto de Panamá por la Naturaleza (Nature Pledge) establishes commitments to achieve targets of zero illegal deforestation and strengthen the economic and environmental value of forests (Government of Panama, 2022). This pledge integrates climate, biodiversity and sustainable development under a green economy vision. 5) Positive economic incentives (carbon markets and ecosystem services) Panama has promoted mechanisms such as: Carbon markets. Payments for ecosystem services. Fondo Panamá Natural. These instruments strengthen the economic value of standing forests, aligning conservation with financial benefits (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). 6) Environmental control and enforcement MiAMBIENTE carries out forest control operations and applies sanctions for illegal logging in accordance with current regulations (National Assembly, 1994; National Assembly, 1998). Strengthening enforcement is key to achieving the goal of zero illegality. 7) Integration with land-use planning and planning The incorporation of conservation criteria in land-use planning and watershed management plans reduces unplanned agricultural expansion and pressure on forests.

NT16.challenges: 1) Identification and precise mapping of organic soils One of the main challenges is to have updated inventories and detailed mapping of peatlands and organic soils. At the global level, the IPCC (2019) notes that measuring soil carbon requires standardized methodologies and solid baselines to assess real changes. Likewise, the Ramsar Convention highlights the importance of identifying and delimiting wetlands for their effective protection (Ramsar Secretariat, 2016). Without clear technical delimitation, measuring the “70% protected” is complex. 2) Pressure from land-use change Agricultural expansion and wetland drainage represent significant threats to organic soils. The IPCC (2022) warns that the conversion of wetlands and peatlands releases large amounts of stored carbon, contributing to climate change. The CDB (2022) also recognizes that the degradation of carbon-rich ecosystems compromises biodiversity and climate targets. 3) Monitoring of soil organic carbon (SOC) Increasing organic carbon by 10% requires: Scientific baseline. Periodic sampling protocols. Long-term monitoring systems. FAO emphasizes that soil organic carbon varies according to management practices, climate and texture, so its monitoring requires technical continuity (FAO, 2017). 4) Limited adoption of agroforestry and silvopastoral practices Agroforestry is recognized as an effective practice to increase soil carbon and improve resilience (FAO, 2020). However, its adoption faces barriers such as initial costs, access to financing and limited technical assistance. The IPCC (2019) highlights that sustainable management practices can increase carbon storage, but require adequate incentives. 5) Interinstitutional coordination The protection of wetlands and agricultural soils involves multiple sectors: environment, agriculture, land-use planning and climate change. The Global Biodiversity Framework (CDB, 2022) emphasizes intersectoral integration as an enabling condition for success. 6) Vulnerability to climate change Prolonged droughts and fires can degrade organic soils and accelerate their oxidation. The IPCC (2022) warns that rising temperature and extreme events increase risks of carbon loss in ecosystems rich in organic matter. 7) Sustainable financing The restoration and monitoring of organic soils require constant investment in research and training. The CDB (2022) recognizes that resource mobilization is key to achieving targets related to restoration and climate mitigation.
NT16.progress: Since 2019, Panama’s progress toward the protection of organic soils and the increase of soil organic carbon is evident in three main lines: (1) identification and inventory of wetlands and peatlands, (2) strengthening of wetland conservation and restoration frameworks (including mangroves), and (3) development of technical and sectoral bases to increase soil organic carbon in agricultural and livestock systems. First, Panama has advanced in the identification and national estimation of wetlands, which constitutes the basis for recognizing and protecting organic soils. The Ministry of Environment reported a national estimate of wetlands of 4,063.004 km² (406,300.4 ha), noting that the country has strengthened its inventory through new technologies and spatial analysis tools; in addition, an increase has been perceived in the coverage of mangrove vegetation, due to monitoring and restoration efforts, reporting 187,064 Ha in mangroves, which means at least 10, 000 more hectares in relation to the studies carried out in the year 2012 (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). This progress makes it possible to have a national reference to guide conservation actions and land-use planning linked to wetlands and associated organic soils. Additionally, Panama maintains significant wetland coverage under the Ramsar Convention, with 285,487 ha declared as Ramsar Sites, which represents an important component of international recognition and management of these ecosystems (Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, n.d.). Although Ramsar designation does not automatically equate to strict protection, it does constitute a formal framework for management and periodic reporting that contributes to the conservation of wetlands with organic soils. A key and recent advance in this line is the explicit start of the process for the identification of peatlands. In 2024, the National Secretariat of Science, Technology and Innovation announced a research project aimed at creating for the first time the national inventory of peatlands of Panama, as well as updating the country’s wetland map (SENACYT, 2024). This milestone is particularly relevant for the target, since fulfillment of the objective of “70% of organic soils protected” depends on the delimitation and formal characterization of peatlands, a type of organic soil that historically had not been systematically inventoried in Panama. Second, progress is observed in the conservation and restoration of wetlands, especially mangroves, which are ecosystems with organic soils of high climate and biodiversity relevance. Since 2020, Panama has had the Manual de técnicas de restauración para áreas degradadas de manglar, prepared by the Ministry of Environment with support from UNDP and published as a regulatory reference, which standardizes approaches to hydrological rehabilitation, active restoration and monitoring (UNDP & MiAMBIENTE, 2020/2021). This instrument has been disseminated through official platforms (SINIA and Transparencia Climática), strengthening national technical capacity to restore and conserve coastal organic soils. From the scientific perspective, the priority given to mangroves is supported by robust evidence showing that these ecosystems are among the richest in carbon at the tropical level, with a significant proportion stored in soils (Donato et al., 2011). Therefore, mangrove conservation and restoration actions contribute directly both to the protection of organic soils and to climate change mitigation. Third, Panama has advanced in the development of technical bases to measure and manage soil organic carbon in agricultural lands and grasslands, a necessary condition to assess the objective of increasing SOC by at least 10%. In 2024, the digital map of organic carbon content in Panama’s soils was published, prepared from 837 soil profiles corresponding to the 0–30 cm layer, a generalized linear model was fitted through regression Kriging interpolation, resulting in the carbon map that predicts a stock of 308,26 Teragrams of soil organic carbon in Panama (Villarreal-Núñez & Ramos Zachrisson, 2024). This product constitutes a relevant technical input to establish national baselines and guide sustainable soil management policies. Complementarily, Panama has a sectoral framework that promotes practices compatible with increasing soil carbon, such as the National Climate Change Plan for the Agricultural Sector (PNCCSA 2018–2030), officially adopted through the Official Gazette in 2019. This plan guides the transition toward agroforestry systems, silvopastoral systems and other sustainable management practices that, according to the scientific literature and IPCC guidelines, can increase soil organic carbon when applied in a sustained manner (IPCC, 2019).
NT16.actions: 1) Legal framework and protection of wetlands (including peatlands) Panama is Party to the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, which implies commitments for the conservation and wise use of wetlands, including those with organic soils and high carbon content (Ramsar, 1971). The designation and management of Ramsar sites strengthens the protection of peatlands and strategic wetlands. At the domestic level, the General Environmental Law (Law 41 of 1998) establishes principles for the protection of fragile ecosystems and regulates activities that may degrade wetlands and soils (National Assembly, 1998). This framework enables restrictions and conservation measures that contribute to protecting organic soils. 2) National REDD+ Strategy and LULUCF sector The National REDD+ Strategy integrates actions to reduce emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, including forest conservation and restoration, which directly affects the protection of organic soils associated with forest ecosystems and wetlands (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). By reducing the conversion of ecosystems with carbon-rich soils, significant emissions from the Land Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry (LULUCF) sector are avoided. 3) Reforesta Panamá Fund and restoration of degraded lands Law 69 of 2017 created the Reforesta Panamá Fund, aimed at financing forest restoration and recovery of degraded lands (National Assembly, 2017). Restoration contributes to: Increasing vegetation cover. Improving soil organic carbon content. Reducing erosion and degradation. 4) Promotion of agroforestry and silvopastoral systems Agro-environmental policies and cooperation projects have promoted agroforestry and silvopastoral systems, which increase biomass and organic carbon in agricultural soils and grasslands (FAO, 2020). These practices: Integrate trees on farms. Improve infiltration and carbon retention. Reduce soil degradation. FAO recognizes agroforestry as a key strategy to increase soil carbon and climate resilience (FAO, 2020). 5) National Adaptation Plan (NAP) The National Adaptation Plan to Climate Change incorporates ecosystem-based measures, including wetland restoration and sustainable management of agricultural lands (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). These actions strengthen the protection of organic soils and increase carbon capture capacity. 6) Conservation of coastal wetlands and mangroves The protection and restoration of mangroves and coastal wetlands contributes significantly to the conservation of “blue carbon,” stored in saturated organic soils (CBD, 2022). Conservation measures in marine-coastal protected areas reduce drainage and degradation of these soils. 7) Integration with the Global Biodiversity Framework The target aligns with: Target 2: Restore 30% of degraded ecosystems. Target 8: Minimize impacts of climate change and increase resilience. Target 11: Maintain and enhance nature’s contributions to people (CBD, 2022).

NT17.challenges: 1) Governance and interinstitutional coordination to operate “at district scale” The simultaneous transformation of climate-smart agriculture, agroforestry, aquaculture and silvopastoralism requires sustained coordination among multiple entities (agricultural extension, environment, climate, water, research, financing and local governments). The PNCCSA was conceived as a participatory instrument and with interinstitutional arrangements, but its territorial implementation requires stable coordination and monitoring mechanisms to avoid fragmented actions (MIDA & MiAMBIENTE, 2017). 2) Lack of sufficient financing and incentives for massive adoption Moving from pilots to covering ≥50% of priority agricultural areas requires investment in technical assistance, inputs (live fences, forage banks, trees, efficient irrigation), infrastructure (collection, cold, water) and access to credit/insurance. Regional evidence shows that the adoption of “CSA” (climate-smart agriculture) depends heavily on adequate incentives and financing, in addition to institutional capacities (FAO, 2013). 3) Barriers to technological adoption and continuous technical assistance Climate-smart agriculture and agroforestry/silvopastoral systems require management changes, a learning curve and technical support over several production cycles. In Panama, technical materials and projects show the benefits of silvopastoral systems, but also demonstrate the need for training and comprehensive management to sustain productivity and ecosystem services (MiAMBIENTE, 2021; IDIAP, 2025; Fundación Natura et al., 2022). 4) Effective integration of climate information into productive decisions (agroclimatic services) For the transformation to be resilient, producers must plan with forecasts, alerts and agroclimatic recommendations. Panama has strengthened tools such as Mesas Técnicas Agroclimáticas, but the challenge is to expand coverage, periodicity, data quality and translation of information into practical decisions (planting, irrigation, health, harvest) in the 21 districts (MIDA, 2025; MiAMBIENTE, 2024). 5) Real inclusion in indigenous comarcas: safeguards, cultural relevance and rights In indigenous comarcas and territories, the challenge is not only to “reach” them, but to ensure cultural relevance, effective participation and safeguards (including consent and community governance where applicable). The biodiversity agenda recognizes the role of indigenous peoples and local communities in sustainable solutions and resilience, which requires institutional arrangements and appropriate processes for implementation (CDB, 2022). 6) Tenure, planning and pressure from land-use change To sustain agroforestry and silvopastoralism, security over land use, control of unplanned expansion and coherence with territorial planning are needed. Without this, investments in sustainable practices may be displaced by changes in use or land-use conflicts, affecting the 50% coverage target (IPCC, 2019). 7) Growing climate risks and more frequent extremes Droughts, floods, intraseasonal variability and increased pests/diseases can reduce yields and discourage adoption if not accompanied by risk management (insurance, efficient irrigation, diversification, adapted seeds/breeds). The IPCC identifies tropical agriculture and livestock as highly exposed to climate extremes, reinforcing the need for resilience based on diversified practices and systems (IPCC, 2019; IPCC, 2022). 8) Sustainable aquaculture: biosecurity, water and standards Expanding sustainable aquaculture implies challenges of biosecurity, water quality, feeding, effluent management and regulatory compliance. Without standards and monitoring, it can generate environmental impacts and health risks that contradict the “sustainable and inclusive” approach (FAO, 2013). 9) Measurement and demonstration of “transformation” (verifiable indicators) The target requires demonstrating coverage (≥50% of priority areas), adoption of practices and benefits (resilience, emissions reduction, productivity, biodiversity). The challenge is to have a monitoring system that is interoperable, with baselines by district and periodic verification—something that the PNCCSA proposes as part of sectoral planning, but which demands sustained capacities and resources (MIDA & MiAMBIENTE, 2017).
NT17.progress: The Ministry of Agricultural Development (MIDA) has direct participation (as sectoral authority and implementing body) in the targets related to the transformation of agrifood systems toward sustainable, resilient and biodiversity-positive models. In practice, its involvement is concentrated in the following targets: This target calls for areas under agriculture and other productive sectors to be managed sustainably, substantially increasing “biodiversity-friendly” practices, including agroecological and innovative approaches that increase resilience and productivity, with conservation and restoration of biodiversity (Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), 2022; CBD, n. d.-a). In Panama, MIDA is a central actor because it leads agricultural policy and extension (including family farming and agrifood chains), and because the country formalized climate guidelines for the agricultural sector through the adoption of the National Climate Change Plan for the Agricultural Sector (PNCCSA 2018–2030) and the creation of an interinstitutional committee for its implementation, monitoring and evaluation (Digital Official Gazette, 2019). In addition, recent public actions oriented toward sustainable practices and territorial inclusion (including indigenous comarcas) reinforce this contribution: for example, the launch of the Sustainable and Inclusive Agricultural Innovation Program (PIASI) to initially benefit 5,000 small producers in 21 districts with components of sustainable productive innovation, inclusive markets and digital management (Ministry of Agricultural Development (MIDA), 2024). In the PIASI formulation documents, a scope of 9,000 small family farmers and a financial plan of US$41 million in the IDB component/financing is also proposed, with a territorial approach and gender and diversity targets, reinforcing the link with sustainability and resilience (Agricultural Innovation Institute of Panama (IDIAP), n. d.). This target seeks to minimize the impacts of climate change on biodiversity and increase resilience through mitigation, adaptation and risk reduction, including nature-based solutions/ecosystem-based approaches (CBD, 2022; CBD, n. d.-b). MIDA is linked because part of agricultural adaptation requires climate planning, information systems and technical assistance for producers. In practice, sectoral management has included Agricultural Climate Technical Roundtables in MIDA regional directorates (10 roundtables reported, with approximate participation of 50 people per roundtable among producers and technicians), aimed at technical recommendations based on climate forecasts to reduce productive risks (MIDA, 2024). Ecosystem-based adaptation initiatives with climate financing and interinstitutional coordination for producers in specific watersheds are also reported (MIDA, 2024). Complementarily, there are demonstration adaptation projects in livestock farming that promote silvopastoral systems (live fences, tree strips, improved pastures, etc.) as a resilience strategy in the face of climate variability (Adaptación MiAmbiente, 2021).
NT17.actions: 1) National Climate Change Plan for the Agricultural Sector (PNCCSA) Panama has advanced in the formulation and implementation of sectoral instruments for adaptation and mitigation in agriculture, integrated into the National Adaptation Plan and national climate policy (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The PNCCSA guides the incorporation of: Climate-smart agriculture. Sustainable soil management. Reduction of productive vulnerability. Integration of biodiversity in productive systems. Climate-smart agriculture is recognized by FAO as an approach that integrates productivity, adaptation and mitigation (FAO, 2013). 2) Promotion of silvopastoral and agroforestry systems Panama has promoted silvopastoral and agroforestry practices as part of the sustainable productive transition, in coherence with the REDD+ Strategy and restoration programs (MiAMBIENTE, 2018). FAO notes that agroforestry: Increases functional biodiversity. Improves soil fertility. Increases carbon capture (FAO, 2020). These systems make it possible to achieve the objective of 50% of priority agricultural areas under sustainable management. 3) Integration of agrobiodiversity Agrifood transformation includes the conservation and sustainable use of local varieties and native species. The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD, 1992) promotes the in situ conservation of agricultural genetic diversity. The Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022) highlights the need to integrate biodiversity into agriculture to reduce species loss and strengthen resilience. 4) Strengthening of sustainable aquaculture Panama has promoted aquaculture practices with a sustainability and climate adaptation approach, aligned with principles of responsible production (FAO, 2020a). This contributes to productive diversification and food security. 5) Integration with climate policy and NDC Agrifood transformation contributes to the implementation of the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) in the agriculture and land use sector, strengthening resilience and reducing emissions (IPCC, 2019). 6) Strengthening of Agroclimatic Technical Roundtables Panama has consolidated territorial coordination mechanisms, such as the Agroclimatic Technical Roundtables, which integrate climate information into productive decisions (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). These bodies facilitate the adoption of resilient practices in prioritized districts.

NT18.challenges: 1) Pressure from urban expansion and land use change The accelerated growth of cities and urban peripheries generates competition for available land, limiting the creation or conservation of green areas. The IPCC (2022) warns that urban expansion without climate planning increases vulnerability and reduces urban natural spaces. Likewise, the 2030 Agenda recognizes that unplanned urbanization affects equitable access to public spaces (United Nations, 2015). 2) Effective integration in Local Land Use Planning Plans (PLOT) Although Panamanian environmental regulations establish the integration of environmental criteria in land use planning (National Assembly, 1998), challenges persist in: Technical homogeneity among municipalities. Local technical capacity. Real incorporation of urban biodiversity in planning instruments. The Global Biodiversity Framework emphasizes that the integration of biodiversity in urban planning requires multisectoral coordination (CBD, 2022). 3) Municipal financial limitations The creation and maintenance of green and blue infrastructure implies: Land acquisition. Ecological restoration. Permanent maintenance. Monitoring. Local financing is usually limited, which hinders long-term sustainability (IPCC, 2022). 4) Lack of baseline and urban monitoring systems Increasing by 30% compared to the 2025 baseline requires: Precise measurement of green and blue cover. Indicators by district. Updated geospatial systems. Without robust monitoring, the evaluation of progress may be imprecise. 5) Territorial inequality in access to green areas SDG 11.7 promotes universal access to safe green spaces (United Nations, 2015). However, there is inequality in the distribution of parks and green areas between central and peripheral neighborhoods. Guaranteeing equitable access requires an environmental justice approach and inclusive planning. 6) Conservation of urban wetlands and mangroves in the face of economic pressures Urban wetlands face pressure from landfills, infrastructure, and real estate development. The Ramsar Convention underscores that wetland degradation compromises critical ecosystem services (Ramsar Secretariat, 2016). 7) Growing climate vulnerability Extreme events (floods, urban droughts, heat waves) can degrade green infrastructure if it is not designed with resilience criteria (IPCC, 2022). 8) Interinstitutional coordination The target involves: Environment. Housing and land use planning. Local governments. Public health. Infrastructure. The lack of coordination can generate duplication or implementation gaps.
NT18.progress: Since 2019, Panama’s progress toward National Target 18 (increase by 30% the area of urban green and blue spaces and integrate climate, biodiversity and sustainability criteria into Local Land Use Plans) is observed mainly in: (1) urban territorial planning with an environmental approach, (2) instruments and technical guidelines to green cities, and (3) national systems to monitor adaptation, although gaps in baseline data and comparable national metrics persist to demonstrate the 30% target. Panama (especially the District of Panama) advanced in spatial planning that explicitly connects biodiversity, climate change and ecological connectivity within urban planning. The Local Land Use Plan (PLOT) of the District of Panama (executive summary, March 2021) incorporates the Open Spaces System (SEA) with explicit objectives on biodiversity, climate change, resilience, connectivity and ecosystem services, and proposes a “macro” structure (protected areas/corridors/ecological structure) and “micro” structure (parks, urban green areas and public space), including connectors such as river corridors and reference to projects such as the Cinta Costera (Municipio de Panamá, 2019). Secondly, the technical basis for measuring and managing urban green infrastructure was strengthened. A useful milestone (because it offers a comparable figure) is the academic-technical report on urban tree cover: using a consistent methodology for several cities, it reports that Panama City would have around 21.2% tree cover relative to its urban footprint (according to the comparative table in the report) (FOBUR, 2021). In parallel, the Municipio de Panamá has documented and promoted a Tree Planting Plan aimed at quantifying, maintaining and monitoring urban trees, linking it to mitigation/adaptation and safety (risk management from falling trees) (Municipio de Panamá, 2019). In addition, there are operational inputs such as local programs/inventories (e.g., at corregimiento level) that aim to establish baselines for tree management (Municipio de Panamá, 2019). Thirdly, at the national level, Panama consolidated instruments for climate planning and monitoring, which are an enabling condition to demonstrate progress on target 18 (especially the part on “integrating climate criteria” and reporting results). The National Climate Action Plan (PNAC) (framework instrument to implement climate commitments) formalizes lines of action and monitoring by sectors, which serves as an umbrella so that the urban/territorial component can have verifiable measures and metrics. (MiAmbiente – Plataforma de Transparencia Climática, 2022). Complementarily, Panama approved a Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) System for Adaptation, designed to track plans/measures and indicators; among its indicators it includes relevant aspects for territory and local governance (e.g., planning instruments that integrate climate risks and municipalities with local regulations that consider adaptation) (MiAmbiente, 2022). Finally, the current national biodiversity framework also supports the direction of target 18, by recognizing the need to integrate biodiversity into spatial planning and policies (which, brought into the urban context, is consistent with expanding and managing green/blue spaces and connectivity) (Gaceta/FAOLEX, 2018). Synthesis (2019–2025): Panama shows clear progress in instruments (PLOT/SEA with biodiversity and climate), technical capacities (tree cover diagnostics and tree planting plans) and M&E architecture (national system to measure adaptation). However, to demonstrate compliance with the target (30% vs. 2025 baseline” and “access for low urban population”), it is necessary for institutions to publish periodically and comparably: (a) the 2025 baseline of green/blue surface area (and/or m² per inhabitant) by city/district; (b) the official measurement method (remote sensing + municipal cadastre + audits of urban parks/rivers/coasts); and (c) a dashboard that connects POT/PLOT → interventions (parks, riverbanks, green drainage, trees, urban wetlands) → indicators of access, equity and risk reduction using the Monitoring and Evaluation System.
NT18.actions: 1) National Climate Action Plan (PNAC) The National Climate Action Plan (PNAC) (framework instrument to implement climate commitments) formalizes lines of action and monitoring by sectors, which serves as an umbrella so that the urban/territorial component can have verifiable measures and metrics. (MiAmbiente – Climate Transparency Platform, 2022). 2) Tree planting plan The Municipality of Panama has documented and promoted a Tree Planting Plan aimed at quantifying, maintaining and monitoring the urban tree cover, linking it to mitigation/adaptation and safety (Municipality of Panama, 2019). 3) Integration of biodiversity in land-use planning The Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022) in its Target 12 promotes the increase of green spaces and urban planning that integrates biodiversity for human well-being. The Local Land-Use Planning Plans (PLOT) have begun to incorporate: Urban biological corridors. Water protection zones. Conservation of urban mangroves and wetlands. 4) Conservation and restoration of urban wetlands and mangroves The protection of urban wetlands is linked to commitments under the Ramsar Convention (Ramsar Secretariat, 2016). These ecosystems function as: Water regulators. Carbon sinks. Resilient urban blue spaces.
