NT19.challenges: 1) Effective data integration and interinstitutional coordination Multi-hazard systems require interoperability among meteorological, hydrological, civil protection, health, agriculture, and local government services. The World Meteorological Organization (OMM) (WMO, 2018) notes that one of the main challenges of EWS is technical and operational coordination among multiple institutions and levels of government. Likewise, the Sendai Framework emphasizes that the lack of institutional integration can limit the effectiveness of warning systems (UNDRR, 2015). 2) Financial sustainability and local climate financing The implementation and maintenance of monitoring stations, digital platforms, and communication networks requires sustained financing. The IPCC (2022) warns that warning systems are cost-effective, but depend on continuous investment in infrastructure and technical capacities. In addition, coordination with local climate financing mechanisms still faces challenges in access to and efficient execution of resources. 3) Accessibility and relevance of information An EWS is not effective if the information is not understood or used by communities. The OMM (2018) indicates that systems must guarantee clear, culturally appropriate, and timely communication. In rural and indigenous contexts, the digital and linguistic gap can limit the effectiveness of early warning. 4) Technical capacity and infrastructure maintenance The installation of meteorological stations and monitoring systems requires constant technical maintenance. The IPCC (2022) highlights that lack of maintenance can generate critical failures at times of extreme events. 5) Integration of anticipatory action The target includes anticipatory action mechanisms. However, the Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) notes that many countries face difficulties in translating warnings into concrete actions prior to impact, due to: Lack of clear protocols. Weak intersectoral coordination. Budget limitations. 6) Precise identification of vulnerable regions Selecting and prioritizing the 10 vulnerable regions requires: Updated risk maps. Assessment of exposure and social vulnerability. Integrated climate and socioeconomic data. The IPCC (2022) highlights that risk-based planning requires updated and multidimensional scientific information. 7) Community trust and local participation The effectiveness of EWS depends on public trust in institutions and in the truthfulness of warnings. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) underscores the importance of community participation in the design and validation of systems. 8) Increase in the frequency and intensity of extreme events Climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme events (IPCC, 2022), which can: Exceed the capacity of current systems. Generate multiple simultaneous threats (multi-hazard). Require constant updating of models and protocols.
NT19.progress: A key structural advance for the country was the creation of the Instituto de Meteorología e Hidrología de Panamá (IMHPA) (approved in 2021, according to the national risk management plan), as the official authority to generate technical-scientific information on hydrometeorological hazards and for the management of early warning systems (SAT), filling an institutional gap that became evident after the extreme events of 2020 (e.g., Eta and Iota) (SINAPROC, 2022). Panama reports Early Warning Systems (SAT) operational and monitored by SINAPROC with a territorial basis. In an institutional publication (2024) it is indicated that there are 15 Early Warning Systems actively functioning and that monitoring is supported by 320 hydrometeorological stations of ETESA (conventional and satellite) (SINAPROC, 2024). The same report details the distribution of SAT by provinces/zones and examples of rivers/basins, which shows real implementation in exposed territories: Colón (1): Costa Abajo. Darién (1): Río Chucunaque–Yaviza. Panamá (4 active): Juan Díaz, Río Villalobos, Pacora, Chepo. Panamá Oeste (1): Río Santa Rosa. Veraguas (2–3 listed): Santa Fé, Río Santa María, Calobre–Río Cocla. Chiriquí (4): 2 in Tierras Altas and 2 in Barú (basin of the Chiriquí Viejo). Coclé: in the process of installation (basin of the Río Antón), with support from cameras/monitoring and linkage to operations centers. These data are consistent with the component “at least 10 vulnerable regions,” in the sense that the country already reports more than 10 operational SAT (15). In practice, several advances point to moving from “hydrometeorological” alerts toward multi-actor and community approaches (an essential component of multi-hazard and anticipatory action): In 2024 a project was launched to implement a community SAT for floods in the basin of the Río Pacora, developed by CATHALAC + SINAPROC + IMHPA, with financing from SENACYT (Call FID 2023). The project emphasizes “timely, simple and efficient” alerts, with community and institutional administration, and local coordination (SENACYT, 2024). On drought (slow-onset risk), the Plan Nacional contra la Sequía de Panamá explicitly sets out the need to prepare and implement a drought SAT, standardize information, generate specialized indices and develop an interactive risk atlas (MiAMBIENTE, n.d.). Panama has consolidated Mesas Técnicas Agroclimáticas, which translate climate information into productive recommendations for farmers (MIDA, 2023). These tables strengthen the dimension of “relevant information” for rural producers. Local climate financing (available numerical evidence) Although the target requires “local climate financing” associated with alerts/anticipatory action, the strongest and most quantitative public evidence available (2019–2025) is found in the climate tagging of public investment: according to UNDP, according to the Sistema Nacional de Inversiones Públicas (SINIP/MEF), in 2023 23.4% of the investment budget of the Sistema Financiero Público Nacional (SPNF) represented climate financing and in 2024 it rose to 25.4%, with 332 projects (UNDP, 2024).
NT19.actions: 1) Regulatory and institutional framework for risk management Panama strengthened its legal framework with Law 7 of 2005, which reorganizes the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) and establishes coordination for disaster prevention, preparedness and response (National Assembly, 2005). This framework enables the operation of EWS at the national and territorial levels. Likewise, the National Policy for Comprehensive Disaster Risk Management and sectoral plans promote the incorporation of alert systems and early response protocols (Government of Panama, 2011). 2) Integration with the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) The National Climate Change Adaptation Plan incorporates the strengthening of climate information systems and early warnings as an axis of territorial resilience (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The NAP promotes: Integration of meteorological and hydrological information. Territorial approach in vulnerable areas. Coordination with local authorities. The IPCC (2022) recognizes early warning systems as one of the most cost-effective measures to reduce losses and damages. 3) Strengthening meteorological and hydrological services The strengthening of the monitoring network of the Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (IMHPA) and integration with SINAPROC allow for: Seasonal climate forecasts. Flood and drought alerts. Hydrometeorological monitoring systems. The WMO (WMO, 2018) highlights that multi-hazard systems require data interoperability and clear communication protocols. 4) Agroclimatic Technical Roundtables and sectoral climate services Panama has consolidated Agroclimatic Technical Roundtables, which translate climate information into productive recommendations for farmers (MIDA, 2023). These roundtables strengthen the dimension of “relevant information” for rural producers. FAO emphasizes that sectoral climate services are essential to reduce agricultural vulnerability (FAO, 2013).

NT20.challenges: 1) Vulnerability of hydroelectric generation to prolonged droughts The Panamanian energy system maintains a significant share of hydroelectric generation. The IPCC (2022) warns that climate change increases the frequency and intensity of droughts in tropical regions, affecting water availability for electricity generation. Hydrological variability reduces system reliability when climate scenarios are not adequately integrated into energy planning. 2) Effective integration of climate scenarios into sectoral planning Although the National Adaptation Plan (MiAMBIENTE, 2021) establishes general guidelines, one of the main challenges is translating climate scenarios into: Operational energy models. Generation expansion planning. Electricity dispatch scheduling. The International Energy Agency (IEA, 2021) notes that many energy systems still do not fully incorporate climate risk analysis into long-term planning. 3) Energy infrastructure exposed to extreme events Substations, transmission networks, and thermal generation are exposed to: Floods. Landslides. Heat waves. Intense storms. The IPCC (2022) highlights that critical energy infrastructure requires structural adaptation and continuous maintenance to withstand extreme events. 4) Need for sustained investment in resilience The modernization of infrastructure, undergrounding of lines, reinforcement of networks, and smart systems entails high costs. The international literature indicates that lack of financing is one of the main obstacles to energy adaptation (IEA, 2021). 5) Limited interinstitutional coordination Energy resilience requires coordination among: National Secretariat of Energy. Electricity Transmission Company. Ministry of Environment. National Civil Protection System. The Paris Agreement promotes integrated adaptation approaches, but its sectoral implementation requires permanent technical coordination (United Nations, 2015a). 6) Growth in energy demand The increase in urban and industrial electricity demand increases pressure on the system, reducing room for maneuver in the face of interruptions caused by extreme climate events. 7) Risks associated with rising temperature Rising temperature affects the efficiency of: Thermal power plants. Transmission systems. Peak demand for cooling. The IPCC (2022) warns that heat stress can affect both electricity supply and demand. 8) Need for diversification and energy storage Diversification toward non-conventional renewables improves resilience, but requires: Storage systems. Smart grids. Intermittency management. The IEA (2021) notes that the integration of renewables must be accompanied by modernization of the electricity system to guarantee stability.
NT20.progress: Since 2019, Panama has experienced significant progress in the integration of climate change into energy planning, whose objective is to strengthen the climate resilience of the energy system through the incorporation of climate scenarios into its planning and operation. The first relevant milestone was the approval of the Strategic Guidelines of the Energy Transition Agenda 2020–2030, which explicitly establish the need to link energy planning with climate change mitigation and adaptation (Secretaría Nacional de Energía, 2020). This approach was reaffirmed when the updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) in 2020 recognized the Energy Transition Agenda as a central instrument for moving toward a resilient and low-emission energy system (Ministerio de Ambiente, 2020). Subsequently, the approval of the National Climate Action Plan (PNAC) in 2022 consolidated the alignment between climate policy and the energy sector, considering energy as a strategic axis for increasing the country's resilience to extreme climate events (Ministerio de Ambiente, 2022). During this period, complementary strategies for energy efficiency, electric mobility, and distributed generation were also strengthened, which indirectly contribute to reducing structural vulnerabilities of the electricity system (Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo, 2023). Between 2023 and 2025, Panama moved toward the formulation of a specific sectoral instrument: the Energy Sector Adaptation Plan. The Climate Change Directorate of the Ministerio de Ambiente documented in its institutional report 2019–2024 the development of the project to prepare that plan, supported by the NDC Partnership, thus marking the beginning of a technical process to identify climate risks, vulnerabilities, and adaptation measures in critical energy infrastructure (Dirección de Cambio Climático, 2024). This effort was complemented by the issuance of Resolution MIPRE-2025-0013776, in which the Secretaría Nacional de Energía approved an initial set of technical recommendations to guide the adaptation of the energy sector, emphasizing the need to integrate climate risk analysis into decision-making (Secretaría Nacional de Energía, 2025). Likewise, international organizations have contributed to the country's technical strengthening. The Latin American Energy Organization (OLADE) developed between 2024 and 2025 the Screen–ALC II initiative, whose objective is to incorporate climate vulnerability assessment methodologies into energy planning, including technical visits to hydroelectric infrastructure as part of the risk assessment (OLADE, 2024). Complementarily, a joint analysis by the Ministerio de Economía y Finanzas and the World Bank (2024) highlighted Panama's efforts to improve energy resilience through regulatory reforms, climate financing, and institutional strengthening. Recently (2026) Panama will begin updating its National Energy plan PEN. Taken together, the recorded progress shows a progression from the establishment of the strategic framework toward the creation of tools and technical processes aimed at adaptation. However, although there is a coherent path, the systematic incorporation of climate scenarios into the daily operation of the energy system is still under development, depending on the completion and full adoption of the Energy Sector Adaptation Plan. Nevertheless, the progress achieved since 2019 demonstrates the country's growing commitment to moving toward a more robust, diversified, and resilient energy system in the face of the impacts of climate change.
NT20.actions: 1) Incorporation of the energy sector into the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) Panama is developing the National Adaptation Plan to Climate Change (NAP), which includes the energy sector as a priority area for reducing vulnerabilities to extreme events, prolonged droughts, and floods (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The NAP promotes: Integration of climate scenarios into sectoral planning. Assessment of physical risks to energy infrastructure. Structural and operational adaptation measures. The IPCC (2022) underscores that energy infrastructure is highly vulnerable to climate change and requires risk-based planning. 2) Integration of climate scenarios into electricity planning National energy planning has incorporated analysis of: Hydrological variability. Temperature projections. Impacts on hydroelectric generation. The International Energy Agency (IEA, 2021) notes that integrating climate scenarios into electricity planning is key to system resilience. 3) Strengthening of critical infrastructure Measures have been adopted for: Vulnerability assessment of transmission networks. Protection of substations against floods. Modernization of distribution systems. The IPCC recognizes that adaptation of critical infrastructure reduces systemic risks (IPCC, 2022). 4) Integration with the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) Energy resilience is linked to both mitigation and adaptation within Panama’s NDC, strengthening coherence between energy transition and climate adaptation (United Nations, 2015). 5) Promotion of distributed generation and renewable energy The expansion of solar energy and other decentralized renewables reduces the vulnerability of the centralized system to extreme events (National Secretariat of Energy, 2016). 6) Intersectoral coordination Energy resilience requires coordination among: Energy. Environment. Water. Risk management. The Paris Agreement promotes sectoral integration in adaptation (United Nations, 2015a).

NT21.challenges: 1) Interoperability and data quality One of the main challenges is to ensure that data from different institutions (meteorology, environment, agriculture, land-use planning) are compatible, updated, and standardized. FAO (2013) highlights that climate information systems require clear interoperability and validation protocols to ensure reliability. The IPCC (2022) notes that risk-based decision-making depends on consistent data with high spatial and temporal resolution. 2) Financial and technological sustainability The continuous operation of a national geospatial platform entails: Technological updating. Server maintenance. Training of technical personnel. The international literature indicates that financial sustainability is one of the main challenges in consolidating sectoral climate services (FAO, 2013). 3) Technical capacities at the territorial level Although OSIGA operates at the central level, its effectiveness depends on technical capacities in provinces and districts. The IPCC (2022) emphasizes that effective adaptation requires local institutional strengthening to interpret and use climate information. 4) Effective integration of the Climate Risk Atlas The integration of the Climate Risk Atlas into productive and territorial planning decisions requires: Periodic updating of scenarios. Technical translation into practical recommendations. Alignment with agricultural planning instruments. The National Adaptation Plan (MiAMBIENTE, 2021) recognizes that the effective use of climate information depends on its incorporation into sectoral policies. 5) Participation and ownership by producers The effectiveness of OSIGA depends on producers and local actors using the information generated. FAO (2013) notes that agricultural climate services must be co-designed with users to ensure relevance and adoption. The Mesas Técnicas Agroclimáticas are an advance, but their sustainability depends on continuous participation and institutional trust. 6) Digital divide and access to information In rural areas and indigenous comarcas, limitations in connectivity and digital literacy persist, which may restrict access to geospatial platforms. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) emphasizes that universal access to risk information is a condition for reducing vulnerability. 7) Sustained interinstitutional coordination The consolidation of OSIGA requires coordination among: Ministry of Agricultural Development (MIDA). Ministry of Environment (MiAMBIENTE). Meteorological institute. Local governments. The Paris Agreement (United Nations, 2015a) promotes sectoral integration in adaptation, but its implementation requires formal and permanent coordination mechanisms. 8) Updating in the face of accelerated climate change Climate change modifies historical rainfall and temperature patterns. The IPCC (2022) warns that planning based on historical data may become insufficient without constant updating of projections.
NT21.progress: By 2027, Panama will have consolidated the Oficina del Sistema de Información Geoespacial Agropecuaria (OSIGA) as the Central National Platform for Monitoring and Management of Agroclimatic Information, integrating data from the Atlas de Riesgo Climático and coordinating territorially through the Mesas Técnicas Agroclimáticas. Progress status (2019–to date): In consolidation. Panama has shown concrete progress in the creation, implementation, and strengthening of the Oficina del Sistema de Información Geoespacial Agropecuaria (OSIGA) within the Ministerio de Desarrollo Agropecuario (MIDA). These advances include its official inauguration, initial operational deployments, and technical training activities, as well as the progressive integration of its agroclimatic monitoring functions, contributing to the national database needed for climate risk management in the agricultural sector (MIDA, n.d.). The Oficina del Sistema de Información Geoespacial Agropecuaria (OSIGA) was formally established by MIDA with the mission of collecting, processing, and analyzing geospatial data from the agricultural sector to strengthen decision-making, monitor territorial and climatic conditions, support the resilience of the sector, and assess impacts and trends of agroclimatic variables through advanced technological tools (MIDA, n.d.). The purpose of this office is to serve as a strategic tool for the geospatial monitoring of policies, plans, and projects that benefit agricultural holdings and promote sectoral sustainability. In January 2025, MIDA officially inaugurated the Oficina de Información Geoespacial, marking a milestone in institutional consolidation and the beginning of more structured operations for OSIGA. During the inauguration ceremony, the importance of OSIGA was highlighted for improving the monitoring of agroclimatic conditions, support for early warning programs, and evaluation of soils and crops through remote data, as well as the availability of digital tools such as the Agroclima app, which is already integrated into the MIDA website within the OSIGA section (MIDAa, 2025). In addition to its physical and organizational establishment, OSIGA has begun concrete technical activities that show progress in its operational consolidation. For example, in February 2025 a stage of technical training was carried out on the use of drones for geospatial data collection, aimed at OSIGA staff and associated officials, with support from the Instituto Interamericano de Cooperación para la Agricultura (IICA). This training is part of the generation of internal capacities that will allow OSIGA to produce high-resolution spatial data and establish dynamic field monitoring jobs, such as moisture assessment, soil quality, and crop health (MIDAb, 2025). These actions show that the consolidation of OSIGA is in an advanced implementation phase and not only at the stage of regulatory or conceptual formulation: there are already regular activities of data generation, use of geospatial technologies, technical training, and online deployment of tools such as the Agroclima app that support the expected functions of the office (MIDA, n.d.; MIDAa, 2025). Regarding the integration of national climate data, OSIGA is linked to the use of information from the Atlas de Riesgo Climático and other monitoring modules available on the Plataforma Nacional de Transparencia Climática (PNTC) of the Ministerio de Ambiente (MiAMBIENTE, n.d.). This national platform allows access to, consultation of, and visualization of different climate data and products, including vulnerability and risk maps, which can be used as part of the set of geospatial inputs that OSIGA incorporates into its analysis and decision-making processes. Although the target for 2027 mentions territorial coordination through Mesas Técnicas Agroclimáticas, no complete public compilation has been found that formally and systematically quantifies OSIGA’s participation in all the Mesas Técnicas Agroclimáticas in the country. However, the existence of these tables and the national emphasis on agroclimatic information, especially as a component of the climate resilience of the agricultural sector, are recognized as a strategic priority in specialized publications on climate-smart agriculture in Panama (CCAFS, 2021).
NT21.actions: 1) Creation and strengthening of OSIGA as a sectoral information system Panama has strengthened the Agricultural Geospatial Information System (OSIGA) as a tool for territorial and climate management of the agricultural sector, integrating productive, climatic and risk data into an interoperable platform (MIDA, 2023). The integration of territorial information systems is consistent with the evidence-based management principles promoted by FAO for resilient agriculture (FAO, 2013). 2) Integration of the Climate Risk Atlas The development of the Climate Risk Atlas has made it possible to map vulnerability, exposure and climate threats at the territorial level, facilitating decision-making in agricultural planning (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The IPCC (2022) notes that sectoral planning based on risk maps is essential to reduce climate vulnerability in agrifood systems. 3) Consolidation of Agroclimatic Technical Roundtables (MTA) Panama has institutionalized Agroclimatic Technical Roundtables as a coordination mechanism among meteorology, agriculture and producers (MIDA, 2023). These roundtables: Translate forecasts into productive recommendations. Facilitate two-way communication with producers. Improve the territorial relevance of information. FAO recognizes the MTA as a key agricultural climate services tool (FAO, 2013). Integration with the National Adaptation Plan (PNA) The National Climate Change Adaptation Plan includes the strengthening of sectoral climate information systems as an enabling condition for effective adaptation (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The consolidation of OSIGA directly contributes to the implementation of the agricultural component of the PNA. 4) Digitization and modernization of agricultural data The digital transformation of the agricultural sector includes: Georeferenced databases. Crop monitoring. Tracking of climatic and productive variables. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) highlights the importance of accessible information systems for disaster risk reduction. 5) Interinstitutional coordination OSIGA functions as an articulating node among: Ministry of Agricultural Development (MIDA). Ministry of Environment (MiAMBIENTE). Meteorological Institute. Local governments. The Paris Agreement promotes the sectoral integration of climate information to strengthen adaptation (United Nations, 2015a).

NT22.challenges: 1) Effective integration into territorial planning instruments One of the main challenges is to ensure that the PLRA are not isolated documents, but are formally integrated into: Municipal development plans. Territorial land-use plans. Watershed management plans. The IPCC (2022) warns that adaptation fails when it is not institutionalized in local regulatory and budgetary frameworks. Likewise, the 2030 Agenda emphasizes the need for coherence between sectoral and territorial planning (United Nations, 2015). 2) Technical limitations and local capacities Many local governments have limitations in: Technical capacities to interpret climate scenarios. Management of geospatial information. Vulnerability and risk assessment. The National Adaptation Plan (MiAMBIENTE, 2021) recognizes that strengthening subnational institutions is an enabling condition for effective adaptation. The IPCC (2022) underlines that multilevel governance is key to territorial resilience. 3) Availability and updating of climate information Adaptive planning requires: Updated climate scenarios. Territorial risk maps. Hydrological and socioeconomic data. The IPCC (2022) notes that climate uncertainty and the lack of high-resolution data can hinder local planning. 4) Sustainable financing for implementation The design of plans does not guarantee their execution. The lack of specific budget allocation and limited access to climate financing can delay territorial implementation. The Paris Agreement recognizes the need to strengthen financial and technical support for adaptation (United Nations, 2015a). 5) Interinstitutional coordination The goal implies coordination among: Ministry of Environment. Local authorities. Watershed authorities. Sectoral institutions (water, energy, agriculture). The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) highlights that risk reduction requires effective intersectoral coordination. 6) Differential approach in indigenous territories and coastal zones The prioritization of indigenous territories and coastal zones requires: Intercultural approach. Consultation and effective participation. Integration of traditional knowledge. The IPCC (2022) recognizes that coastal and indigenous communities face disproportionate climate risks and require differentiated adaptive approaches. 7) Accelerated change in climate risks The intensification of extreme events may exceed the scenarios initially considered in the plans, requiring periodic review. The IPCC (2022) emphasizes that adaptation must be dynamic and flexible in the face of changing climate scenarios. 8) Follow-up, monitoring and evaluation The absence of clear indicators and monitoring systems can make it difficult to assess the real impact of territorial plans. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) establishes the importance of continuous monitoring to reduce human and economic losses.
NT22.progress: Since 2019, Panama has progressed progressively (although still in a fragmented manner) toward national Target 8 (design, validate and implement local and regional adaptation plans prioritizing watersheds, protected areas, coastal zones and indigenous territories, and integrate them into development and watershed management plans) through (i) strengthening of the national adaptation planning framework, (ii) territorial/municipal instruments that already incorporate adaptation and risk, and (iii) adaptation programs in prioritized watersheds with technical products and measurable results. A recent milestone is the formal launch of the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) process in 2023 (with reported financing of USD 2.9 million for 2023–2026), whose explicit objective is to plan, finance, implement, monitor and report adaptation, and articulate sectoral plans (for example, water resources, agriculture/food security, infrastructure and health), which creates enabling conditions to “bring down” adaptation to the territorial and sectoral scale (MiAmbiente, 2023). In parallel, concrete progress can be observed in territorial instruments that function as “building blocks” for local/regional adaptation plans, especially in prioritized districts and destinations. In 2021, the Autoridad de Turismo de Panamá (ATP) reported the tender to prepare “Land Use Plans (POT) and Climate Change Scenario Studies” in six districts (Pedasí, Bocas del Toro, Boquete, Tierras Altas, Soná and Taboga), highlighting that these facilitate local adaptation actions and a roadmap in the face of risks (Autoridad de Turismo de Panamá, 2021). Subsequently, MIVIOT reported in 2024 the approval of the tourism Plan Local de Ordenamiento Territorial (PLOT) of Soná, noting that it forms part of the “six tourism plans” and that it incorporates a climate change mitigation and adaptation approach; in addition, it reported the progress/completion status of other plans (Taboga already approved; Boquete and Tierras Altas completed; Bocas del Toro pending municipal agreement; Pedasí being submitted to the Planning Board) (MIVIOT, 2024). In terms of “figures,” this shows at least 6 territorial instruments designed with climate scenarios (and at least 2 approved in the tourism package as of April 2024), which can serve as the basis for local adaptation plans. At the regulatory-operational level, a key advance in 2025 is that, in the consultation process for an adaptation decree, it was consolidated that local adaptation plans may be prepared at the municipal, watershed or comarca scale, and that they must maintain coherence with land use plans; in addition, it is explicitly recognized that the six PLOT prepared by ATP/MIVIOT can be used as the technical basis for local adaptation plans in their regions (MiAmbiente, 2025). This is relevant because it formalizes the “bridge” between climate planning and territorial/watershed planning, and enables (in the regulatory design) integration into development and territorial management instruments. In prioritized watersheds, Panama also reported quantifiable implementation results linked to adaptation and territorial water governance. For example, MiAmbiente reported in 2023 that El Programa de adaptación al Cambio Climático, through the Manejo Integrado del Recurso Hídrico, in the watersheds of the Chiriquí Viejo and Santa María rivers, implemented actions on 120 farms with silvopastoral systems (≈600 ha), established agroforestry systems on 226 ha, installed 50 rainwater harvesting systems, developed eight climate-resilient water management instruments (including adaptation plans), and installed more than 40 automatic agrometeorological and hydrological stations; in addition, it linked Mesas Agroclimáticas that benefited more than 6,000 producers in five prioritized regions (MiAmbiente, 2023).
NT22.actions: 1) National strategic adaptation framework Panama adopted the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (PNA) as the guiding instrument to strengthen sectoral and territorial resilience, establishing guidelines for subnational planning and prioritization of vulnerable areas (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The PNA promotes the territorialization of adaptation through local instruments consistent with updated climate scenarios. The IPCC (2022) notes that effective adaptation requires multilevel and risk-based planning. 2) Incorporation of the watershed approach The prioritization of watersheds responds to an ecosystem-based adaptation approach, integrating water management, land use, and biodiversity conservation in the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (PNA) (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The IPCC (2022) recognizes that integrated watershed management reduces vulnerability to droughts and floods. 3) Integration with Land Use Plans Panama has promoted the integration of climate variables into Local Land Use Plans (PLOT) and municipal development plans, strengthening coherence between urban planning and climate adaptation (United Nations, 2015). The 2030 Agenda highlights the importance of integrating resilience into local planning (United Nations, 2015). 4) Focus on coastal and marine-coastal areas Coastal areas vulnerable to sea level rise and erosion have been prioritized in sectoral adaptation instruments National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The IPCC (2022) identifies tropical coastal areas as highly vulnerable to climate change. 5) Development of technical support instruments Tools such as the following have been strengthened: Climate Risk Atlas. Geospatial information systems. Sectoral vulnerability assessments. The IPCC (2022) highlights the importance of having robust technical tools for adaptive planning.

NT23.challenges: 1) Acceleration of sea level rise and extreme events The IPCC (2022) warns that sea level rise and the intensification of storms may exceed initially projected scenarios, increasing risks of coastal flooding and erosion. This requires constant updating of projections and flexible adaptation of measures. 2) Historical loss and continued pressure on mangroves Although Panama has made progress in restoration, there is evidence of loss of cover in specific coastal sectors, associated with urbanization, tourism expansion and changes in land use (MiAmbiente, 2023). Anthropogenic pressure limits the effectiveness of NbS if it is not accompanied by land-use planning and control of illegal activities. The CBD (2022) notes that the degradation of coastal ecosystems reduces their capacity to act as natural barriers against climate change. 3) Sustainable financing for large-scale implementation NbS require: Ecological restoration. Continuous monitoring. Long-term maintenance. The Paris Agreement recognizes that adaptation depends on sustained access to climate financing (United Nations, 2015a). The territorial scale of the marine-coastal plan implies investments greater than current pilot projects. 4) Interinstitutional coordination and coastal governance Marine-coastal management involves multiple actors: Environment. Maritime authorities. Coastal municipalities. Fisheries. Tourism. Infrastructure. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) underscores that risk reduction requires effective multisectoral coordination to avoid duplication and conflicts of competence. 5) Formal integration into land-use planning instruments Effective implementation requires that the measures of the marine-coastal plan be integrated into: Local development plans. Coastal land-use plans. Land-use regulations. The IPCC (2022) indicates that adaptation fails when it is not institutionalized in binding regulatory frameworks. 6) Monitoring and evaluation of Nature-based Solutions Although Panama has made progress in blue carbon baselines and restoration, the challenge remains of: Measuring effectiveness in risk reduction. Evaluating ecological co-benefits. Establishing clear resilience indicators. The IPCC (2022) emphasizes that NbS require systematic monitoring to demonstrate their effectiveness. 7) Saline intrusion and impacts on livelihoods Saline intrusion impacts: Coastal agriculture. Aquifers. Artisanal fisheries. The IPCC (2022) warns that these impacts affect food security and the local economy, which requires comprehensive adaptation approaches. 8) Conflicts between economic development and conservation Urban and tourism expansion in coastal areas may conflict with the conservation of wetlands and mangroves. The CBD (2022) and the 2030 Agenda (United Nations, 2015) highlight the need to harmonize economic development with ecosystem protection.
NT23.progress: Since 2019, Panama’s progress toward the goal of implementing the Marine–Coastal Adaptation Plan (in areas vulnerable to sea level rise, erosion, mangrove loss, and saline intrusion, incorporating green infrastructure and nature-based solutions (NbS)) is evident in three main lines: (1) sectoral planning and generation of climate evidence, (2) governance and monitoring instruments, (3) implementation in the territory through NbS (especially restoration of mangroves and coastal wetlands). Panama shows the following progress: Panama advanced in sectoral planning and in the production of technical inputs to implement marine-coastal adaptation measures. The National Climate Action Plan had already identified the need to develop instruments for the marine-coastal sector with adaptation components (and bases for a sectoral guide/plan toward 2025), recognizing risks such as sea level rise and damage to coastal infrastructure (MiAmbiente, 2022). Along these lines, specific studies of climate change scenarios and sea level rise toward 2050 were prepared to support decision-making and the definition of adaptation measures in coastal areas, including workshops with national actors; with spatial and quantitative data it shows that Panama’s marine-coastal areas will face increasing cumulative impacts associated with sea level rise, coastal erosion, salinization, and the loss of natural ecosystems, the projection of an average rise of up to 0.30 m in the Caribbean and 0.22 m in the Pacific, together with extreme levels that could exceed 3.8 m (MiAmbiente, 2023). Subsequently, the process for the Climate Change Adaptation Plan for the marine-coastal sector was formalized with terms of reference that explicitly require an NbS approach, cost estimation, and integration with Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) and governance (GWP, 2024). Progress is observed in outreach, governance, and preparation for implementation of the sectoral plan. In 2025, outreach workshops on the Climate Change Adaptation Plan (PACC) for the marine–coastal sector were reported in several provinces, the process of preparing the PACC has integrated the efforts of various government entities, non-governmental organizations, academia, the private sector, and local communities, to ensure the considerations of each coastal region and the inclusion of sectors such as environment, fisheries, tourism, and infrastructure (February 2025) (GWP, 2025a) and a public event presenting the plan, indicating that the process was led by MiAmbiente with NDC financing and technical support from Global Water Partnership (GWP) (GWP, 2025b). Additionally, the monitoring architecture was strengthened with the Panama Adaptation Monitoring and Evaluation System (hybrid approach to measure implementation of plans and measures), which is key to reporting real implementation progress (MiAmbiente, 2024). Panama presents evidence of implementation of NbS in priority coastal sites, especially mangroves (protection against erosion and flooding, and blue carbon co-benefits). In Bahía de Chame, MiAmbiente reported a project to restore 250 hectares of mangrove and documented that between 2012 and 2019, 358.94 hectares of mangrove were lost in that area due to illegal logging, which contextualizes the intervention as a response to loss and degradation (MiAmbiente, 2022). In 2025, MiAmbiente reported restoration progress in Chame with 150 hectares restored through reforestation/enrichment of red mangrove ( Rhizophora spp. ) with community participation, which constitutes concrete implementation data (MiAmbiente, 2025a). In parallel, restoration actions were promoted in Darién (MangRes project), with forensic diagnosis in an 11 ha polygon and a second phase where restoration measures will be implemented in around 32 ha (MiAmbiente, 2025b). To support the technical standardization of these NbS, Panama has a Manual of restoration techniques for degraded mangrove areas (published as a regulatory reference in the Gazette) (PNUD & MiAmbiente, 2020/2021). Panama has developed concrete actions for the restoration of coastal and inland wetlands, mainly through projects implemented with the support of Wetlands International – Oficina Panamá, with two documented projects, which together total approximately 156.2 hectares restored or in the process of restoration. The first project corresponds to the restoration of mangroves on Isla Galeta (province of Colón), carried out between 2018 and 2024, with a restored area of 6.2 ha and the second project was carried out in Laguna de Las Lajas (San Félix, province of Chiriquí) between 2017 and 2025, covering an approximate area of 150 ha. (Blanco & Yellachich, 2023). In the wetlands/mangroves and evidence-based management approach, the “Patrimonio Natural Azul” project (MiAmbiente–Audubon) stands out, financed by the United Kingdom Blue Carbon Fund and administered by the IDB, with a reported budget of USD 2.3 million, aimed at valuing, protecting, and improving marine-coastal ecosystems, the project is implemented in two key pilot sites: the Refugio de Vida Silvestre Humedal Bahía de Panamá and Bahía de Parita; among its achievements are studies on the role of mangroves in carbon capture, the active community participation of more than 1,000 community leaders, environmental education through the Aulas Verdes project to more than 10,200 students and 360 teachers from 19 schools in the pilot areas, the strengthening of Panama’s international leadership in conservation and the creation of a national inventory to optimize mangrove restoration (MiAmbiente, 2024). Project materials also report generation of blue carbon baselines in pilot sites (e.g., Bahía de Parita and Bahía de Panamá), strengthening the technical basis for prioritizing NbS (Somos Impacto Positivo, 2024). Complementarily, a StoryMap of the project documents natural regeneration of 136.27 ha of mangrove in a site associated with sedimentary dynamics (Estero Palo Blanco, Natá, Coclé) and that the extent of mangrove in Bahía de Parita has increased by approximately 1,014 ha from the nineties to date. On the other hand, in Bahía de Panamá the results indicate a decrease in mangrove cover, with the exception of the period between the years 2000 – 2009 where there is an increase of 14.13 ha due to the accumulation of sediments on the coastline of Juan Díaz and Punta Manglares, a decrease of 98.13 ha of mangrove forest was identified due to coastline loss in the sector of Isla Cocotillo and Los manglares de Río Hondo, in the Corregimiento de Chimán; which points to NbS opportunities supported by natural processes when pressure is reduced and the territory is managed (MiAmbiente/Audubon, n.d.). Panama participates in regional initiatives and portfolios that include saline intrusion, coastal erosion, and sea level rise, explicit risks of this goal. Adaptation Fund proposals that include saline intrusion and monitoring components (for example, monitoring sea level and soil/water quality) show the type of measures that Panama is structuring and financing for territorial implementation (Adaptation Fund, 2023; Adaptation Fund, 2025). Likewise, the Adaptation Fund itself records a binational Costa Rica–Panama project to strengthen the resilience of coastal communities (including Bocas del Toro) through NbS for local livelihoods, which aligns directly with the goal of implementing the marine-coastal plan with NbS (Adaptation Fund, 2024).
NT23.actions: 1) Development of the National Adaptation Plan (PNA) with a coastal approach Panama adopted the National Adaptation Plan to Climate Change (PNA), which identifies the marine-coastal sector as a priority due to its high vulnerability to sea level rise and extreme events (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The IPCC (2022) notes that tropical coastal zones are among the most exposed to climate risks, which justifies the territorial prioritization adopted. 2) Restoration and conservation of mangroves Panama has promoted mangrove restoration programs as an adaptation and climate mitigation measure, given their role in: Protection against storm surges and storms. Reduction of coastal erosion. Blue carbon capture. The IPCC (2022) recognizes that mangroves significantly reduce wave energy and coastal vulnerability. Likewise, the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD, 2022) promotes the restoration of coastal ecosystems as part of the Global Biodiversity Framework. 3) Implementation of Nature-based Solutions (NbS) The green infrastructure approach —including restoration of dunes, coastal wetlands and natural barriers— is aligned with the scientific evidence that positions NbS as cost-effective adaptation strategies (IPCC, 2022). NbS simultaneously allow: Reduction of climate risks. Conservation of biodiversity. Protection of coastal livelihoods. 4) Integration into territorial planning instruments Panama has promoted the incorporation of climate risk criteria into coastal and territorial planning instruments, in coherence with the 2030 Agenda and the territorial resilience approach (United Nations, 2015).
