NT24.challenges: 1) Technical integration of climate and health data One of the main challenges is achieving interoperability between meteorological databases and epidemiological surveillance systems. WHO (2015) notes that climate-resilient health systems require systematic integration of climate data into surveillance platforms, which implies standardization, validation, and permanent updating. The IPCC (2022) warns that the quality and resolution of climate data condition the effectiveness of predictive models of climate-sensitive diseases. 2) Technical capacities and training of health personnel The incorporation of climate projections requires that public health personnel understand: Interpretation of climate scenarios. Epidemiological predictive models. Early warning systems in health. WHO (2015) emphasizes that strengthening human capacities is a critical component for operationalizing health adaptation. 3) Unequal territorial coverage Reaching 80% of public health facilities implies overcoming gaps in: Technological infrastructure. Digital connectivity. Human resources in rural areas and indigenous comarcas. The IPCC (2022) recognizes that vulnerable populations face greater exposure and lower adaptive capacity, which increases the challenge of national coverage. 4) Completion and updating of the Climate Vulnerability and Risk Study The Vulnerability Study requires: Updated epidemiological models. Regionalized climate projections. Identification of populations at risk. The IPCC (2022) indicates that health vulnerability is dynamic and must be updated periodically in the face of changes in climate and demographic patterns. 5) Sustainable financing The modernization of surveillance systems, acquisition of specialized software, and continuous training require sustained investment. The Paris Agreement recognizes that adaptation depends on access to adequate and continuous financing (United Nations, 2015a). 6) Intersectoral coordination Climate-informed epidemiological surveillance requires coordination between: Ministry of Health. Ministry of Environment. Meteorological services. Civil Protection. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) highlights that disaster risk reduction requires effective multisectoral coordination. 7) Increase in climate-sensitive diseases Climate change is expanding the geographic distribution of vectors such as mosquitoes that transmit dengue and other diseases (IPCC, 2022). This implies: Greater pressure on the health system. Need for more complex predictive models. Permanent surveillance. 8) Protection of health infrastructure against extreme events Health facilities are also vulnerable to floods, heat waves, and storms. WHO (2015) underscores that the structural resilience of hospitals is an integral part of health adaptation.
NT24.progress: Since 2019, Panama has shown clearer progress in (a) strengthening the foundation of the epidemiological surveillance system and (b) producing technical evidence on climate vulnerability and health; in contrast, there is little public evidence (with verifiable national indicators) that would allow confirmation of compliance with the milestone “80% of public health facilities” with systematic integration of climate variables/projections in surveillance. By 2019, the country’s epidemiological surveillance system already had a formal reporting network (presented by the system itself), reporting 280 reporting units and a reference population of 3,504,483 inhabitants in the system’s technical training documentation (Taller de Vigilancia Epidemiológica, 2019). This is relevant because the goal does not start from “zero”: the challenge is to explicitly integrate climate variables and projections into that surveillance (for example, temperatures, precipitation, ENSO, seasonal forecasts, scenarios) and standardize their use for alerts, analysis, and response. A substantive advance is the publication of the MINSA technical document “Vulnerabilidad al Cambio Climático en la República de Panamá y su Repercusión en la Salud” (published on the institutional portal in 2022), which develops a vulnerability analysis by health regions using components of exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity, and sets out steps to guide intervention and adaptation plans in health. The Study constitutes the first systematic national analysis linking climate variables, epidemiological risks, and health system capacity, covered 100% of the country’s health regions (14 regions), and analyzed climate and epidemiological information corresponding to the period 2000–2020, using data from ETESA, the MINSA Department of Epidemiology, and national health records. Likewise, statistical correlations were identified between climate variables and climate-sensitive diseases, such as dengue (2010–2020), malaria (2000–2021), leishmaniasis (2000–2020), and acute respiratory diseases, demonstrating the potential of climate models to anticipate epidemiological outbreaks. It also consolidated climate-health vulnerability and risk maps for the 14 health regions, prioritizing territories with high social vulnerability such as Bocas del Toro, Darién, Ngäbe Buglé, Guna Yala, and rural areas of the Pacific, where poverty, climate exposure, and limited adaptive capacity converge (Ministerio de Salud (MINSA), 2022). In terms of the goal, this does align with the component “complete the climate vulnerability and risk study” (at least as a baseline/diagnosis), although the goal speaks of “Estudio de Vulnerabilidad y Riesgo Climático” as a final product; in practice, the MINSA document constitutes a central input that can be considered verifiable progress. An indirect indicator of integration (although not equivalent to a “formal system” with protocols and 80% coverage) is that MINSA has publicly communicated analyses where climate variables (temperature, irregular rainfall pattern) are linked to the cycle of the Aedes aegypti vector and dengue behavior. In 2025, MINSA reported that “last year” 32,077 cases and 52 deaths from dengue were recorded; in addition, it communicated clinical distributions (89% without warning signs; 9% with warning signs; 2% severe; lethality 0.16%) and partial figures for the current year (e.g., ~3,500 confirmed cases up to a reported epidemiological week) (MINSA, 2025). These figures suggest that the country is already connecting climate-health in its technical-operational discourse, but the goal requires institutionalizing that integration in the surveillance system (not only in communications or specific analyses). The MINSA Environmental Health Analysis 2025 includes a section on “climate change vulnerability and its effects on health,” citing international evidence (e.g., exposure to heat waves) and placing climate change as a relevant determinant for public health; it also recognizes national adaptation frameworks (MINSA, 2025).
NT24.actions: 1) Formulation of the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) with a health component Panama adopted the National Adaptation Plan to Climate Change, which recognizes the health sector as a priority in the face of risks associated with heat waves, vector-borne diseases, extreme events, and water insecurity (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The IPCC (2022) notes that the integration of climate information into public health systems is key to reducing health vulnerability. 2) Development of the National Adaptation Plan for the Health Sector The health sector has advanced in the formulation of a sectoral adaptation plan aligned with the NAP, incorporating: Identification of priority climate risks. Assessment of the vulnerability of health facilities. Strengthening of climate-sensitive epidemiological surveillance. The World Health Organization (WHO, 2015) recommends that health systems integrate climate projections into planning and risk management. 3) Integration of climate variables into epidemiological surveillance Panama has strengthened coordination between: Ministry of Health (MINSA). Institute of Meteorology. Ministry of Environment. This makes it possible to correlate climate variables (temperature, precipitation, humidity) with the incidence of climate-sensitive diseases (dengue, malaria, respiratory diseases). The IPCC (2022) highlights that climate-based early warning systems in health make it possible to anticipate outbreaks and reduce mortality. 3) Preparation of the Climate Vulnerability and Risk Study The process of assessing climate vulnerability in health includes: Identification of populations at risk. Territorial mapping of exposure. Analysis of critical health infrastructure. WHO (2015) indicates that vulnerability studies constitute the technical basis for developing health adaptation policies. 4) Strengthening resilient health infrastructure Adaptation includes: Assessment of the structural resilience of hospitals and health centers. Protocols for floods and extreme events. Climate contingency plans. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) highlights the importance of protecting critical infrastructure, including health facilities. 5) Training of health personnel Capacity-strengthening actions have been promoted for: Identification of climate risks in health. Use of meteorological information in epidemiological surveillance. Management of climate-related health emergencies. WHO (2015) emphasizes that health adaptation requires continuous training of medical and technical personnel. 6) Integration with international commitments The incorporation of adaptation in health responds to: The Paris Agreement, which promotes reducing vulnerability and strengthening resilience (United Nations, 2015a). The Sustainable Development Goals, especially SDG 3 (Health and Well-being) and SDG 13 (Climate Action) (United Nations, 2015).

NT25.challenges: 1)    Interoperability and data quality One of the main challenges is to guarantee interoperability between sectoral platforms (water, health, agriculture, infrastructure) and the Climate Risk Observatory. Methodological standardization and data quality are fundamental to avoid inconsistencies in the measurement of adaptation and losses (IPCC, 2022). The IPCC (2022) warns that the lack of clear metrics can limit the effective evaluation of impacts and adaptation results. 2)    Definition of adaptation and resilience indicators Measuring adaptation is more complex than measuring mitigation. It requires: •    Outcome indicators (reduction of vulnerability). •    Process indicators (implementation of measures). •    Impact indicators (losses avoided). The Paris Agreement recognizes the need to improve adaptation monitoring and reporting systems (United Nations, 2015a). 3)    Quantification of non-economic losses and damages An important challenge is measuring non-economic losses such as: •    Loss of cultural heritage. •    Loss of biodiversity. •    Human displacement. •    Psychosocial impacts. The IPCC (2022) notes that non-economic losses are difficult to quantify, but critical for public policies. 4)    Sustainable financing of the system Maintaining a national monitoring system requires: •    Technological infrastructure. •    Specialized technical personnel. •    Periodic updating of platforms. The Paris Agreement emphasizes that adaptation depends on continuous access to climate financing (United Nations, 2015a). 5)    Interinstitutional coordination and multilevel governance The system involves coordination among ministries, local governments and the private sector. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) highlights that risk reduction requires multilevel coordination and clarity of responsibilities. Institutional overlaps can delay effective implementation. 6)    Design and implementation of the Planned Relocation Protocol Planned relocation is a measure of last resort and presents significant challenges: •    Guarantee informed consent. •    Avoid human rights violations. •    Ensure sustainable livelihoods. •    Prevent social conflicts. The IPCC (2022) recognizes that relocation may be necessary in contexts of extreme risk, but it must be designed with a justice and equity approach. 7)    Social acceptance and legitimacy Relocation can generate social resistance if there is no effective participation. The 2030 Agenda emphasizes that the protection of vulnerable populations must guarantee dignity and equity (United Nations, 2015). 8)    Risk of maladaptation Without adequate monitoring, some measures may generate counterproductive effects (for example, infrastructure that increases future vulnerability). The IPCC (2022) warns about the need for continuous evaluation to avoid maladaptation.
NT25.progress: Since 2019, Panama’s progress toward the goal of developing and implementing a National Monitoring System for Adaptation and for Loss and Damage, interoperable with a climate risk Observatory/System, can be grouped into three lines: (1) regulatory institutionalization and data platforms, (2) planning and risk management (GIRD) with implementation instruments, and (3) preparation of protocols for planned relocation (Executive Decree No. 135, 2021; SINAPROC, 2022; Ministry of Environment, 2025). The most concrete milestone of the period is Executive Decree No. 135 (13 May 2021), which regulates adaptation to climate change and explicitly creates the National Climate Change Adaptation Data System (SNDACC) as a platform for the management and monitoring of climate risk and vulnerability; in addition, it establishes the National Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting System for Adaptation and links these instruments to the National Climate Transparency Platform (PNTC) as the official mechanism for the management, monitoring, reporting and registration of initiatives (Executive Decree No. 135, 2021). Within that same architecture, the decree incorporates a historical record of loss and damage within the components of the national programme “Construye Tu Resiliencia” (Executive Decree No. 135, 2021), which aligns directly with the part of the goal relating to Loss and Damage and the monitoring of progress. From the perspective of implementation and inter-institutional coordination, the National Policy/Strategic Plan for Comprehensive Disaster Risk Management (GIRD) 2022–2030 recognizes as a gap the need to strengthen information management and proposes the development/improvement of systems such as an integrated system for risk management, with measures aimed at the recording and availability of information for decision-making (SINAPROC, 2022). In the official documents reviewed, this component is treated more as capacity under construction (framework and measures) than as evidence of “full coverage” achieved for the entire country, so progress is substantive in institutional design and planning, but still requires consolidated public evidence (for example, periodic national reports with indicators and coverage) to demonstrate “full implementation” at the level required by the goal (SINAPROC, 2022; National Climate Transparency Platform, n.d.). Regarding the component of dignified and just planned relocation, there are signs of recent progress: the Ministry of Environment reported in 2025 progress in the development of a National Protocol for Planned Relocations, conceived as guidance for authorities and communities, with an approach focused on prevention, management and the guarantee of rights (Ministry of Environment, 2025). This is consistent with the logic of the goal (activating a protocol when protecting lives is the only alternative), but, based on the public information consulted, it is described as a process under development, not necessarily as a protocol already officially adopted and operational at the national scale (Ministry of Environment, 2025).
NT25.actions: 1) Development of the National Adaptation Monitoring System Panama has advanced in the design of a National Adaptation Monitoring and Evaluation System, aimed at: Recording adaptation projects and measures. Evaluating progress in sectoral and territorial resilience. Measuring results and impacts. The National Adaptation Plan (MiAMBIENTE, 2021) establishes the need to have a robust monitoring system to guarantee effective implementation. The IPCC (2022) emphasizes that systematic monitoring is fundamental to evaluate the effectiveness of adaptation and avoid maladaptation. 2) Integration with the Climate Risk Observatory Interoperability with the Climate Risk Observatory strengthens: Integration of climate and socioeconomic data. Monitoring of losses and damages associated with extreme events. Identification of priority territories. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015 ) highlights the importance of integrated information systems for reducing human and economic losses. 3) Incorporation of the Loss and Damage approach Panama has aligned its efforts with the international Loss and Damage approach under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (CMNUCC), recognizing the need to measure residual impacts of climate change (United Nations, 2015a). The IPCC (2022) underscores that the quantification of economic, social, and ecosystem losses is key for future planning and access to international financing. 4) Consolidation of information on climate investments The monitoring system makes it possible to track: National and international climate financing. Sectoral adaptation projects. Resilience indicators. This responds to the principle of transparency and accountability promoted in the Paris Agreement (United Nations, 2015a). 5) Design of a Planned Relocation Protocol Panama has advanced in conceptualizing planned, dignified, and just relocation mechanisms for communities highly exposed to irreversible risks (permanent flooding, severe coastal erosion). The IPCC (2022) recognizes that, in extreme cases, planned relocation may be a necessary adaptation measure, provided that it guarantees human rights and livelihoods. 6) Human rights and equity approach Planned relocation considers: Protection of fundamental rights. Access to basic services. Guarantee of livelihoods. Community participation. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) and the 2030 Agenda (United Nations, 2015) emphasize the need to protect the most vulnerable populations from climate risks. 7) Institutional strengthening and multisectoral coordination The monitoring system and the relocation protocol imply coordination among: Ministry of Environment. Ministry of Housing. Civil Protection. Local governments. Social sectors. The IPCC (2022) highlights that multilevel governance is essential to manage losses and damages effectively.

NT26.challenges: 1) Insufficiency and updating of baseline data The preparation of national maps of seagrasses and coral reefs requires high-resolution oceanographic, biological, and cartographic data. In many cases, the available information is fragmented or outdated. The IPCC (2022) warns that the lack of continuous monitoring limits the assessment of the resilience of coastal ecosystems to ocean warming and acidification. 2) Technical and technological limitations Marine-coastal monitoring requires: Oceanographic sensors. High-resolution satellite images. Scientific diving equipment. Specialized laboratories. Sustained investment in technology is key to maintaining operational monitoring systems (CBD, 2022). 3) Sustainable financing Monitoring systems require continuous financing for: Specialized technical personnel. Equipment maintenance. Data processing. Periodic field trips. The Paris Agreement recognizes that adaptation and environmental monitoring depend on stable access to climate financing (United Nations, 2015a). 4) Interinstitutional coordination The system involves coordination among: Ministry of Environment. Aquatic Resources Authority. Academia. NGOs. Coastal communities. The Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022) emphasizes the need for multilevel governance for effective monitoring systems. 5) Growing vulnerability of coastal ecosystems Reefs and seagrasses face threats such as: Coral bleaching. Pollution. Sedimentation. Overfishing. The IPCC (2022) notes that many tropical reefs could suffer severe losses under temperature increase scenarios, which increases the urgency of monitoring. 6) Anthropogenic pressures on wetlands Urban expansion, coastal infrastructure, and agricultural and livestock activities affect wetlands and mangroves. The Ramsar Convention (1971) underscores that wetland loss is one of the fastest environmental degradation processes globally. 7) Standardized monitoring of sea turtles Turtle monitoring requires: Uniform scientific protocols. Nesting monitoring. Regional coordination. Panama, as a Party to the Inter-American Convention for the Protection and Conservation of Sea Turtles (IAC, 1996), must maintain scientific standards compatible with other countries. 8) Integration of information in interoperable platforms A technical challenge is to consolidate information on reefs, wetlands, and turtles in an integrated and accessible platform. The CBD (2022) promotes the strengthening of national biodiversity information systems as a basis for evidence-based decisions. 9) Community participation and social sustainability The sustainability of monitoring depends on the active participation of coastal communities. Without adequate incentives and continuous training, efforts may weaken (United Nations, 2015).
NT26.progress: Since 2019, Panama has advanced gradually toward the creation of a National Integrated Marine-Coastal and Wetlands Monitoring System, although to date this system has not yet been fully implemented. One of the main advances has been the strengthening of the documentary and regulatory base on marine-coastal ecosystems. Panama continues to use as a technical reference the Inventory of Continental and Coastal Wetlands of Panama, prepared by the Regional Ramsar Center in 2010, which constitutes the baseline for wetland management at the national level (CREHO, 2010). However, as of 2025 no official update of the inventory has been published, which represents a gap for the full achievement of the target. In parallel, Panama has promoted important advances in the conservation of marine species. The approval of Law 371 of 2023 established the country’s most robust legal framework for the protection of sea turtles, reinforcing measures against illegal capture, trade in by-products, and the degradation of nesting beaches (MiAmbiente, 2023). Likewise, the Ministry of Environment reported in its 2024 institutional report advances in the “support for sea turtle monitoring in the San San Pond Sak International Wetland,” including patrols, environmental education, and collection of community data (Dirección de Cambio Climático, 2024). Although these efforts represent important progress, there is still no unified national monitoring system that consolidates real-time information on sea turtle populations in all the country’s nesting areas. In relation to marine-coastal ecosystems, the Dirección de Cambio Climático indicates as a sectoral climate target the preparation by 2027 of the National Seagrass and Coral Reef Map, a key tool for monitoring climate change in coastal areas (MiAmbiente, 2022). To date, these maps have not been officially published, although various state and academic institutions have carried out local studies that could feed the future monitoring system. Complementarily, in 2025 the first Interinstitutional Marine-Coastal Monitoring Center was inaugurated, aimed at the surveillance of marine ecosystems and environmental protection through the integration of information from various state institutions (Red Pacífico, 2025). This center represents an institutional milestone toward the consolidation of the integrated system required by the national target. At the technical level, Panama participates in regional platforms such as SPINCAM (Southeast Pacific Data and Information Network in Support of Integrated Coastal Area Management), coordinated by the Autoridad de los Recursos Acuáticos de Panamá (ARAP), which provides indicators, databases, and tools for the analysis of coastal areas (ARAP, n.d.). Although SPINCAM does not replace a national monitoring system, it does constitute a significant advance in data interoperability and coastal monitoring at the regional scale.
NT26.actions: 1) Strengthening marine-coastal monitoring within the National Adaptation Plan Panama incorporated the marine-coastal component within the National Adaptation Plan to Climate Change (PNA), recognizing the vulnerability of reefs, seagrasses and wetlands to sea level rise, acidification and temperature increase (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The IPCC (2022) notes that the systematic monitoring of coastal ecosystems is essential to assess resilience and guide adaptation measures. 2) Preparation of technical studies on reefs and seagrasses Technical and cartographic studies have been developed to improve knowledge on: Distribution of coral reefs. Health status of coral ecosystems. Location and extent of seagrasses. These efforts respond to national commitments under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CDB, 2022) and to recognition of the role of these ecosystems in blue carbon capture and coastal protection (IPCC, 2022). 3) Progress towards the National Wetlands Inventory Panama has strengthened wetland management through: Identification and characterization of Ramsar sites. Technical studies of inland and coastal wetlands. Integration of geospatial information. The Ramsar Convention (1971) establishes the obligation to inventory and monitor wetlands as a basis for their conservation. 4) Sea Turtle Monitoring System The country has implemented sea turtle monitoring and protection programmes in collaboration with: MiAMBIENTE. Non-governmental organizations. Local communities. Panama is Party to the Inter-American Convention for the Protection and Conservation of Sea Turtles (CIT, 1996), which promotes scientific monitoring and the conservation of critical habitats. 5) Integration of geospatial information platforms Progress has been made in consolidating interoperable environmental databases, including: Satellite information. Geographic information systems (GIS). Marine biodiversity records. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (CDB, 2022) emphasizes the importance of robust monitoring systems to assess progress in conservation. 6) Community participation and citizen science Turtle and mangrove monitoring programmes have incorporated coastal communities, strengthening: Environmental surveillance. Environmental education. Local governance. The 2030 Agenda promotes inclusive participation in environmental management (United Nations, 2015). 7) Linkage with climate and biodiversity commitments The monitoring of seagrasses, reefs and wetlands contributes to: Reports under the UNFCCC. Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC). Targets of the Global Biodiversity Framework (CDB, 2022). The IPCC (2022) highlights that these ecosystems are critical for mitigation (blue carbon) and adaptation.

NT27.challenges: 1) Financial and budgetary sustainability The continuous operation of the Observatory's regional offices requires stable financing for: Specialized technical personnel. Technological infrastructure. Updating platforms and maintenance of equipment. The Paris Agreement recognizes that adaptation and institutional strengthening depend on adequate and sustained financial resources (United Nations, 2015a). Likewise, the IPCC (2022) warns that the lack of financing limits long-term adaptation capacity. 2) Interoperability and standardization of data One of the main challenges is to ensure that the regional offices use: Homogeneous protocols. Comparable indicators. Systems compatible with each other. The IPCC (2022) emphasizes that the lack of standardization can generate inconsistencies in risk assessment and decision-making. 3) Strengthening local technical capacities Decentralization implies that regional technicians manage: Climate risk models. GIS tools. Regionalized climate scenarios. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) highlights that disaster risk reduction requires strengthening technical capacities at the local level. 4) Multilevel interinstitutional coordination The Observatory must coordinate with: Local governments. Sectoral systems (health, agriculture, energy). National Civil Protection System. The 2030 Agenda emphasizes that climate action requires effective coordination among levels of government (United Nations, 2015). 5) Constant updating of climate scenarios Risk scenarios must be updated periodically as scientific projections evolve. The IPCC (2022) indicates that climate risks are dynamic and require adaptive monitoring systems. 6) Access to and effective use of information Although the information is available, one challenge is to ensure that: Local authorities use it in planning. Productive sectors integrate early warnings. Communities understand and use the information. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) emphasizes that information must be accessible, understandable, and actionable. 7) Reduction of the risk of maladaptation Without rigorous evaluation, some decisions could increase future vulnerability (for example, urban expansion in risk zones). The IPCC (2022) warns about the risk of maladaptation if planning is not based on updated evidence. 8) Territorial gaps and regional inequality Rural regions or indigenous comarcas may present: Less technological infrastructure. Less digital connectivity. Limited institutional capacity. The 2030 Agenda recognizes that resilience must prioritize the most vulnerable populations (United Nations, 2015).
NT27.progress: The national target states that by 2035 Panama will have adopted and put into operation at least 10 branches of the Climate Risk Observatory, strengthening decentralized management of monitoring and response to climate risks. Up to December 2025, public evidence on concrete implementations shows technical and information platform progress, although there are no official reports documenting the operation of 10 complete institutional branches with personnel, infrastructure, and fully operational functions. A substantive advance is the consolidation of climate and risk information tools and systems within the framework of the National Climate Transparency Platform (PNTC), managed by the Ministry of Environment (MiAMBIENTE). Within this platform there is a specific Climate Vulnerability and Risk module, which integrates mathematical and geospatial information on hazards (temperature, precipitation, floods, landslides, etc.) and supports the development of technical solutions for use in territorial and sectoral planning, oriented toward sensitive sectors such as agriculture, water resources, health, and others (MiAMBIENTE, n.d.). A key product of this management is the Interactive Climate Risk Atlas of the Republic of Panama, officially presented on 2 December 2024, developed by MiAMBIENTE with support from the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and more than 15 collaborating institutions. This atlas provides cartographic data and analysis on floods, landslides, droughts, and forest fires that make it possible to strengthen planning, adaptation, and response capacity in the face of climate change throughout the country. Its launch constitutes significant technical progress in the operation of strategic information that a risk observatory should provide. In addition, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) approved technical cooperation in June 2023 (TC PN-T1330) to support the Panamanian government in the modernization of climate information and planning systems, including aspects of monitoring and evaluation of climate risks. The project has a budget of USD 300 000 and is expected to contribute to improving the database and analysis tools for strategic decision-making in various sectors in the face of climate risks. In addition, the implementation of policies and legislative tools that integrate climate risk into environmental processes, such as the incorporation of climate change analysis in Environmental Impact Studies through Executive Decree No. 1 of 1 March 2023, indirectly strengthen the operational structure of risk management by requiring vulnerability and risk analysis in environmental decisions. The Procedures Manual for generating climate change scenarios was also approved by resolution in August 2023, generating the technical guidelines required to assess climate risk. Complementarily, within the framework of institutional follow-up and monitoring, Panama has the National Climate Change Adaptation Data System (SNDACC) as a platform to manage, evaluate, and monitor climate risk and vulnerability, participating as one of the basic tools for an operational observatory (MiAMBIENTE, n.d.).
NT27.actions: 1) Creation and strengthening of the Climate Risk Observatory Panama has promoted the development of the Climate Risk Observatory as a national platform to integrate climate, territorial, and sectoral information, in coherence with the National Adaptation Plan (PNA) (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The IPCC (2022) underscores that territorialized climate information systems are essential to strengthen local resilience and reduce vulnerability. 2) Integration with national information systems The Observatory has been conceived as an interoperable platform with: National geospatial systems. Climate risk atlas. Sectoral platforms for agriculture, health, and infrastructure. The strengthening of integrated information systems responds to the recommendations of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR, 2015), which promotes evidence-based early warning and monitoring systems. 3) Territorial decentralization of climate monitoring Panama has promoted the decentralization of climate management through: Agroclimatic Technical Roundtables. Coordination with local governments. Regional training for risk analysis. The 2030 Agenda establishes that effective climate action requires multilevel implementation (United Nations, 2015). 4) Incorporation of climate scenarios in sectoral planning The Observatory's units allow sectors such as energy, agriculture, and water resources to integrate climate projections into their planning (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The IPCC (2022) highlights that the integration of climate scenarios into sectoral planning reduces maladaptation risks. 5) Development of regional technical capacities The implementation of territorial units implies: Training of local technicians. Use of GIS tools. Analysis of regionalized climate scenarios. The Sendai Framework (UNDRR, 2015) emphasizes the strengthening of local capacities as a key element of resilience. 6) Coordination with the National Adaptation Monitoring System The Observatory is linked with the National Monitoring System for Adaptation and Loss and Damage, allowing territorialized monitoring of impacts and investments (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The Paris Agreement establishes that countries must strengthen their adaptation monitoring and evaluation systems (United Nations, 2015a). 7) Transparency and public access to information The Observatory promotes open access to climate information, strengthening: Transparency. Data-based decision-making. Citizen participation. The IPCC (2022) notes that the availability of reliable climate information improves adaptive governance.

NT28.challenges: 1) Sustained capitalization and financial governance (Panama Natural Fund) Ensuring that capitalization is stable and long-term (not only one-off contributions), and that the vehicle maintains transparent governance, clear allocation rules, and credibility with donors and investors is an ongoing challenge (MiAMBIENTE, 2025; MiAMBIENTE, 2025b). Use the results of BIOFIN’s BER to demonstrate financing gaps and guide capitalization strategies. 2) “Full operation” of the Reforesta Fund: reactivation, regulation, and implementation Although the Reforesta Fund is established by Law 69 of 2017, the practical challenge is to sustain its effective operation (capacity to manage incentives, implement and follow up), including reactivation and coordination with institutional actors and civil society (Law 69, 2017; MiAMBIENTE, 2025a). 3) Environmental and social integrity of the instruments (avoiding “financing without results”) Channeling USD 300 million requires demonstrating verifiable results (hectares restored, biodiversity conserved, risk reduction), and avoiding reputational risks associated with projects with low additionality or unmanaged social impacts. The Roadmap for the National Carbon Market emphasizes precisely the need to clarify functioning and environmental/social impacts aligned with Article 6 (CMNUCC/UNFCCC, n.d.). 4) Regulatory framework and “launch” of the National Carbon Market The development of the National Carbon Market depends on a legal and implementation framework (e.g., the mandate in Executive Decree No. 100 of 2020, according to the official platform), in addition to rules, registries, MRV, and interinstitutional coordination to operate with integrity (MiAMBIENTE, 2024). 5) Measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) and transaction costs The mechanisms (carbon, PES, biodiversity credits) require robust MRV. The challenge is to cover transaction costs (baselines, monitoring, audits) without excluding small producers, communities, and local governments. The carbon market roadmap discusses precisely the need to organize the system and its requirements (CMNUCC/UNFCCC, n.d.). 6) Legal certainty and rights (land, tenure, FPIC and benefit-sharing) To attract private investment and avoid conflicts, clarity on tenure/use and social safeguards (including effective participation) is required. In forest incentive schemes such as Reforesta, the legal framework itself provides for management mechanisms (e.g., the possibility of fiduciary administration), but the challenge is to turn it into operation with clear rules and social acceptance (Law 69, 2017; MiAMBIENTE, 2025a). 7) Design and institutionalization of Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) The challenge is to move from definitions/studies and pilots to sustainable programs with clear payment sources, eligibility criteria, territorial targeting, and monitoring. There are technical documents that address the feasibility and concept of PES/PSA in Panama, but institutionalizing it at the national scale implies coordination and recurrent financing (SDG Fund, n.d.; ACP, 2018). 8) “Biodiversity credits”: standardization and demand As an emerging instrument, the challenge is to develop national standards (what is measured, how double counting is avoided, how permanence is ensured), and to build real demand from the private sector (beyond declarations). The Global Biodiversity Framework promotes mechanisms and incentives for resource mobilization, but translating this into operational instruments requires rules and capacities (CBD, 2022). 9) Coordination of “synergistic” portfolios (climate-biodiversity-land) without fragmentation Channeling “synergistic” resources implies assembling integrated portfolios (conservation, restoration, resilience) while avoiding dispersion into small projects without scale. This requires prioritization criteria and portfolio governance, consistent with the long-term financing approach proposed for the PFP/Panama Natural Fund (MiAMBIENTE, 2025; Natura Panamá, 2026). Use the results of BIOFIN’s PIR to improve policy coherence and interinstitutional coordination.
NT28.progress: Since 2019, Panama's progress toward the target of mobilizing 30% more resources and channeling at least USD 300 million for climate-biodiversity-land synergetic actions is observed mainly in: (a) regulatory and financial enabling of environmental funds and trusts; (b) reactivation and strengthening of national mechanisms (e.g., Reforesta and trusts); and (c) growing mobilization of cooperation linked to conservation, restoration, and oceans. However, a consolidated “statement of account” has not yet been identified (in public sources) demonstrating that the country has already channeled USD 300 million specifically through the capitalization of the Fondo Panamá Natural and the full operation of the Fondo Reforesta (MiAmbiente, 2025a; MiAmbiente, 2025b). Fondo Reforesta Panamá (framework and seed capital). A relevant milestone is the consolidation to finance conservation, operational plans, and capitalization of environmental instruments. Executive Decree No. 4 of 13 November 2023 (published in the Gazette) modifies the regulations for operations and investments of funds constituted by MiAmbiente for the benefit of the environmental trust, detailing sources of income and distribution rules. Within that framework, it is established that the trust patrimony, inextinguishable and subject to capitalization, includes B/.3,500,000 as seed capital (B/.2,000,000 from the MiAmbiente budget and B/.1,500,000 contributed by the GEF) associated with Grant Agreement TF-018972 (República de Panamá, 2023). In addition, sources that can feed mechanisms such as the Fondo Reforesta are specified (e.g., ecological compensation from the Fondo de Protección y Desarrollo Forestal, compensation agreements from the private sector, and funds from concessions in protected areas), as well as a general allocation rule whereby 30% enters a capitalization/investment fund and 70% goes to the execution of operational plans (República de Panamá, 2023). In 2025, MiAmbiente explicitly reported the push to reactivate the Fondo Reforesta Panamá (established by Law No. 69), directing it to finance reforestation, restoration, and conservation with access for small producers, communities, researchers, and civil society (MiAmbiente, 2025a). Fondo Panamá Natural (inspired by the Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) model): construction and first mobilizations. From 2024–2025, the Government has communicated the “construction” of the Fondo Panamá Natural as a Project Finance for Permanence (PFP)-type mechanism intended to ensure lasting financing to strengthen the SINAP, with emphasis on innovative solutions (sustainable tourism, carbon markets, debt swaps, and other sources) (MiAmbiente, 2025b). Although the public communications describe the model and partnerships, they do not publish a total capitalized amount; specific contributions are observed, for example, an announced contribution of USD 3 million to the “Panamá Natural Fund” to strengthen conservation and expansion of protected areas (Rainforest Trust, 2025). Complementarily, organizations linked to the PFP explain the approach of leveraging public-private financing and cooperation to strengthen terrestrial and marine protected area systems (ANCON, n.d.; Enduring Earth, n.d.). Large-scale operations and commitments driving the “USD 300 million” target. In 2025, CAF approved a USD 300 million loan for Panama aimed at improving forest management, supporting sustainable management policies, conservation of ecosystems, and green financing, aligned with national forest strategies (CAF, 2025). In the regional marine-coastal sphere with Panama's participation, the “Connect to Protect” coalition reported commitments of USD 118.5 million in 2022 for conservation of the Eastern Tropical Pacific (Enduring Earth, 2023), and the Bezos Earth Fund communicated regional commitments of USD 165.3 million to expand and strengthen marine protected areas in Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, and Panama (Bezos Earth Fund, 2025). In December 2025, the world's largest philanthropic organization (Reuters) reported new USD 24.5 million in grants for marine conservation in the region, including Panama (Reuters, 2025). These amounts show an environment of accelerated mobilization of resources for biodiversity and climate in which Panama participates. Carbon markets and other innovative mechanisms (mobilization enablers). Panama advanced in the regulatory framework of the National Carbon Market with decrees creating the Reduce Tu Huella Program (2020) and progressively establishing the National Carbon Market (MNCP) (2021), with a registration system and components for compensation and trading of credits (Dirección de Cambio Climático, n.d.). The Roadmap (2025) documents that the country received specific technical and financial support for the development of the market and describes the status of its components, with one operational and others under development (CMNUCC, 2025). This type of instrument is consistent with the target by facilitating the scaling up of climate financing and synergies with restoration and biodiversity (MiAmbiente, 2025b). BIOFIN progress: evidence for decision-making and closing gaps Within the framework of the Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN), Panama has generated key inputs to strengthen resource mobilization: The Policy and Institutional Review (PIR) identified opportunities to improve policy coherence, strengthen financial governance, and create enabling conditions for instruments such as environmental funds, carbon markets, and positive economic incentives. The Biodiversity Expenditure Review (BER) estimated current public expenditure on biodiversity and showed significant financing gaps, providing a baseline to guide the prioritization of investments and dialogue with the Ministry of Economy and Finance and international partners. These analyses have strengthened the technical basis for resource mobilization, the integration of biodiversity into fiscal planning, and the design of the Biodiversity Finance Plan.
NT28.actions: 1) Capitalization and strengthening of the Fondo Panamá Natural Panama has promoted the strengthening of the Fondo Panamá Natural (FPN) as a financial mechanism to support the sustainable management of protected areas and conservation projects. The Fund acts as an instrument to channel public and private resources toward biodiversity and climate goals (Fondo Panamá Natural, 2023). Within the framework of the Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN), the Policy and Institutional Review (PIR) has identified opportunities to improve policy coherence, strengthen financial governance, and optimize institutional mechanisms that facilitate the channeling of resources toward instruments such as the FPN. Likewise, the Biodiversity Expenditure Review (BER) has made it possible to estimate the current level of public expenditure on biodiversity and to reveal financing gaps that justify the need to strengthen and capitalize this type of fund. The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022) promotes the mobilization of innovative financial resources to close biodiversity financing gaps. 2) Bringing the Fondo Reforesta into operation The Fondo Reforesta has been conceived as a financial instrument aimed at forest restoration and rehabilitation of degraded lands, aligned with the National Forest Strategy and Panama’s climate commitments (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). Forest restoration contributes to carbon capture and climate resilience, in line with the Paris Agreement (United Nations, 2015a) and the IPCC (2022). 3) Development of the national carbon market Panama has advanced in structuring a voluntary carbon market, allowing the generation of carbon credits from: Forest restoration. Forest conservation. Sustainable land management. These mechanisms are aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which promotes international cooperation through carbon markets (United Nations, 2015a). 4) Implementation of Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) schemes have been promoted to encourage the conservation of forests, watersheds, and biodiversity. The PIR has pointed out the need to strengthen the institutional framework and positive economic incentives, while the BER shows the potential to redirect public resources and mobilize private financing toward incentive schemes such as PES. The CBD (2022) recognizes positive incentives as a key tool to conserve biodiversity and restore ecosystems. 5) Promotion of biodiversity credits Panama has explored emerging financial instruments such as biodiversity credits, which seek to: Finance results-based conservation. Mobilize private capital toward protected areas and biological corridors. The Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022) urges increasing positive incentives and innovative financing mechanisms. 6) Integration with climate commitments and NDC The funds and financial mechanisms are aligned with the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) and the National Adaptation Plan, making it possible to integrate mitigation, adaptation, and biodiversity in the same investment portfolio (MiAMBIENTE, 2021). The BIOFIN PIR has contributed to strengthening coherence between climate and biodiversity policy instruments, promoting integrated financial planning within the framework of the Promesa de Panamá con la Naturaleza. The IPCC (2022) highlights that nature-based solutions generate multiple benefits (climate, biodiversity, and livelihoods). 7) Mobilization of international financing Panama has accessed multilateral climate financing, including climate funds and international cooperation, to complement national resources. The results of the BER provide a baseline of existing financing and facilitate dialogue with international partners, while the PIR strengthens the enabling environment for the mobilization and effective management of external resources. The Paris Agreement recognizes the importance of international financing to support climate actions in developing countries (United Nations, 2015a).

NT29.challenges: Critical gaps persist for the comprehensive fulfillment of the target, including: (a) The absence of a formalized and operational national mechanism for the protection of environmental defenders (with risk protocols, protection measures, legal assistance, and financing); (b) The lack of national indicators and monitoring systems that make it possible to measure real coverage of access to information and environmental justice in vulnerable groups; (c) The nonexistence of a consolidated national report on gender representation in decision-making bodies in conservation; and (d) The need to harmonize and standardize safeguards protocols for traditional knowledge for their systematic application in conservation and decision-making processes.
NT29.progress: Since 2019, Panama has significantly strengthened the enabling regulatory framework for this target through the approval of the Escazú Agreement as a law of the Republic (Law 125 of 2020), (ECLAC, n.d.). The Escazú Agreement adopted in Escazú, Costa Rica in 2018, aims to guarantee the full and effective implementation in Latin America and the Caribbean of the “rights of access to environmental information, public participation in environmental decision-making processes and access to justice in environmental matters, as well as the creation and strengthening of capacities and cooperation”. Latin America and the Caribbean being one of the regions worldwide with the fewest transparency and access to environmental information mechanisms where more crimes against environmental human rights defenders are recorded. It also establishes the protection of the human rights of environmental human rights defenders, a measure that reflects the challenges they face in Latin America and the Caribbean. In the institutional sphere, interinstitutional coordination actions have been recorded, highlighting the rapprochement between the Ministry of Environment and the Ombudsman’s Office to strengthen the guarantee of the right to a healthy environment and the protection of defenders (Ombudsman’s Office, 2025a). Likewise, Panama has actively participated in the regional spaces of the Escazú Agreement, including the organization of the Second Annual Forum on Women Environmental Defenders and Environmental Defenders in Latin America and the Caribbean held in Panama in 2023 (MiAMBIENTE, 2023). In terms of access to environmental information, Panama has continued strengthening the National Environmental Information System (SINIA) as a public platform for access to official environmental data, aligned with open government and transparency commitments (SINIA, n.d.; Open Government Partnership, n.d.). Additionally, the National Authority for Transparency and Access to Information (ANTAI) maintains oversight mechanisms and transparency portals applicable to entities in the environmental sector, which contributes to the availability of information for citizens (ANTAI, n.d.). Regarding access to environmental justice, in addition to the Escazú framework, there are reference instruments such as the environmental jurisprudence compendiums of the Judicial Branch, which document relevant precedents and criteria in the resolution of environmental conflicts (Judicial Branch–CENDOJ, n.d.). However, there are no consolidated public statistics available that make it possible to measure effective access to environmental justice disaggregated by condition of vulnerability. The 2024 adjustments document of the Institutional Strategic Plan (PEI) 2021–2026 of the Ombudsman’s Office, a national human rights institution with constitutional rank, addresses the environmental perspective on the human right to a healthy environment, integrating the ecological approach within the PESTEL analysis and in specific institutional targets. The main environmental challenges identified are: Mining transition following the cessation of mining activities and the need for fair and sustainable management. Inadequate waste management and open-air dumps, generating pollution and fire risks. Climate change, with effects on: food security, displacement of communities and greater social vulnerability. These challenges being environmental opportunities to: promote social dialogue during the mining transition, integrate a human rights approach in local waste management policies, align local policies with national and international commitments on environmental matters, participation in dialogue roundtables on mining, environmental education with a human rights approach and accompaniment of communities affected by socio-environmental conflicts; in addition, the institutional structure includes a National Directorate of Environmental Affairs, which formally demonstrates the incorporation of the environmental component in the institutional mandate. Some of the outstanding environmental targets of the PEI are: Target 1.20: strengthen coordination mechanisms with institutions and organizations to develop projects in vulnerable communities from the perspective of the human right to a healthy environment. Target 4.19: train populations on possible environmental crimes and offenses. In relation to the safeguarding of traditional knowledge, Panama has a robust legal framework that includes Law 20 of 2000 on the collective rights of Indigenous peoples and rules on access to genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge, updated through Executive Decree No. 19 of 2019, aligned with the Nagoya Protocol (Executive Branch, 2019). Likewise, community biocultural protocols have been developed and disseminated, such as that of the Ipetí Emberá people, which operationalize safeguards at the territorial level (CBD–ABS Clearing-House, 2020). As for equitable representation with a gender perspective, Panama adopted the National Gender and Climate Change Plan (published in the Official Gazette), which promotes the equitable participation of women in environmental and climate decision-making (Republic of Panama, 2022). Complementarily, in 2024 a practical guide was launched to incorporate the gender approach in the Watershed Committees, a relevant instrument for decision-making spaces in conservation at the territorial level, identifies the barriers that limit female participation in these spaces, while proposing concrete methodologies for their effective integration (MiAMBIENTE, 2024; UNDP, 2024).

NT30.challenges: 1) Regulatory and institutional harmonization One of the main challenges is to guarantee coherence between the Framework Law on Climate Change (Law 41 of 2021) and other sectoral laws (energy, mining, land-use planning, biodiversity, agriculture). The lack of harmonization can generate regulatory gaps or contradictions (National Assembly, 2021). The IPCC (2022) notes that intersectoral integration is fundamental to avoid contradictory policies and achieve climate effectiveness. 2) Effective implementation beyond enactment Publication in the Official Gazette does not guarantee implementation. The following are required: Secondary regulations. Technical guidelines. Budget allocation. Monitoring mechanisms. The Paris Agreement (United Nations, 2015a ) emphasizes that legal frameworks must be translated into measurable operational actions. 3) Actual functioning of interministerial governance The establishment of an interministerial body and of CONACLABIT implies permanent coordination among ministries and autonomous entities. The Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022) warns that cross-cutting governance requires clarity of roles, decision-making mechanisms, and accountability. 4) Political sustainability and institutional stability The continuity of the regulatory package depends on political stability and multisectoral support. The 2030 Agenda underscores that strong institutions and policy coherence are essential for long-term sustainability (United Nations, 2015). 5) Application of the principle of environmental non-regression The principle of non-regression faces legal and political challenges, especially when there are economic pressures to relax environmental standards. International environmental law recognizes progressivity as a key element of sustainable development (United Nations, 2015). 6) Technical capacities and human resources The implementation of the regulatory package requires: Technical training in sectoral ministries. Strengthening of monitoring systems. Climate and environmental assessment tools. The IPCC (2022) highlights that institutional capacity is decisive for the effectiveness of climate policies. 7) Integration of climate–biodiversity–lands in sectoral planning A structural challenge is to prevent climate and biodiversity from continuing to operate as separate agendas. The CBD (2022) promotes the integration of biodiversity at all levels of decision-making, which requires administrative and budgetary reforms. 8) Effective participation and social legitimacy Participatory governance requires: Inclusion of indigenous peoples. Participation of the private sector. Public transparency. The 2030 Agenda and the Sendai Framework highlight the importance of inclusive processes to strengthen resilience (UNDRR, 2015).
NT30.progress: 1. Progress toward the Framework Law on Climate Change and Green Transition 1.1. The Framework Law as a political mandate from 2020–2022 The National Gender and Climate Change Plan, approved by Executive Decree and published in the Official Gazette in 2022, explicitly includes the “creation of the Framework Law on Climate Change (LMCC)” as one of the structural actions to align the climate agenda with national public policy (Ministry of Environment, 2022). In parallel, Executive Decree No. 100 of 20 October 2020 created within the country’s legal framework the National Climate Transparency Platform (PNTC) as the official instrument for monitoring, reporting and verification of climate action, anticipating the type of institutional architecture that the Framework Law would have to consolidate (Ministry of Environment, 2024). These political decisions function as “regulatory precursors” of the current Framework Law bill and can be considered indirect progress toward the goal of having a comprehensive legal framework for the Panama Nature Pledge. 1.2. Drafting and publication of the Framework Law bill (2025) The clearest progress occurs in 2025, when the Ministry of Environment makes the “Framework Law on Climate Change and Green Transition,” May 2025 version, publicly available as a Bill. The document appears both on the MiAmbiente portal and on public consultation platforms and describes a legal and institutional framework for mitigation, adaptation, ecosystem restoration and green transition, emphasizing the protection of human rights and nature (Ministry of Environment, 2025a; Panamá Legal Group, 2025). The bill explicitly recognizes the Panama Nature Pledge (Nature Pledge) as a priority instrument, aligning the Framework Law with the country’s commitments under the three Rio Conventions (climate, biodiversity and desertification). The Pledge is composed of a political declaration and three technical annexes, which set out the national targets for mitigation, adaptation, conservation and restoration. These include the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC), the National Biodiversity Strategy (ENBSAP) and the Land Degradation Neutrality Strategy (NDT) (Ministry of Environment, 2025b). 1.3. Public consultation process (2024–2025) Between 2024 and 2025, a public consultation process is carried out, which is concrete progress toward approval of the Law: In June 2025, MiAmbiente holds a territorial workshop at the Technological University of Panama; 55 people from social, academic, institutional and community sectors participate to analyze and enrich the draft Framework Law (Ministry of Environment, 2025c). In July 2025, the Regional Directorate of MiAmbiente in East Panama organizes a consultation workshop with students and public officials at the Regional University Center of East Panama, as part of the participatory process for the draft bill (Ministry of Environment, 2025d). The Municipality of Panama holds a public hearing at the Electoral Tribunal to discuss the “Framework Law on Climate Change and Green Transition Bill,” where municipal commitments are presented and contributions are gathered from community boards and other local actors (Municipality of Panama, 2025). A monthly report from MIDA records the ministry’s participation in public consultations on the Framework Law together with universities and public institutions in the provinces of Los Santos, Herrera and Coclé, noting that “during the consultation the draft of the Framework Law on Climate Change and Green Transition Bill was prepared” (Ministry of Agricultural Development, 2025). In addition, the “Public Consultation Report” of October 2025 summarizes the participation process on the National Green Transition Strategy, the Panama Nature Pledge and the National Adaptation Plan, linked to the development of the Framework Law bill. Multisectoral participation and systematized analysis made it possible to adjust the legislative proposal to align it with international best practices and national expectations. However, challenges persist in the integration of interinstitutional competencies and in coordination with key economic sectors, issues that the law will have to address during its implementation (Ministry of Environment, 2025e). All this indicates that, although the Law is still a “Bill” and does not appear as a law enacted in the Official Gazette, the country has advanced to a complete legislative text, submitted to territorial and sectoral consultations. 2. Progress toward a unified governance framework and CONACLABIT The goal requires creating “a unified governance framework with an interministerial decision-making body and the National Committee on Climate, Biodiversity and Land (CONACLABIT).” Here the progress is mainly in institutional design, not yet formalized by law. 2.1. Diagnosis and proposal in the Panama Nature Pledge The Panama Nature Pledge, presented in 2025 as an integrating document of NDC 3.0, the National Biodiversity Strategy and the Land Degradation Neutrality Strategy, identifies that there are currently three separate bodies: the National Climate Change Committee, the Interinstitutional Biodiversity Commission and the National Committee to Combat Drought and Desertification, which operate in a fragmented manner (Ministry of Environment, 2025b). In response, the Pledge proposes that the draft Framework Law on Climate Change and Green Transition will create a National Green Transition Cabinet as a high-level body, supported by the National Committee on Climate, Biodiversity and Land (CONACLABIT), which will integrate the existing committees into a single national body and strengthen coordination with basin committees and local authorities (Ministry of Environment, 2025b; 2025f). A note from the National Climate Transparency Platform (PNTC) and from the presentation of the Nature Pledge before the Rio Conventions underscores that the country seeks “integrated governance” to coordinate climate, biodiversity and land commitments under a single framework, reinforced by the Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system articulated in the PNTC (Ministry of Environment, 2022; Ministry of Environment, 2025g; Republic of Panama, 2025). 2.2. Institutions already operational Although CONACLABIT still does not appear as a body formally created by law or decree, progress has been made in the institutional architecture that would accompany it: The PNTC was publicly launched in 2022 as a portal that integrates GHG inventories, tracking of the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) and monitoring modules, being the operational basis of the transparency and MRV system that the Pledge envisages for all environmental agendas (Wetlands International, 2022; Ministry of Environment, 2024). The Panama Nature Pledge was consolidated in 2025 as an integrating framework for Panama’s commitments on climate, biodiversity and desertification, with joint targets (for example, restoring 100 000 ha of ecosystems by 2035 and reducing GHG emissions by 11 % compared with the trend scenario) that require precisely the unified governance proposed by the Framework Law (Ministry of Environment, 2025b; Republic of Panama, 2025). In September 2025, MiAmbiente reports that the public consultations on the Panama Nature Pledge have become the country’s largest citizen participation initiative on environmental and climate issues, which strengthens the social legitimacy of the future CONACLABIT and the Green Transition Cabinet (Ministry of Environment, 2025h; Somos Impacto Positivo, 2025). In summary, there is a clear and widely consulted design of the new governance (Cabinet and CONACLABIT), but by December 2025 no legal progress has been achieved. 3. Progress toward the Environmental Non-Regression Law The goal also requires an “environmental non-regression law.” 3.1. Bill and public consultation (2024) On 19 August 2024, MiAmbiente publishes the “Public Consultation on the Bill entitled ‘By which the principle of environmental non-regression and the right to public participation in the creation and modification of protected areas are guaranteed’”, including a draft bill document (Ministry of Environment, 2024b). This bill seeks to incorporate into the Panamanian legal system the principle of environmental non-regression, understood as the prohibition of stepping back from levels of environmental protection already achieved, in line with the regional doctrine compiled by Peña Chacón and UNDP (Peña Chacón, 2013). The opening of public consultation marks concrete progress toward the goal: the country moves from a doctrinal reference to the principle of non-regression to a specific legislative draft, with emphasis on protected areas and public participation. 3.2. Status to date By December 2025, this Bill does not appear enacted in the Official Gazette; everything indicates that it is still in the discussion and review phase, similar to the Framework Law on Climate Change and Green Transition.
NT30.actions: 1) Enactment of the Framework Law on Climate Change Panama adopted Law 41 of 1 July 2021 (Framework Law on Climate Change), which establishes principles, obligations and institutional mechanisms for mitigation and adaptation, including instruments such as the National Adaptation Plan and the carbon market (National Assembly, 2021). The law strengthens the integration of climate change into sectoral policies, in coherence with the Paris Agreement (United Nations, 2015a). 2) Recognition of the Panama Pact with Nature The Panama Pact with Nature has been incorporated as a high-level strategic framework that integrates biodiversity, climate and land commitments, aligned with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022) and the 2030 Agenda (United Nations, 2015). This instrument positions biodiversity as a structural axis of sustainable development. 3) Creation of unified climate and environmental governance The Framework Law establishes an interinstitutional coordination scheme to: Integrate climate and environmental decisions. Harmonize sectoral policies. Guarantee monitoring and accountability. The IPCC (2022) highlights that multilevel governance is essential to effectively implement adaptation and mitigation. 4) Establishment of the National Committee on Climate, Biodiversity and Land (CONACLABIT) As part of institutional strengthening, the creation or consolidation of participatory technical bodies that integrate climate, biodiversity and land management has been promoted, favoring intersectoral coherence. The Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022) recommends integrated national structures that facilitate cross-cutting coordination. 5) Incorporation of the principle of environmental non-regression The principle of environmental non-regression seeks to ensure that environmental standards do not weaken over time. This approach is grounded in international environmental doctrine and aligns with the environmental progressivity commitments recognized in the 2030 Agenda (United Nations, 2015). 7) Articulation with international instruments The regulatory package is aligned with: Paris Agreement (United Nations, 2015a). Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022). Sendai Framework for risk reduction (UNDRR, 2015). Regulatory integration strengthens coherence between multilateral commitments and national legislation. 7) Strengthening of the climate planning framework The Framework Law enables instruments such as: Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC). National Adaptation Plan. Monitoring and reporting systems. The IPCC (2022) emphasizes that the legal institutionalization of climate action improves the stability and predictability of public policies.

a-cy-1-forest-area-as-a-proportion-of-to.comments: The 2021 Forest Cover Map of the Ministry of Environment of Panama (MiAMBIENTE) estimated that forest cover and other wooded lands were around 5,945,470 ha (59,454.7 km²), equivalent to about 68% of Panamanian territory.

mecanismo-nacional-de-protecci-n-a-defen.comments: Panama approved the Escazú Agreement through Law 125 of 4 February 2020, which integrates the “access rights” (information, participation, justice) and the protection of defenders in environmental matters. The legal framework and an implementation roadmap have been established and are operational, including the obligation to protect persons defending environmental matters, together with institutional actions and coordination spaces.

n-mero-de-planes-locales-y-regionales-de.comments: In Panama we have 4 local adaptation plans and currently the Climate Change Directorate of MiAMBIENTE is designing 5 plans. tasa-anual-de-deforestaci-n-ilegal.comments: An official assessment indicates that between 2022 and 2023 Panama lost 352,873 ha of forests and other wooded lands, which is equivalent to a reduction of about 4% of forest cover in that period (Panama, Panama Deforestation Rates & Statistics | GFW)

tasa-de-reciclaje-de-residuos-pl-sticos.comments: The national plastic recycling rate is estimated at approximately 1% of the total generated, according to the Baseline of the National Plastic Action Platform (NPAP, 2022). Panama currently does not have a consolidated annual national reporting system on tons recycled by material, so the value is maintained as a reference until new measurements are available.
